5.6 NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF OPEN SCHOOLING (NIOS): 
5.6.1 The Department has informed that National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, rooted in the 
pillars of access, equity, quality, and affordability, lays a strong foundation for transforming 
India's education system. The National Institute of Open Schooling (NIOS) plays significant role 
in achieving the objectives of the NEP 2020. By offering flexible, learner-centered educational 
opportunities, NIOS aligns with the key pillars of NEP 2020: access, equity, quality, and 
affordability. Through its innovative programs and diverse offerings, NIOS is positioned to 
bridge gaps in formal education, provide alternatives learning opportunities, and enhance the 
overall educational landscape of India. NIOS offers learner-centered education that caters to the 
unique needs of school dropouts, marginalized groups, and differently-abled individuals. To 
enhance accessibility, NIOS has developed over 1000 Indian Sign Language (ISL) videos and 
talking books, covering 23 subjects at both the Secondary and Senior Secondary levels. ISL has 
also been introduced as a language course at the Secondary level, with plans to expand to Senior 
Secondary and Open Basic Education (OBE) levels.Furthermore, NIOS has launched a 100-day 
Teacher Training Programme known as SAMARTHYA, along with a Gender Green Teacher 
course for the professional development of teachers. These initiatives support the continuous 
learning and upskilling of teachers. Additionally, NIOS offers 25 courses in the Bhartiya Jnana 
Parampara stream, which includes five courses each at the Secondary and Senior Secondary 
levels, and 15 at the OBE level.To ensure wider reach, Self Learning Materials are available in 
14 mediums at the Secondary level and 8 mediums at the Senior Secondary level. However, 
NIOS has developed an Inclusive Education Policy for Open Schooling as well as a Gender 
Policy to address the diverse needs of its learners. As part of the implementation of the National 
Education Policy (NEP) 2020, NIOS has revised its examination pattern, which was 
implemented from the 2024 public examinations. No Budgetary support is provided to NIOS by

5.7 NATIONAL COUNCIL FOR TEACHER EDUCATION (NCTE): 
5.7.1 The National Council for Teacher Education (NCTE) was established as a statutory body 
by an Act of Parliament (Act No. 73 of 1993) with a view to achieve planned and coordinated 
development of teacher education throughout the country, the regulation and proper maintenance 
of norms and standards in the teacher education system and for matters connected therewith. The 
NCTE Act 1993 (NCTE Act) came into force w.e.f. 1st July 1995 and NCTE came into existence 
on 17th August 1995 with its Head Office in New Delhi. The Council is the highest decision 
making body of NCTE consisting of 43 Members comprising of the Chairperson, Vice-
Chairperson, Member Secretary on full time basis besides the Education Secretary of the MoE, 
GoI, Adviser (Education), Planning Commission, Education Secretaries of the State 

79 
 
Governments, eminent academicians and Heads of National Educational Institutions like 
NCERT, NIEPA, UGC, CBSE, AICTE etc. The Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson and Member 
Secretary are appointed by the GoI. The NCTE is headed by the Chairperson who is vested with 
executive powers and, along with the RCs, is responsible for implementing the provisions of the 
NCTE Act, Rules and Regulations made thereunder, and also the policy decisions of the Council 
taken from time to time. 
5.7.2 As per Section 20 of the NCTE Act, the 4 RCs i.e. Eastern, Western, Northern and 
Southern deal with matters related to grant of recognition / permission to the TEIs under Section 
14/15 of the NCTE Act in the States/UTs under their jurisdiction. The RCs receive applications 
from the applicant institutions for starting a new teacher education programme or for 
introduction of another teacher education programme in an existing TEIs or for additional intake 
in an existing teacher education programme under Section 14/15 of the NCTE Act. The RCs also 
exercise powers to withdraw recognition/permission of a recognized institution under Section 17 
of the NCTE Act, provided it is established that the concerned institution has contravened the 
provisions of the NCTE Act / Rules / Regulations under which recognition/permission was 
granted to it. The RCs, besides the functions under Section 14, 15 and 17 of the NCTE Act, 
perform such other functions as may be assigned to it by the Council or as may be determined by 
Regulations. No Budgetary support is provided to NCTE by the Department of School Education 
& Literacy. However, grants under Samagra Shiksha are provided to NCTE for specific projects. 
5.7.3 The details of NEP 2020 mandates pertaining to NCTE are as under: 
(i) Integrated Teacher Education Programme (ITEP): As outlined in Para 15.5 of NEP 2020, 
the Integrated Teacher Education Programme (ITEP) is a pioneering initiative that combines 
education with a specific discipline and stage-specific specialization.  
(ii) National Mission for Mentoring (NMM): National Mission for Mentoring (NMM) as 
envisaged in para 15.11 of NEP 2020, envisioned the creation of a large pool of outstanding 
professionals willing to provide mentoring to schoolteachers. These potential mentors, regardless 
of the age or position, will contribute towards realizing 21st century developmental goals of 
nation building.  
(iii) National Professional Standards for Teachers (NPST): National Professional Standards 
for Teachers (NPST), as envisioned in Para 5.20 of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, 
aims to enhance the personal and professional development of teachers by providing clear 
expectations and guidelines for performance improvement. It seeks to ensure that all students are 
taught by passionate, motivated, highly qualified, professionally trained and well-equipped 
teachers

5.7.7 The Committee observes that there are persistent teachers' shortages, outdated 
training methodologies, and curriculum gaps have weakened the education system. 
Aligning teacher training programs with 21st-century pedagogies is crucial for improving 
education quality and recommends that the Department/NCTE should:- 
(i) Enhance teacher training budgets, focusing on blended learning, 
competency-based education, and continuous professional development; 
(ii) Expand AI-driven adaptive learning systems, supporting differentiated 
instruction and personalized learning experiences; and 
(iii) Strengthen NCTE guidelines for teacher qualification to ensure national 
uniformity while allowing state-specific modifications. 
5.7.8 The Committee observes that as the organization overseeing teacher education and 
training, the NCTE has access to networks and data that can be of help to education 
planning in the country. For instance, data provided for KVs and JNVs by the Department

and prospective teachers, each one with an APAAR Id or some equivalent unique 
identification, that tracks teachers, their training, experience, and disciplinary expertise. 
This can help clear inefficiencies in the labour market for teachers, and provide clear data 
on where career opportunities exist for prospective teachers.

to protect child rights. Accordingly, teachers need to be sensitised and trained to be among 
the first points of contact in cases of child abuse, trafficking, marriage, etc. Teachers need 
to be trained and capacitated accordingly, and the NCTE must take a lead in ensuring the 
same.

of teacher quality across states. Teacher quality must become something we can study and

SAMAGRA SHIKSHA ABHIYAN (SSA) 
 
 
8. The Committee observes that to achieve near-universal primary education, Government 
of India spent several years pursuing policies that focused on the goal and provided 
adequate resourcing to back it up. The Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan and the Right to Education 
Act, 2009 were notable interventions in this regard. While near-universal levels of primary 
education have been reached, there still remain 11.7 lakh children across the country who 
are Out of School (OoSc). The Committee is of the view that this is partly because there is 
no proper mechanism to ensure that these children are retained in school. Section 4 of the 
RTE Act, 2009 primarily focuses on a ‘curative/rehabilitative approach’ in the form of 
bridge courses, etc., after the child has dropped out for several months – there is no 
protocol for timely preventive action by authorities to retain children in schools. This 
absence of a preventive protocol is incompatible with the concept of a Fundamental Right. 
(Para 3.4.4) 
9. The goal of the Samagra Shiksha Abhiyan is to enable RTE implementation in state 
schools. However, the Committee is pained to note that 15 years after the RTE Act was 
passed, we have still not reached universal achievement of RTE norms by schools and 
teachers. In far too many schools, the pupil-teacher ratio, the number of classrooms, or the 

85 
 
availability of water and sanitation facilities and/or playgroundsis inadequate. The 
Committee notes the tremendous achievements of the Samagra Shiksha Abhiyan butcalls 
for a revamping of the scheme to function on mission mode. The mission must be to achieve 
near-saturation of the RTE’s requirements by 2029. The Finance Minister’s Budget 
announcement of achieving universal broadband connectivity for rural secondary schools 
within the year offers a model for the scale and timeline at which the Government should 
be operating at to upgrade the physical and human resources offered by schools. 
 
At the same time,it is not advisable to impose the RTE’s norms and requirements on 
schools without forethought.There are several schools, especially in underserved, remote, 
and Adivasi-majority areas, which may be unable to meet the formal requirements 
demanded by the RTE. Recently, the only Gondi-language school in Maharashtra, in 
Gadchiroli district, was forced to shut down since it did not have the requisite approval 
from the State Government as mandated by the RTE.Similar stories have emerged from 
ST dominant areas in Assam. Recognizing that the only feasible alternative to these schools 
is no school, the Department must relax RTE norms in such instances.Relaxation of RTE 
norms can only be done with a view to preserve schools – not with a view to consolidate 
them or to continue to under-resource them. 
(Para 3.4.5)

Department for school education, it is responsibility of the Department to collect data on school 
closures and consolidations and Committee should be apprised thereof. The lack of data precludes 
any systematic study or policy of the impact that such school closures may have on students.The 
Committee, therefore, directs the Department to develop a policy on school closure and 
consolidation. Some features of such a policy may include –  
 Clear guidelines on when it is acceptable to consider school consolidation, ensuring 
that RTE guidelines are not violated 
 Mandatory impact assessment of each school closure 
 Mandatory centralised collection of all data relating to school closures, since the 
Department has been entrusted with overseeing RTE implementation 
 Protocol for tracking students impacted by school closures and ensuring they are 
transferred to another school 
 Provision of transport allowance for students impacted by closure of neighborhood 
schools to travel to a more distant school complex 
The Committee also feels that any school consolidations or closures should not violate RTE 
norms on the physical proximity of primary schools to children. The Committee notes that in its 
discussion of school complexes, the NEP does not reiterate the RTE’s guidance on the necessity to 
have primary schools (Grade I-V) within 1 km of a neighborhood and upper primary schools 
(Grade VI-VIII) within 3 km of a neighborhood. However, this does not mean that the NEP’s 
proposed school complexes overrule or modify the provisions of the RTE Act, 2009. The Committee 
emphasizes that the RTE is a law passed by Parliament which deals with the fundamental rights of 
Indian children and. Department should evolve a mechanism to ensure that School consolidations

reservation in Government jobs to SC, ST, OBC, EWS, PwD etc. Since, the funds under

the Department of School Education and Literacy to seek data from the State/UT

monitor filling up of vacancies of teachers in SSA funded schools by respective State/UT

of teachers should be ensured in a time bound manner i.e. within six months from the

27. The Committee has taken serious note of the non-release of SSA funds to certain 
States which have not signed MoUs for implementation of PM Shri scheme. The total funds 
pending under this scheme to the states are considerable, with over Rs 1,000 crores to West 
Bengal, Rs. 859.63 crore to Kerala, and Rs. 2,152 crores to Tamil Nadu. The committee also 
notes that 33 out of 36 States/UTs have signed the MoU for PM SHRI and are 
implementing the scheme and developing NEP exemplar schools, so as, to create 
anequivalence in assessment and curriculum at the national level. The Committee,

Governments concerned and release the pending funds on priority basis. 
The Department has also informed the Committee that PM SHRI is the model 
school scheme developed under the NEP and the SSA is the program to achieve the NEP 
goals. This appears to be the reasoning behind the decision to halt SSA grants to states not 
signing the PM SHRI MoU. However, the Committee takes the view that this reasoning is 
not factual or justified. The SSA predates PM SHRI and is intended to help States to 
achieve the targets of the Right to Education Act. The RTE is a law duly passed by 
Parliament and confers education as a fundamental right onto every child. The SSA, as a 
scheme that enforces the fundamental right-based RTE, cannot be bypassed by the NEP, 
which was an executive policy statement.

pay salaries to teachers and resource personnel due to delays in release of central

39. The Committee is of the view that to secure rights to these children, we must 
develop a robust protocol to identify and mainstream OoSc children. The Department 
should conduct a review of the protocols enforced by States across the country – like the 
well-regarded protocol in Karnataka –and suggest a model set of rules for all States. Some 
features may include –  
 The current definition of a drop-out is pegged at 45 days of unexcused 
absence.This extended period delays the detection and flagging of the 
prospective drop-out until two-three months after the fact, a crucial time period 
in which the child may have migrated out, or engaged in work. The Karnataka 
protocol defines a ‘drop-out’ as a child with ‘unexcused absence of seven days.’ 
This shortened time-span allows for a more proactive response rather than a 
reactive response 
 The Karnataka protocol places accountability on a specific designated state 
official – an ‘attendance authority’ – who is tasked with ensuring that the Child 
Welfare Committee addresses the reason for the drop-out in a timely manner 
and mainstreams all local OoSc children within a specified time-frame 
 Currently, there is no instiutionalised or statutory mechanism for ensuring that 
child gets education if measures instituted by the Child Welfare Committe fail to

bring back a child to school. In such cases, it may be appropriate for the state to

populations that inhabit or adjoin forested lands, community settlements are not

children belonging to such communities are not counted as OoSc since their habitations are

children, and that it is incumbent upon the Department to work with the State 
Governments to ensure primary schooling is available to all residents of such habitations.

42.  The Committee recognizes that large parts of India are disaster-prone, with 
recurring natural disasters on an annual basis – including floods in Assam and parts of 
Bihar, landslides in ecosensitive regions of the Western Ghats and Himalayas, and cyclones 
on the eastern coast of the country. However, it notes that there is no existing, 
comprehensive policy guidance on how school education should respond to a natural 
disaster. There is a need to do so given that most schools become relief camps in the event 
of a disaster, and schooling activities come to a stop, sometimes for months at a time. This 

96 
 
leads to a learning loss, in addition to damage to school property. Accordingly the 
Committee recommends the formulation of a policy for school education in disaster-hit 
areas in coordination with Ministry of Home Affairs and the National Disaster 
Management Authority. Some features of this policy could include –  
 Provision for additional textbooks and uniforms in disaster-hit areas; 
 Extension of financial provisions for schools in disaster-hit areas, encompassing not 
just the structure but also the fixtures and furnishing; 
 Examination relief for students in disaster-hit communities, who cannot give exams 
on the same timeline as the rest of the state or country; 
 An assessment of the learning loss that occurs in such areas and formulation of a 
strategy to minimise the damage in the medium-term; and 
 Integration of disaster management into curriculum. 
(Para 3.4.50) 
 
43. The Committee reiterates the importance of Article 350(a) of the Indian 
Constitution, which mandates that the state shall endeavour to provide adequate facilities 
for instruction in the mother-tongue at the primary stage of education to children 
belonging to linguistic minority groups. It also emphasises Article 29 of the Indian 
Constitution, which guarantees minority (linguistic, ethnic, and/or religious) communities 
the Fundamental Right to conserve culture, language and script, and administer 
educational institutions of their choice. The Committee observes that the NEP 
acknowledges the importance of teaching students in the mother tongue, especially in the 
early years. However, by arguing that “[H]ome language is usually the same language as 
the mother tongue or that which is spoken by local communities,” the NEP doesn’t 
adequately grapple with the circumstance of linguistic minorities who speak a language 
different from that of their state and/or region. As a result, as the Department has 
acknowledged,Samagra Shiksha has no special focus or programs for students belonging to 
linguistic minorities. This has a cascading impact on state-level policies to support linguistic 
minorities.For instance, Maharashtra – which has ~4.6 lakh Gondi speakers as of 2011 – 
does not have a single Gondi-medium school.  
Accordingly, the Committee recommends that the Department should create a special 
program within Samagra Shiksha that supports states in the following –  
 Coordinate with NCERT, NBT, and SCERT to ensure that TLM and all other 
resources are widely available (online for free and marketable) in all key languages 
– especially those spoken by Adivasi and tribal communities; 
 Develop and financially support bridge courses to teach the state’s dominant 
language as a second language to children belonging to linguistic minorities; 
 Develop pedagogy, teacher training, and TLM for instruction in multiple languages; 
and 
 Support recruitment of new teachers from the local linguistic communities that the 
school caters to. 
(Para 3.4.51)

47. Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE)-The Committee observes that 90% of 
an infant’s brain development occurs between 2-5 years. Universal ECCE, as envisioned in 
the NEP is therefore critical to securing lifelong thinking and reasoning capabilities for all 
of India’s children. However, the Committee observes that universal ECCE by 2030, as 
envisioned by NEP, remains a distant dream five years after the adotion of the NEP. The 
Committee regrets that the Kasturirangan Committee’s recommendation that ECCE be an 
integral part of RTE Act did not find space in the NEP. It therefore strongly recommends 
the expansion of the RTE to include ECCE for children aged 3 years to 6 years. The 
Committee is deeply concerned about the limited progress the Ministry has made in 
achieving universal ECCE. Physical convergence of Bal Vatikas and Primary Schools with 
Anganwadishas not occurred. More importantly, neither has operational convergence.The 
Committee observes that children enrolled in Bal Vatikas (pre-schools in the Education 
Department) get mid-day meals through PM POSHAN while those in Anganwadis get it 
through the Saksham Anganwadi scheme. In Anganwadis, children are offered a welcome 
snack in addition to the meal. Children in Bal Vatikas get only a meal. Nutritional 
guidelines for both appear to be different, as are the cost normsSEL has prepared the 
Integrated Teacher Education Program for ECCE and NISHTHA ECCE. However, 
Anganwadi workers are being trained by NIPCCD under Poshan Bhi Padhai Bhi scheme. 
The Committee is very keen on ensuring that regardless of which department runs the 
ECCE program, children need to be guaranteed the same food and the teachers need to be 
trained in a standardized fashion. The Committee also emphasizes that ECCE includes 
early childhood care and education – care is an integral part of what must be available to 
children, and Anganwadi workers are therefore part of the solution. The Department must 
work with the WCD Ministry to achieve universal ECCE. The Committee observes that 
Department of SEL and WCD have created a Joint Task Force to implement universal 
ECCE, but it appears to be ineffective. Given the demonstrated inadequacy of the two 
departments concerned, i.e., SEL and WCD, in making progress on universal ECCE, the 
Committee recommends a national-level mission under the supervision of the PM to 
operationalize and accelerate convergence between the Bal Vatikas and Anganwadis.   
(Para 3.4.55) 
48. The Committee observes that over the past five years, ECCE has consistently received only 
about 2% of the total budget allocated under the Samagra Shiksha Scheme. Such limited budgetary 
provisions compromise the availability of essential resources such as quality teaching-learning 
materials (TLM), training and capacity-building programs for educators, and recruitment of 
adequate human resources to effectively implement ECCE initiatives. Inadequate funding 
undermines the capacity of ECCE programs to deliver impactful and quality early education, 
which is crucial for fostering cognitive and social skills among young learners. To 
effectivelystrengthen ECCE, enhance classroom interactions, and ensure foundational 
preparedness of young children for formal schooling, an increased budgetary commitment is 
imperative. Therefore, it is recommended that the budget allocation dedicated to ECCE be 
increased substantially, ideally to at least 5% of the total Samagra Shiksha budget. Such enhanced 
investment will significantly contribute to achieving the overarching goals of holistic child 

99 
 
development, inclusive educational access, and improved foundational learning outcomes 
nationwide. 
(Para 3.4.56)

(Para 3.4.65) 
58. The Committee notes that teachers are at the heart of the NEP – and none of the ideas 
discussed in the policy are possible without re-establishing “teachers, at all levels, as the most 
respected and essential members of our society” (NEP). The Committee believes that the first step 
towards restoring the status of teachers is to ensure that all teachers have the same service 
conditions, regarding pay, in-service teacher-training, transfers and other benefits. The dual system 
of regular teachers and contractual teachers creates a system of different pay for equal work, which 
goes against the spirit of the constitutional guarantee of equal pay for equal work. The hiring of 
contractual teachers also undermines the Constitutional right of SCs, STs, and OBCs to reservation 
in public employment. The Committee notes that the NEP 2020, unlike the draft version released in 
2019, does not make any unequivocal statement on discontinuing the practice of hiring contract 
teachers. The Committee therefore recommends that the Department direct the utilisation of 

101 
 
Samagra Shiksha funds by states towards the hiring of regular teachers alone, or the regularisation 
of contractual teachers. The Department must develop a clear roadmap for transitioning 
contractual teachers into permanent positions within the next five years.States must also be 
encouraged to count years on contract as being part of a teacher’s service when considering 
promotions. 
(Para 3.4.66) 
 
59. The Committee notes that single-teacher schools continue to exist despite years after the 
passage of the RTE. It notes that the RTE’s stipulated Pupil Teacher Ratio of 30:1 for primary 
schools and 35:1 for upper primary schools took the focus away from the importance of having one 
teacher per grade. Thus, the Committee unequivocally advocates for a new policy of requiring one 
teacher per grade. 
(Para 3.4.67) 
60. The Committee recommends increased funding for regional language learning resources in 
school and higher education curriculums to implement NEP’s vision of instruction in the child’s 
mother tongue.” 
(Para 3.4.68) 
PRADHAN MANTRI POSHAN SHAKTI NIRMAN (PM POSHAN) SCHEME  
61. The Committee observes that Rs. 12,467.39 crores were allocated under PM-
POSHAN at BE 2024-25 which was reduced to Rs. 10000.00 crores at RE 2024-25 stage. 
The actual utilization as on 18.02.2025 is only Rs. 5,421.97 crores which is 43.48% and 
54.21% of BE and RE 2024-25 respectively. The Committee recommends that the 
Department should issue directions to State Governments to submit utilization certificates 
on time and strive for ensuring full utilization of allocation of Rs. 12,500.00 crores during 
FY 2025-26. 
(Para 3.5.6)   
62. The Committee notes that while PM POSHAN has contributed significantly to 
school enrollment and attendance, the scheme remains incomplete in coverage and lacks 
effective monitoring mechanisms to ensure meal quality etc.. Additionally, adolescent 
malnutrition continues to be a concern, as students in secondary and senior secondary 
schools are excluded from the program. Strengthening nutritional support will directly 
impact student performance and retention. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
the Department of School Education and Literacy should take initiatives on the following:- 
(i) Expansion of PM POSHAN to Secondary Education: PM POSHAN coverage 
should be extended to students upto Class 12th (upto the age of 18 years), 
with a focus on preventing adolescent dropouts and addressing gender 
disparities in nutrition. This is a natural corollary of the Committee’s 
recommendation to extend the RTE until the age of 18. 
(ii) Breakfast Inclusion: A national breakfast program should be introduced to 

102 
 
combat morning hunger and enhance cognitive performance, particularly in 
rural and economically weaker sections. This has already been envisioned in 
the NEP but is yet to be implemented by the Department. 
(iii) Decentralized Procurement & Localized Meal Planning: Community-led 
food sourcing, integrating locally grown grains, vegetables, and dairy should 
be promoted to improve nutrition while supporting local farmers as well. 
(iv) Third-Party Quality Audits: Quarterly meal quality, hygiene, and taste of the 
mid-day meal checks should be conducted through independent agencies, 
ensuring compliance with dietary standards and addressing reported issues 
in real-time. 
(v) Nutritional Fortification: Iron and protein fortification in mid-day meals 
should be implemented to tackle widespread deficiencies in school-aged 
children.  Provision of a glass of milk daily should be ensured under the 
scheme, adopting the Karnataka model of Ksheera Bhagya in view of the fact 
that around 40 to 50% of children in the country are stunted. 
(vi) Revision of Nutritional Norms:The nutritional norms should be revised for 
the meals under PM POSHAN on the line of recommendations by the ICMR.  
(vii) The Department should significantly hike the compensation paid to mid-day 
meal workers. 
 
(Para 3.5.10)   
63. The Committee is of the view that there is inadequate convergence with other 
Ministries/ Departments and Schemes being run by them which is adversely affecting 
effective implementation of crucial schemes like PM POSHAN. The Committee 
recommends that the Department of School Education and Literacy should make sincere 
efforts for convergence amongst various Ministries, like Ministries of Education, Health 
and Women and Child Development, for seamless implementation of schemes of various 
Ministries related to children and their development.  
(Para 3.5.11)   
 
64. The Committee appreciates that the Department has revised the existing rates of 
material cost to Rs. 6.19 per child per day for Bal Vatika and  Primary classes and Rs. 9.29 
per child per day for upper primary classes w.e.f. 1st December, 2024. However, the 
Committee strongly feels that Rs. 6.19 per child per day for Bal Vatika and  Primary 
classes and Rs. 9.29 per child per day for upper primary classes, are too meagre amounts to 
feed nutritious food to the children of the country  in view of inflationary trends in the 
country. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should relook into 
the revision of rates of material cost per child per day and revise it  to a reasonable limit 
per child per day, so that, provision of a glass of milk, iron and protein fortification and 
breakfast can be ensured for the school children. 
(Para 3.5.12)   
 
65. The Committee observes that though Public Financial Management System 
(PFMS) has been introduced by the Government under which State Government needs to 
open State Nodal Agency (SNA) Account and the funds released by Central Government 
are transferred to SNA account which in turn releases the funds to Implementing 

103 
 
Agencies directly through electronic mode, as a result, delay in the release of funds to the 
implementing agencies by the States are being reported. The Committee recommends that 
the Department should take up the issue of delay in the release of funds to the 
implementing agencies with the State/UT Governments immediately to redress the same 
for ensuring the effective implementation of the scheme. 
(Para 3.5.13)   
66. The Committee takes serious note of the complaints received regarding poor 
quality of meals, corruption/misappropriation, casteism and other irregularities under 
PM POSHAN scheme and recommends that the Department should sensitize the State/UT 
Governments on regular intervals for speedy and fair enquiry into the complaints and 
disposal thereof as per the provisions of Law. 
(Para 3.5.14)   
PM SCHOOLS FOR RISING INDIA (PM SHRI) -   
67. The Committee appreciates the enhanced allocation for PM SHRI scheme during 
FY 2025-26. However, the Committee observes that Actual utilization of Rs. 2186.42 crores 
as on 18th February, 2025 against the BE 2024-25 of Rs. 6,050.00 crores and reduced 
allocation at RE 2024-25 of Rs. 4,500.00 crores is very meagre under the PM SHRI scheme 
for exemplar/ model schools. Similarly, Actual utilization during FY 2023-24 is Rs. 1214.68 
crores only against BE of Rs. 4,000.00 crores and reduced RE of Rs. 2,800.00 crores for the 
same FY. 
The Committee is compelled to note that utilization of allocated funds is very poor 
and Department was able to utilize only 30.36% of the total allocation in BE 2023-24 and 
36.13% (as on 18th February, 2025) of the total allocation made in BE 2024-25. Similarly, 
the actual utilization against RE 2023-24 is only 43.38% and 48.58% only against RE 2024-
25 (as on 18th February, 2025). The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
Department should take effective steps for complete utilization of funds allocated under 
PM SHRI scheme at BE 2025-26 and to ensure the efficacy of the scheme. 
(Para 3.6.6)   
68. During the Study-visit to Guwahati, the Committee observed that schools witness 
higher enrolment of students after being given the status of PM-SHRI. This can have 
negative effects on the quality of education since the number of teachers remains the same. 
PM-SHRI funds are largely for infrastructural upgradation and schools are unable to use 
them to hire teachers. The Committee, therefore, recommends that norms for selection of 
PM SHRI schools in the country should be relaxed to accommodate at least 2 PM SHRI 
schools per block in the district based on the population density and number of students to 
reduce burden on specific schools and to accommodate students from every section of the 
society in these exemplar/model schools. 
(Para 3.6.7)   
69. The Committee notes that aspirational schools are needed to reform the image of 
public schooling in popular perception but it distracts from the necessity of large-scale 
improvements in quality. PM-SHRI should therefore be extended to average schools also 
by relaxing the norms – the Ministry cannot afford to concentrate resources on improving 
the top performing schools alone. The first step in this regard would be to exclude the KVs 

104 
 
and JNVs from the scheme since as schools run by the Union Government, they should 
automatically be resourced and organised along the lines of the NEP rather than needing 
additional support to do so. The Committee also recommends that Department should 
makeassessment of functioning and performance of PM SHRI schools on the impact that 
PM-SHRI status has had on schools and apprise the Committee in this regard. 
(Para 3.6.8)   
70. The Committee recommends that the Department should evolve a mechanism to 
encourage exemplar PM SHRI schools for handholding other schools of Central/ State 
Government in their geographical proximity, so that, these schools can also be transformed 
into exemplar schools for popularizing school education. 
(Para 3.6.9) 
71. The Committee observes that the PM SHRI initiative aims to establish model 
schools across India, but certain States like Tamil Nadu, Kerala and West Bengal have 
raised concerns regarding the imposition of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 
along with other concerns with respect allied conditions for participation in the scheme. 
Additionally, these States have raised the issue of lack of transparency in PM SHRI fund 
allocation and delays in disbursement. The Committee therefore, recommends the 
following:- 
(i) The Department should take sincere efforts to bring onboard amicably, the States like 
Tamil Nadu, Kerala and West Bengal by allowing them the flexibility to adopt their own 
education models while still benefiting from infrastructure and resource allocations. 
Besides, continued and adequate funding be ensured under schemes like Samagra Shiksha 
Abhiyan (SSA) for States such as Tamil Nadu, West Bengal, and Kerala.  
(ii) The Department should ensure Transparent Funding Mechanisms and real-time 
utilization reports for PM SHRI funds are made publicly accessible to prevent disparities 
and ensure accountability.  
(iii) The Department should prioritize infrastructure grants for smart classrooms, well-
equipped libraries and teachers' recruitment, rather than focusing on administrative 
expenses. 
(iv)The Department should take sincere efforts for Community Engagement in School 
Management and to establish School Development Committees with local representatives, 
including political representatives, teachers, and parents to ensure contextual curriculum 
adaptation and school governance. 
(Para 3.6.10)   
STRENGTHENING TEACHING-LEARNING AND RESULTS FOR STATE (STARS): 
72. The Committee notes that allocation for STARS at BE 2024-25 was Rs. 1,250.00 
crores which was reduced to Rs. 850 crores at RE 2024-25 stage. The Actual utilization as 
on 18.02.2025 is Rs. 611.39 crores only. The scheme has been allocated Rs. 1,250.00 crores 
again in spite of under utilization during 2024-25. The Committee, therefore, recommends 

105 
 
that the Department of School Education and Literacy and other stakeholders should 
ensure optimum utilization of allocation during FY 2025-26. 
(Para 3.7.3)   
73. The Committee observes from the details of Approvals, Central Releases and 
Expenditure given above that Central Releases under the STARS scheme is very low in 
comparison to Approvals since inception of the scheme. Additionally, the utilization is also 
not upto the mark when compared with approvals. The Committee recommends that the 
Department should sincerely look into the reasons for lower release and utilization and 
rectify the trend. 
(Para 3.7.6)   
74. The Committee observes that the STARS project is designed to enhance governance 
and accountability in school education. However, rural and tribal schools have seen limited 
benefits, necessitating better fund distribution and oversight mechanisms. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Department of School Education and Literacy should take 
the following actions:- 
(i) Targeted Rural & Tribal Interventions: Mandatorily at least 50% of STARS 
funding should be directed to rural and tribal schools in order to reduce urban-rural 
disparities in quality education. 
(ii) Data-Driven Learning Improvement Plans: State-level data repositories to track 
student progress, teacher performance, and infrastructure gaps should be implemented. 
(iii) Independent Learning Assessments: Third-party impact assessments of STARS 
projects should be conducted at both the district and school levels to guide course 
corrections. 
 
(iv) Localized Curriculum Enhancements: Regional linguistic and cultural element 
should be incorporated into learning materials to make education more accessible and 
relevant. 
 
(v) Capacity Building for Administrators & Teachers: Specialized training modules 
should be developed for school heads and teachers, emphasizing data-driven decision-
making and innovative pedagogy with the support of AI & other technological 
developments. 
(Para 3.7.7)  
NEW INDIA LITERACY PROGRAMME/ UNDERSTANDING OF LIFELONG 
LEARNING FOR ALL IN SOCIETY (ULLAS)/ULLAS- NAV BHARAT 
SAAKSHARTAKARYAKRAM 
75. The Committee notes that Department was allocated Rs. 157.00 crores during BE 
2023-24 which had been substantially reduced to Rs. 100.00 crores at RE 2023-24. 
Moreover, the Actual utilization under NILP/ULLAS was 39.30 crores only during 2023-24 
which was 39.30% of the allocation at RE stage. The Committee further notes that under 

106 
 
NILP/ULLAS, Rs. 160.00 crores were allocated at BE 2024-25 which was reduced to Rs. 
120.00 crores at RE 2024-25 and the actual utilization as on 18.02.2025 is only 80.76 crores 
which is around 50% of BE 2024-25 and around 66% of RE 2024-25. However, the 
Department has been allocated enhanced BE 2025-26 of Rs. 160.00 crores in comparison to 
RE 2024-25. 
The Committee expresses its anguish over under utilization of allocated funds and 
recommends the Department to utilize enhanced allocation at BE 2025-26 optimally and 
avoid under utilization and rush for expenditure during the last quarter of the Financial 
Year in compliance of Rule 56(3) of General Financial Rules (GFR) of Ministry of Finance.  
(Para 3.8.4)  
76. In response to question of the Committee regarding the number of illiterates in the 
country, the Department informed the Committee that there are around 17-18 crore 
illiterates in the country. Accordingly, the Committee recommends that the Department 
should accelerate the process of literacy programmes like NILP/ULLAS to achieve full 
literacy target within the irreducible minimum time latest by 2029. The Committee further 
feels that any scheme without incentive cannot succeed and accordingly, recommends that 
volunteer teachers registered on ULLAS App should be incentivized to make the scheme 
successful and efficacious. 
(Para 3.8.5)  
77. The Committee observes that despite India’s push for universal literacy, adult 
literacy rates remain a challenge, particularly among women and marginalized 
communities like SC, ST, OBC, EWS and PwD etc. The NILP aims to bridge this gap, but 
low outreach, inadequate learning resources, and underutilization of allocated funds have 
hindered its effectiveness in these communities. There is problem/shortage of volunteer 
teachers for the scheme in Tribal Areas due to digital divide. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Department of School Education and Literacy should ensure the 
following actions: 
(i) District-Level Learning Centers: Atleast one Community Learning Center 
(CLC) should be established per district with dedicated literacy facilitators, 
offering structured adult education programs. 
(ii) Integration with Digital Literacy: Free mobile-based literacy modules should 
be provided and tablets in CLCs should be distributed to support self-paced 
learning and financial literacy training. 
(iii) Customized Literacy Models: Tailored learning pathways should be 
developed for marginalized groups, including women-led literacy circles and 
tribal education modules in local dialects. 
(iv) Partnerships for Skill-Based Literacy: Collaboration with corporates and 
NGOs should be established to integrate vocational skills with literacy 
programs, ensuring economic upliftment. 
(v) Monitoring & Accountability: Real-time literacy tracking systems, with 
quarterly progress assessments should be implemented to measure impact 
and guide policy adjustments. Besides, awareness generation initiatives 

107 
 
should be taken in local languages for better enrolment under the scheme for 
achieving the target of complete literacy. 
(vi) Community Libraries: The Department should evaluate the model of the 
Gram Panchayat libraries and Information Centers in Karnataka to set up a 
nationwide system of community libraries that encourage lifelong learning 
and active literacy.  
(Para 3.8.6)  
 
CENTRAL SECTOR SCHEME 
NATIONAL MEANS-CUM-MERIT SCHOLARSHIP SCHEME (NMMSS): 
 
78. The Committee observes that Rs. 374.00 crores have been allocated at BE 2025-26 
under NMMSS which is Rs. 3.00 crores less than BE 2024-25 and Rs. 22.00 crores higher 
than RE 2024-25. The number of enrollment of students is increasing, however, the amount 
of allocation is stagnant since 2019-20. The Committee feels that it would have adverse and 
demoralizing impacts on students from disadvantageous communities like SCs, STs, OBCs, 
EWS, minority etc. The Committee also observes that the number of scholarships has gone 
down in recent years in comparison to 2019-20. The Committee, therefore, recommends the 
Department to seek additional funds for NMMSS and increase the number of scholarships 
in view of its declining numbers in recent years and increase in number of students. 
(Para 4.1.2)  
79. The Committee is of the view that amount of Rs. 12000.00 per annum as scholarship 
under NMMSS is very low in view of inflationary trends in the country and the 
Department should sincerely consider and increase the amount of scholarship from Rs. 
12,000.00 per annum to Rs. 36,000/- per annum immidetately. The Department should also 
relax the income ceiling criteria under the scholarship in view of inflation and to 
accommodate more children under the scheme. 
(Para 4.1.3)  
80. The Committee observes that scholarships are crucial for economically weaker 
students. Slow disbursal and restrictive eligibility criteria have limited their impact. 
Accordingly, the Committee recommends the Department of School Education and 
Literacy the following:- 
(i) The Department should establish a centralized digital tracking system for 
real-time monitoring of scholarship disbursal and should ensure timely 
disbursal of scholarships to students; 
(ii) The Department should expand eligibility criteria, including students from 
disadvantaged backgrounds beyond income-based filters; 
(iii) The Department should adjust scholarship amounts annually to align with 
inflation and rising education costs, ensuring meaningful financial support; 
(iv) The Department should proactively co-ordinate with  
Ministries/Departments concerned i.e. Ministry of Communication and 

108 
 
Ministry of Finance and address the issue of interruption of internet 
connectivity in Aadhaar Payment Bridge (APB) gateway in rural areas and 
non-seeding of Bank account with Aadhaar due to which payment fails; and 
(v) Department should take efforts for awareness of students regarding process 
of seeding of accounts in Banks through advertisements in print, digital and 
electronic media. 
(Para 4.1.7) 
81. The Committee notes that there is mismatch in data furnished by the Department 
regarding number of year-wise scholarship (fresh + renewal) at Table 34 and 35. The 
Committee expresses its anguish over the casual approach being taken while furnishing 
data/ information to the Committee which is utter disregard to Parliament and its Standing 
Committees. The Committee, therefore, directs the Department that correct reply/ figure 
with due diligence and after proper vetting by the authority concerned be furnished for its 
consideration. 
(Para 4.1.8)  
PRADHAN MANTRI INNOVATIVE LEARNING PROGRAM (PMILP)-DHRUV 
 
82. The Committee notes that Rs. 1 lakh only were allocated under the scheme at BE 2024-
25 stage which was increased to Rs. 7.5 crores at RE 2024-25. However there is nil 
utilization of the allocated fund during 2024-25 as on 18.02.2025 which reflects the pace of 
working of the Department.  The Committee further observes that under DHURUV 
scheme, in spite of, the fact, there is 5500% increase in BE 2025-26 over BE 2024-25 and 
around 800% increase over RE 2024-25, the amount of Rs. 55.00 crores allocated at BE 
2025-26 is very meagre and the Committee, therefore, recommends the Department to 
expedite finalization of guidelines of Central Sector Scheme Pradhan Mantri Innovative 
Learning Programme - DHRUV and ensure optimum utilization of  the allocated amount 
during 2025-26 for nurturing the exceptional potential of gifted and talented students 
across the nation. 
(Para 4.2.4)  
THE NATIONAL MISSION ON FOUNDATIONAL LITERACY AND NUMERACY 
(NIPUN BHARAT MISSION)  
83. The Committee observes that foundational literacy and numeracy skills are critical 
for long-term educational success. However, fund underutilization and insufficient per-
teacher allowances have limited the program’s reach and its impact. Strengthening 
implementation mechanisms can accelerate the improvement of literacy rates and 
numeracy competencies across the States. Accordingly, the Committee recommends the 
Department of School Education and Literacy as under:- 
(i) Enhanced Teacher Resource Allocation: The Department should increase per-
teacher resource allowance from ₹150 to ₹1,500 per year, ensuring sufficient access 
to graded reading materials, manipulatives, and remedial tools; 

109 
 
(ii) Annual Literacy & Numeracy Assessments: The Department should conduct 
standardized, state-level competency assessments, ensuring targeted interventions 
for underperforming schools; 
(iii) Community-Based Learning Support: The Department should establish volunteer-
based reading camps in rural areas, engaging educated youth and retired teachers 
in literacy initiatives; 
(iv) Multilingual Learning Strategies: The Department should develop mother-tongue-
based literacy modules, integrating bilingual learning resources to ease transition 
into formal education; and 
(v) Tech-Enabled Learning: The Department should deploy AI-driven adaptive 
learning tools to track student progress and personalize remedial instruction based 
on real-time learning data. 
(vi) Teaching Learning Material (TLM): Given the absence of at-home learning and 
lack of access to print material at home, students must not have shortage of 
pedagogical material like workbooks etc in class and must have print-rich classroom 
environments. The Department may evaluate the need for increased TLM funding 
from existing norms.  
(Para 4.3.4)  
 
84. The Committee observes that the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 accorded 
the highest priority to FLN, stating that “the rest of this Policy will become relevant for our 
students only if this most basic learning requirement (i.e., reading, writing, and arithmetic 
at the foundational level) is first achieved.” Accordingly, the Committee encourages the 
Department to regard NIPUN Bharat as one of its flagship missions, and provide resources 
and visibility to it accordingly. The Committee recommends that the Department publish 
an annual report on the NIPUN Bharat Mission.  
(Para 4.3.5)  
85. The The Committee notes that the recently released Annual Status of Education 
Report (ASER) survey 2024 showed some encouraging findings for Foundational Literacy 
and Numeracy (FLN), with Grade III students recovering the learning loss in reading 
abilities recorded due to the COVID-19 pandemic, and surpassing pre-pandemic levels of 
quantitative ability. However, NIPUN Bharat aims to have every child in the country attain 
foundational literacy and numeracy by the end of Grade 2, by 2026-27. Despite the 
progress recorded, this is a target that we are highly unlikely to meet. Accordingly, the 
deadline for the NIPUN Bharat Mission must be extended from 2027 to 2032. The 
Committee observes that this is in line with the international norm of running FLN 
missions for a minimum of 10 years. 
(Para 4.3.6) 
86. Given the limited capacity of state governments to spend on education, the 
Department must also continue to provide budgetary support to NIPUN Bharat to ensure 
its success.  
(Para 4.3.7) 

110 
 
87. The Committee notes that the mission has been re-focused recently to exclude oral 
reading fluency as one of its objective. This has ostensibly been done to align the Mission 
with the NEP’s 5+3+3+4 structure, since oral reading fluency was targeted for Grade 3 and 
Grade 3 falls beyond the purview of the first 5 years of schooling under NEP. However the 
Committee notes that the Prime Minister himself highlighted the importance of oral 
reading fluency at the conclave on school education in the 21st century under NEP 2020 on 
September 11, 2020. Oral reading fluency is a foundational life skill critical to the success 
of students. The Committee strongly recommends that the Mission be refocused once again 
to include the attainment of universal oral reading fluency as one of its key objectives.  
(Para 4.3.8) 
88. The Committee also observes that an ambitious goal like FLN requires community 
engagement and support. It therefore recommends an additional allocation of INR 270 
Crores annually (10% of the total allocation currently) for Information Education 
Communication (IEC) Activities. Further,10% of the Composite School Grant should be 
designated for awareness building of NIPUN Bharat Mission in the school’s local 
neighborhood community. This additional resourcing and focus will go a long way in 
aligning all stakeholders, including parents and community elders, with the Mission’s 
objectives.                                                                                                                     (Para 4.3.9)  
AUTONOMOUS BODIES  
National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT):- 
89. The Committee appreciates the enahanced allocation of Rs. 560.77 crores at RE 2024-25 
and healthy utilization of Rs. 506.77 crores as on 18.02.2025. The Committee also 
appreciates the enhanced allocation of Rs. 593.71 crores at BE 2025-26 to NCERT. 
(Para 5.1.4) 
90. The Committee takes note of the vacancies in NCERT and observes that 146 posts of 
academic staffs are vacant against the sanctioned strength 529. The Committee also 
observes that 26, 13, 43 and 25 posts of academic staffs under SC, ST, OBC and EWS 
category, respectively, are vacant. Further, 3 posts of teaching staffs out of total 8 sactioned 
strength in Group 'A' are lying vacant while 121 posts of teaching staffs out of 263 
sanctioned strength in Group 'B' are lying vacant. Similarly, 20, 09 and 25 posts of 
teaching in Group 'B' are lying vacant under SC, ST and OBC category respectively. The 
Committee had recommended the NCERT in its 349th Report, to "complete the process of 
filling up the vacancies with permanent posts in a time-bound manner and latest by the end 
of 2023, so that, NEP 2020 is implemented in letter and spirit. However, NCERT has not 
filled up the huge number of posts lying vacant in NCERT. The Committee, therefore, 
reiterates its recommendation contained in 349th Report and directs the NCERT to fill up 
the all the vacancies including backlog vacancies at the earliest in mission mode and latest 
by end of 2025. The Committee further recommends the Department of School Education 
and Literacy and NCERT to stop contractual appointments in premier institutions like 
NCERT which undermines the Constitutional provision regarding reservation in 
Government jobs to SC, ST, OBC, EWS and PwD etc. 
(Para 5.1.10) 

111 
 
91. The Committee takes note and appreciates the decision of the NCERT mentioned at 
Para 5.1.9 above which states that henceforth, Preamble of the Indian Constitution will be 
included in the preliminary pages of all the school textbooks published by the NCERT. The 
Committee recommends the NCERT to include 'Preamble of the Indian Constitution', 
'National Anthem' and 'Talisman of Gandhi ji' which is regarded as one of the last notes 
left behind by Mahata Gandhi in 1948, expressing his deepest social thought, in the 
preliminary pages of NCERT books from class 1st to 12th invariably.

92. The Committee also feels that an integrated approach to protecting child rights 
should be adopted. The Committee recommends toinclude modules on Nutrition, Sex abuse 
(Good touch, Bad touch), Child marriage, Child labour, Domestic violence, Drug addiction 
and Gender inclusivity, Human trafficking, Disaster response and resilience and Mental 
health in the school curriculum, beginning from Class 1st onwards.  The Committee also 
recommends the inclusion of regional icons and forgotten heros in NCERT textbooks. 
(Para 5.1.12) 
93. The Committee further recommends the NCERT to ensure curriculum revision 
reflecting regional linguistic diversity, social inclusivity, and technological advancements. 
NCERT should also ensure Public and Expert Consultation for Curriculum Development. 
Regular stakeholder engagement sessions to incorporate State/UT Governments, academia, 
and civil society inputs into NCERT textbook revisions should also be done invariably. 
(Para 5.1.13) 
94. The Committee observes that the gap between the curriculum of the 9th and 10th is 
often divorced from that of the 11th and 12th, especially in mathematics and sciences. This 
results in a rupture for students in these disciplines, which the NEP's 5+3+3+4 structure 
seeks to bridge. The Committee recommends that further revisions of the curriculum for 
these grades must be done with the goal of smoothening the transition for students.  
(Para 5.1.14) 
95. The Committee observes that the curriculum for arts, crafts, music, and physical 
education in schools is often done on an ad hoc basis. Accordingly, the Committee 
recommends that the NCERT consult with the requisite experts to provide a framework 
for education in these subjects.

importance. Poor scores in Mathematics are the single biggest indicator of students who 
are likely to drop out. Quality Mathematics teachers are scarce even in the best schools.

Mission on Mathematics, tasked with conducting research on the most effective 
interventions to build Mathematical proficiency in students throughout their school 
education years, building the capacity of teachers in Mathematics, and developing

(Para 5.1.16) 
 

112 
 
97. The Committee recommends that the National Curriculum Framework on Teacher 
Education be published as soon as possible to provide clarity to teacher education under 
the NEP. 
(Para 5.1.17)

recommendation of the Committee contained in its 349th Report, to "complete the process 
of filling up the vacancies with permanent posts in a time-bound manner and latest by the 
end of 2023, so that, NEP 2020 is implemented in letter and spirit". The Committee takes 
serious note of the casual approach of Department and CBSE with respect to 
recommendations of the Committee and directs the Department of School Education and 
CBSE to fill up the vacancies including backlog vacancies in mission mode and in 
timebound manner at the earliest and latest by the end 2025.   
(Para 5.2.7) 
99. The Committee observes that few private schools force students and their parents to 
purchase books, shoes, dresses etc. from specific stores recommended by those schools, on 
very higher prices. Moreover, these schools have no capping on fees and other charges 
collected from students. Private schools are running like commercial business instead of 
community service against the provisions of Clause 9.1.3 of Affiliation Bye Laws of the 
Board. The Committee, therefore, recommends the CBSE to monitor these malpractices in 
private schools affiliated to CBSE and ensure compliance of provisions of Clause 9.1.3 of 
Affiliation Bye Laws of the Board by these profit making schools. 
(Para 5.2.8) 
100. The Committee is expresses its concerns about the CBSE's draft policy for the 
conduct of two annual board examinations, which announces a planned enhancement of 
examination fees. It recommends that the examination fees not be hiked for all students, 
but only for those who are giving an additional attempt in the board examinations. 
Moreover, given CBSE’s considerable surplus revenues, there may be occasion to reduce 
the fees charged to students for exams.  
(Para 5.2.9) 
101. The Committee expresses its concerns about the draft policy’s notification that 
examination for remaining subjects will be conducted on 2 to 3 days. This offers potential 
for question paper leaks and other irregularities which must desperately be avoided. The 
Committee recommends further thought be given to the system to make it foolproof.  
(Para 5.2.10) 

113 
 
 
KENDRIYA VIDYALAYA SANGATHAN (K.V.S)  
102. The Committee observes that Rs. 9,302.67 crores were allocated to KVS at BE 2024-
25, however, it was reduced to 8,727.00 crores at RE stage. The actual utilization as on 18th 
February, 2025 is Rs. 8,105.98 crores. Further, KVS has been allocated Rs. 9,503.84 crores 
under BE 2025-26. The Committee notes that reduction of allocation at RE 2024-25 stage 
when there are huge numbers of teaching and non-teaching posts are lying vacant, is 
unwarranted and avoidable.   
(Para 5.3.4) 
103. From the data given at Table-47 and 48, the Committee notes that the number of 
sanctioned posts of Teaching /Non-teaching Staffs are 50,457 and 6,436 as on 01.08.2024. 
However, the number of operational sanctioned staff of Teaching /Non-teaching has 
reduced to 50,456 and 6,354 respectively in KVS. Similarly, the number of total sanctioned 
staff is 56,893 and 56,810 as 01.08.2024 and 31.12.2024 respectively. Moreover, the number 
of total sanctioned teaching posts for the academic year has been mentioned as 50317 at 
Table-49 provided by Department in response to query regarding contractual 
appointments of teaching staffs under KVS. The Committee  fails to understand the 
rationale for reduction/increase in number of sanctioned teaching and non-teaching staffs 
within a period of 5 months and directs the Department/KVS that correct reply/ figures 
with due diligence and after proper vetting by the authority concerned should be furnished 
for its consideration.                                                                                                    (Para 5.3.8) 
104. The Committee taking into consideration data given at Table-48, observes that out 
of total sanctioned strength of 56,810, there are 8,977 posts of teaching and non-teaching 
staffs are vacant. Out of it, 7,414 posts of teaching staffs and 1563 posts of non-teaching 
staffs are lying vacant under KVS which is 14.69% of total sanctioned teaching positions 
and 24.59 % of total sanctioned non-teaching strength. KVS are exemplar/ model schools 
in the country and such a large number of vacancies inevitably hamper its functioning and 
reputation. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Department School Education and 
KVS that vacancies of teaching and non-teaching staffs should be visualised in advance 
and advertisements for recruitment should be published well ahead of the occurring of 
vacancies. The Committee further recommends that recruitment process and joining of 
teachers should be ensured in a time bound manner and within six months from the date 
of advertisements for filling up the vacancies.   
(Para 5.3.9) 
105. The Committee observes that there were 3,404 contractual teachers in KVS during 
academic year 2023-24 which has increased to 6,734 contractual teachers during academic 
year 2024-25. It reflects that there is around 100% increase in appointment of contractual 
teachers in 2024-25 in comparison to 2023-24.  The Committee is anguished over the 
increasing number of contractual appointments in exemplar/model schools like KVS. The 
contractual teachers cannot give their 100% to their institutions and cannot concentrate on 
teaching jobs when they are in quest of permanent jobs due to insecurity and lesser pay in 

114 
 
contractual jobs. It will also adversely affect the quality of education imparted by them and 
the institution itself. Further, appointments on contractual basis undermines the 
Constitutional provision of reservation for SC, ST, OBC, EWS, PwD etc. in these jobs. The 
Committee, therefore, strongly recommends the Department/KVS to stop appointments on 
contract basis and fill up the vacancies through special recruitment drives in time bound 
manner and latest by March, 2026, ensuring subject matter expertise, and enhancing 
professional development opportunities. 
(Para 5.3.11) 
106. The Committee observes that KVS caters to the educational needs of transferrable 
Central Government employees including Defence and Para-military personnel. The 
Committee notes that 192 KVS do not have permanent buildings and are functioning in 
temporary accommodations. Accordingly, the  Committee recommends that the 
Department should take-up the matter with the State Governments/Agencies concerned 
and pursue and convince them for providing land for the remaining 192 KVS on mission 
mode as Department has been given enhanced  allocation for Financial Year  2025-26. 
Further, for continued financial sustainability of KVs, the Committee recommends that the 
Government should consider focusing on bearing the capital cost of setting up KVs alone. 
(Para 5.3.13) 
107. The Committee appreciates Government's approval of the   proposal for opening of 
85 new KVs in Civil/Defence Sector across the country and expansion of one existing KV 
Shivamogga, Karnataka. While KVS has received increased funding, in view of the 
affecting quality education access for rural students, strengthening recruitment, 
infrastructure, and oversight mechanisms can optimize these institutions' impact. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should ensure Equitable 
Expansion of KVS Schools by identifying districts with high demand but no KVS presence 
and prioritize new schools in underrepresented regions. The Committee also recommends 
that Department should Conduct annual audits of KVS schools, ensuring financial 
accountability and curriculum enhancements. 
(Para 5.3.14) 
108. The Committee also recommends that the local Member of Parliament be added to 
the School Management Committee of the KendriyaVidyalayas falling within their 
constituency. 
(Para 5.3.15) 
 
 
NAVODAYA VIDYALAYA SAMITI (NVS) 
 
109. The Committee notes that allocation under BE 2025-26 is Rs. 5305.23 crores which 
is lower than BE 2024-25 of Rs. 5800.00 crores and RE 2024-25 of Rs. 5370.79 crores. The 
Committee expresses its concerns regarding reduction in allocation at BE 2025-26 for NVS, 
when 23.62% and 26.63% vacancies of teaching and non-teaching staffs, respectively, are 

115 
 
lying vacant. Moreover, Government has sanctioned 28 new NVS in December, 2024 which 
will require additional funds. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Department/NVS 
to seek enhanced budget allocation from Ministry of Finance particularly for filling up of 
all vacancies including backlog vacancies during 2025-26, newly approved 28 JNVs, 
upgradation of hostel facilities, transport provisions, and rural school expansions. 
(Para 5.4.3) 
110. The Committee notes that 6,858 posts of teaching and non-teaching staffs are lying 
vacant in JNVs out of total sanctioned strength of 27,676 which is 24.77% of the total 
sanctioned strength in spite of Committee's recommendation contained in its 349th Report 
to fill up the vacancies in a time bound manner and latest by the end of 2023. The 
Committee further notes that not even a single recruitment for vacant teaching and non-
teaching posts has taken place during 2023-24 and for non-teaching posts nil recruitment 
has been done during 2022-23 in JNVs even though COVID-19 phase has ended. The 
Committee, therefore, directs the Department of School Education and Literacy and NVS 
that vacancies of teaching and non-teaching staffs should be visualised in advance and 
advertisements for recruitment should be published well ahead of the occurring of 
vacancies. The Committee further recommends that recruitment process and joining of 
teachers should be ensured in a time bound manner and within six months from the date 
of advertisements for filling up the vacancies. 
  (Para 5.4.8) 
111. The Committee observes that the number of teachers appointed on contractual basis 
in JNVs is 2403 during 2021-22, 2155 during 2022-23, 2500 druing 2023-24 and 3237 
during 2024-25. Similarly, the number of non-teaching contractual staffs appointed in 
JNVs is 00 during 2021-22, 561 during 2022-23, 350 during 2023-24 and 694 during 2024-
25.  The Committee expresses its concerns over the increasing number of contractual 
appointments in exemplar/model residential schools like JNVs. The contractual teachers 
and staffs cannot give their 100% to their institutions and cannot concentrate on teaching 
jobs when they are in quest of permanent jobs due to insecurity and lesser pay in 
contractual jobs. It will also adversely affect the quality of education imparted by them and 
the institution itself and also undermines the provisions for reservation to SC, ST, OBC, 
EWS etc. contained in the Constitution of India. The Committee, therefore, strongly 
recommends the Department/NVS to stop appointments on contract basis and fill up all the 
vacancies including backlog vacancies through special recruitment drives in timebound 
manner and latest by March, 2026. 
(Para 5.4.9) 
112. The Committe also recommends the Department/NVS to conduct annual audits of  
NVS schools, ensuring financial accountability and curriculum enhancements and 
introduce structured career counseling and vocational training in NVS schools, preparing 
students for diverse career pathways. The Committee futher recommends a shift in the 
criterion for setting up Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalayas to one JNV per district to one JNV 
per 15 lakhs population to accommodate more students from rural areas. 
(Para 5.4.10) 
National Bal Bhavan (NBB): 

116 
 
 
113. The Committee appreciates the healthy utilization of Rs. 21.73 crores by NBB 
against allocation at RE 2024-25 of Rs. 24.33 crores. However, the Committee observes that 
RE 2024-25 has been reduced from 26.00 crores to Rs. 24.33 crores at RE 2024-25 stage in 
spite of large number of vacancies in NBB. The Committee also takes note of the enhanced 
BE 2025-26 of Rs. 27.80 crores. 
(Para 5.5.3) 
114. The Committee expresses its anguish over the fact that NBB has not appointed a 
single personnel on permanent basis since January, 2020 till 31st December, 2024. Only two 
appointments in Group 'A' and Group 'C' have been made by "deputation" during last 
five years which describes the state of affairs in NBB. Further, out of total 213 sanctioned 
posts, 59 posts have been recommended by SIU for abolition, out of total remaining 154 
post, contractual appointments have been made against 83 posts and the total number of 
vacancies is 101 out of total 154 posts which is around 2/3rd of the sanctioned strength in 
NBB. The Committee is pained to note that vision of the NBB is to provide opportunities to 
children that ignite curiosity and possibilities through immersive dynamic experiences in 
visual arts, scientific and physical activities and to foster values that mould self-confident, 
holistic and responsible citizens of the world, but NBB can not realize its vision through 
vacant posts and contractual appointments. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends the Department and NBB to fill up the 
vacancies by permanent appointments at the earliest and by the end of 2025 and apprise 
the Committee in this regard. Further, the recruitment on contractual basis should be 
discouraged and stopped to achieve the vision of the NBB.                                    (Para 5.5.6) 
115. The Committee is not satisfied with the geographic dispersion of Bal Bhavans around 
the country, and recommends that the Ministry move to a goal of one Bal Bhavan per 
district. The Committee also calls for closer coordination between the National Bal Bhavan 
and the state Bal Bhavans. 
(Para 5.5.7) 
NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF OPEN SCHOOLING (NIOS): 
116. The Committee notes that NIOS has recruited against 98 posts since 2019 to 2024 on 
permanent basis. However, there are total 139 vacancies in Group 'A', 'B' and 'C' against 
sanctioned strength of 394 which is 35% of the total sanctioned strength. There are 27% 
vacancies against Group 'A' posts, 45% against Group 'B' and 34% against Group 'C' post 
under NIOS. The Committee, therefore, recommends the NIOS to fill up all the vacancies 
including backlog vacancies at the earliest and latest by the end of the year 2025 on 
permanent basis. 
(Para 5.6.3) 
117. The Committee notes that the NIOS currently offers courses only in Hindi and 
English. To meet the goals of the NEP, it is incumbent upon the NIOS to offer courses in 

117 
 
other languages as well. Further, the NIOS lacks land and a dedicated office space of its 
own for several of its regional centers – for example, in Bengaluru. The Committee notes 
that the NIOS has surplus revenues which it can devote to this purpose.  
(Para 5.6.4) 
NATIONAL COUNCIL FOR TEACHER EDUCATION (NCTE): 
118. The Committee takes note of the submission of Department/NCTE which states that 
"the shortage of staff reflected above impacts the day to day working of NCTE. While the 
shortage is addressed to some extent by engagement of staff through Deputation/ 
Contractual basis, however, the same is not sufficient to meet with the existing shortages." 
The Committee also takes serious note that no new recruitments of permanent teaching, 
non-teaching and administrative staffs have been made by NCTE in view of the directives 
given by Secretary, Department School Education and Literacy, Ministry of Education 
during a meeting on NEP held in September, 2020, till date.  
In this regard, the Committee observes that there are 63 vacancies against total 
sanctioned strength of 123 in statutory body NCTE which is entrusted with realisation of 
objectives of NEP, 2020 and teachers' training. Moreover, the Committee fails to 
understand why Secretary, DoSEL had issued such directives for stoppage of recruitment 
since September, 2020 which has adversely affected the day to day working of NCTE. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends the Department to withdraw the directives for no 
recruitment immediately under intimation to this Committee and NCTE be directed to fill 
up the vacancies in a timebound manner and ensure smooth functioning of the NCTE and 
realization of objectives of NEP 2020.                                                                     
 (Para 5.7.6) 
119. The Committee observes that there are persistent teachers' shortages, outdated 
training methodologies, and curriculum gaps have weakened the education system. 
Aligning teacher training programs with 21st-century pedagogies is crucial for improving 
education quality and recommends that the Department/NCTE should:- 
(iv) Enhance teacher training budgets, focusing on blended learning, 
competency-based education, and continuous professional development; 
(v) Expand AI-driven adaptive learning systems, supporting differentiated 
instruction and personalized learning experiences; and 
(vi) Strengthen NCTE guidelines for teacher qualification to ensure national 
uniformity while allowing state-specific modifications. 
(Para 5.7.7) 
120. The Committee observes that as the organization overseeing teacher education and 
training, the NCTE has access to networks and data that can be of help to education 
planning in the country. For instance, data provided for KVs and JNVs by the Department 
shows that the highest vacancies are for teachers in subjects like physics and chemistry. 
The NCTE could assist with issues such as this by creating a national registry of in-service 
and prospective teachers, each one with an APAAR Id or some equivalent unique 

118 
 
identification, that tracks teachers, their training, experience, and disciplinary expertise. 
This can help clear inefficiencies in the labour market for teachers, and provide clear data 
on where career opportunities exist for prospective teachers.  
(Para 5.7.8) 
121. The Committee notes that schools should be at the center of the Government’s 
efforts to protect child rights. Accordingly, teachers need to be sensitised and trained to be 
among the first points of contact in cases of child abuse, trafficking, marriage, etc. 
Teachers need to be trained and capacitated accordingly, and the NCTE must take a lead 
in ensuring the same.  
(Para 5.7.9) 
122. The Committee recommends that the NCTE undertake an assessment and ranking 
of teacher quality across states. Teacher quality must become something we can study and 
measure, to facilitate interventions that ensure better outcomes for teachers.  
(Para 5.7.10)

INTRODUCTION 
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Education, Women, Children, Youth and Sports, having been authorised by the Committee to 
present the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Three Hundred and Sixty Fourth 
Report of the Committee on the Demands for Grants (Demand No. 26) of the Department of 
Higher Education, Ministry of Education for the year 2025-26.  
2. In accordance with the constitutional requirement under Article 113, the estimated 
expenditure of the Ministries/Departments of the Government of India projected under 
various Demands for Grants for the upcoming financial year needs to be voted by Parliament. 
As a sequel thereto, Demands for Grants of the relevant Ministries/Departments stand 
referred to concerned Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee to make a close 
scrutiny thereof under Rule 270 of Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the 
Council of States (Rajya Sabha). While making scrutiny of the Demands for Grants, the 
Committee has made an appraisal of the performance, programmes, schemes and policies of 
the Department of Higher Education vis-a-vis expenditure made out of Consolidated Fund of 
India in the current financial year. 
 
3. The Budget allocations of the Ministry of Education have been sought under two 
demand Numbers, i.e, Demand No. 25 pertains to the Department of School Education and 
Literacy and Demand No.26 pertains to Department of Higher Education. In this Report, a 
scrutiny of Demand No. 26 pertaining to the Department of Higher Education of the Ministry 
of Education for the Financial Year 2025-26 has been made by the Committee. While 
scrutiny of Demand No. 25 pertaining to Department of School Education and Literacy is 
covered in Report number 363rd of the Committee. 
 
4.  During the course of examination of Demands, the Committee heard the views of the 
Secretary, Department of Higher Education and other Senior Officers of the Department in its 
sitting held on 19th February, 2025. The Department also made available inputs from various 
organizations/agencies, namely, University Grants Commission (UGC); All India Council for 
Technical Education (AICTE), NAAC, IGNOU, JNU, DU, IIT Delhi etc under the 
administrative control of the Department of Higher Education.  
 
5. The Committee, while making its observations/recommendations, has mainly relied 
upon the following documents:- 
(i)  Detailed Demands for Grants (2025-26);  
(ii) Annual Report for the year 2023-24; 
(iii) Annual Plan for the year 2025-26; 
(iv) Appropriation Accounts for the year 2023-24; 
(v) Detailed Explanatory Note (Demand-wise) on the Demands for Grants (2025-
26) pertaining to the Department and Organizations/Institutes under its 
administrative control along with a brief synopsis of the Scheme/Item for which 
Demand is being raised;  
(vi) Output Outcome Monitoring Framework (OOMF) 2025-26, relating to all 
Schemes under the Department; 
(vii) National Education Policy, 2020; 
(viii) Working Committee up Report of NITI AAYOG on 'The Three Year Action Agenda',  
(ix) Presentations made by the Secretary, Department of Higher Education, Ministry of 
Education and other Senior Officers of the Department and bodies under the 
administrative control of the Department of Higher Education;
