The detailed of schemes/initiatives implemented by DoYA, is as under: 
2.2. RashtriyaYuva Sashaktikaran Karyakram: 
2.2.1  Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan: Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan (NYKS) is one of the largest 
youth organisations in the world. NYKS has presence in 623 districts of the country through Nehru 
Yuva Kendras (NYKs). The objective of the programme is to develop the personality and leadership 
qualities of the youth and to engage them in nation-building activities.  
2.2.2 The areas of focus of the NYKS activities include literacy and education, health and family 
welfare, sanitation and cleanliness, environment conservation, awareness on social issues, women 
empowerment, rural development, skill development and self-employment, entrepreneurship 
development, civic education, disaster relief and rehabilitation, etc. The youth associated with Nehru 

9 
 
Yuva Kendras are not only socially aware and motivated, but are also inclined towards social 
development work through voluntary efforts. 
2.2.3 In BE 2024-25 Rs 426.00 crores was allocated but in RE 2024-25 the amount was reduced to 
Rs 412.00 crores. The projection of MoF for BE 2025-26 is Rs 556.50 crores and BE 2025-26 
allocation stands at Rs 423.50 crores.The variations of percentage in allocations from BE 2025-26 
over RE 2024-25 stands at 2.8%. BE 2025-26 over projections of MoF stands at -23.9%. While 
variations of percentage in allocations from BE 2025-26 over BE 2024-25 stands at -0.6%.  
2.2.4 The Committee was informed that for BE 2025-26, an additional requirement are proposed 
because of the cited reasons - (i) for payment of Salary of existing 1146 employees, (ii) for payment of 
salary of 674 new recruits staff expected to join in next FY, (iii) for meeting the retirement dues of 
retired employees in FY 2025-26, (iv) for recruitment exercise to be conducted in next FY, (v) for 
core programmes and operations of project management unit. 
2.2.5 Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan, National Youth Corps, National Programme for Youth and 
Adolescent Development (NPYAD), Youth Hostels (YH), National Young Leaders Programme 
(NYLP), International Cooperation, Assistance to Scouting and Guiding Organisations, these seven 
programmes are under the RYSK.   
2.2.6 The Committee observes that the sanctioned strength for Nehru Yuva Kendra 
Sangathan is 2,273, but that the number of positions filled is only 1,184. There are therefore, 
1,089 vacant positions. The Ministry in its response noted that before Covid, three initiatives 
were taken through which District Youth Officers were given employment in NYKS. The 
Committee was informed that these vacancies are no longer filled through the UPSC or the 
Staff Selection Commission but through the Institute of Banking Personnel Selection (IBPS), 
as per the decision of the Governing Board. The Committee recommends that these vacancies 
must be filled at the soonest.  
2.2.7 The Committee notes with concern that of the sanctioned post of 560 District Youth 
Officer, a total of 240 posts are lying vacant, and that the last direct recruitment process was 
carried out in the year FY 2019-20. The NYKS designs its core programmes keeping the 
District as a base unit for conduct of the programme. The Committee was informed that in 
the absence of regular District Youth Officer, additional charge of the said districts has been 
assigned to officials from neighboring Kendras. The fact that the existing DYOs have been 
tasked with running multiple Nehru Yuva Kendras is a constraint on their ability to 
effectively run the programs under this scheme. Therefore, the Committee recommends that 
the Department conduct recruitment to fill all existing vacancies. An additional demand of 
funds may be submitted to the Finance Ministry at RE stage of FY 2025-26.  
2.2.8 The Committee notes that a separate NYKS has not been established in every district of 
the country. It has been created only in 623 districts, while the number of districts in the 
country totals 788 districts. The new districts do not have staff positions sanctioned yet nor a 
Nehru Yuva Kendra.  Therefore, taking a comprehensive view of staff positions, the 
Committee observes that the current sanctioned positions may be insufficient for the 
discharge of the NYKS responsibilities across all districts in the country. Therefore, in 
addition to the filling of vacancies, the number of sanctioned posts in the NYKS may need to 
be enhanced, and funds need to be provided for expansion of the organization in all districts. 
2.2.9 The Committee queried as to why the RE for the FY 2024-25 was not utilized and as to 
why the BE for the FY 2025-26 was reduced when the resources were direly needed. The 
Committee notes that there is an increase in the budget outlay for the current financial year 
and recommends that the Department take all steps to ensure that the same is not repeated. 
 

10 
 
2.2.10 The Committee was informed that the Nehru Yuva Kendras ran at least 42 core 
programmes and 11 special programmes in the last few years. The Committee is concerned 
that the proliferation of programmes and activities dilutes the brand of the NYKS. The 
Committee was informed that each year, the NYKS core programmes are set by the Annual 
Action Plan approved by the Board of Governors. The Committee recommends that the 
NYKS adopt a few flagship programs that are conducted every year without fail, so as to 
provide a focus to the organization and build its brand positioning among youth. Additional 
special programmes may be instituted as per the decision of the Board of Governors.  
2.2.11 The Committee was informed that the NYKS programs are designed to instill a sense of 
civic responsibility and build personality traits that help participants in their academic and 
professional journeys. However, the Committee was informed that there is currently no 
mechanism to track the professional trajectories of NYKS participants beyond their 
association with the NYKS. The Committee believes that tracking the alumni of the programs 
can help inform the Department about the long-term utility of the program, as well as create 
an alumni network that can benefit the existing volunteers. The same provision can be 
extended to NSS volunteers and NYVs as well. The Committee notes that the MY Bharat 
Platform has provided a dedicated profile page for each youth to describe their professional 
interest.  For Experiential Learning Program conducted on the portal, a certificate of 
participation is also reflected on the youth profile page as an incentive to youth to update 
their profiles from time to time.  This facility can be used to track the NYK volunteers, NSS 
volunteers, and NYVs after their association with the Department and its activities ends.  
2.2.12 The Committee noted with satisfaction that more than 2,000 Padyatras were organised 
across the country to commemorate the Constitution Day 2024 celebrating 75 years of Indian 
constitution, in which more than 1.5 lakh youth and others participated where oath of the 
Preamble to the Constitution was integral part of the Padyatra. The theme of these padyatras 
was Humaara Samvidhaan, Humaara Swabhimaan. On the same lines, the Committee 
recommends that all youth programs must begin with oath taking of the Preamble to the 
Constitution, and the recitation of the National Pledge. Similarly, all NYKS building and 
other structures operated by the Department must feature a copy of the Preamble to the 
Indian Constitution to build a culture of Constitutional morality among our youth. 
 
2.2.13 The Committee recommends that the Department should work more closely with the 
District Collectors, the State administration, and elected representatives to involve them in 
programmes being conducted at the district level so that they can leverage their own networks 
to enhance youth participation in the schemes.  
 
2.2.14 The Committee notes the work done by NYKS, NSS, and local Youth Clubs in 
promoting peace and social harmony in Manipur, and in bringing internally Displaced 
Persons into relief camps. The Committee encourages the Department to continue supporting 
these groups in these endeavours and to provide them with capacity building support to 
promote social harmony at the grassroots level.  
2.3 National Youth Corps: 
2.3.1 The Scheme of National Youth Corps (NYC) is being implemented through NYKS. The main 
objectives of the Scheme are – 
i. To set up a group of disciplined and dedicated youth who have the inclination and spirit to 
engage in the task of nation-building; 
ii. To facilitate the realization of inclusive growth (both social and economic); 

11 
 
iii. To act as focal points for dissemination of information, basic knowledge in the community; 
iv. To act as group modulators and peer group educators; and 
v. To act as role models for the younger cohort, especially towards enhancement of public ethics, 
probity and dignity of labour.  
2.3.2 Under the Scheme, youth in the age-group of 18-25 years are engaged as volunteers to serve 
up to a maximum of 2 years in nation-building activities at block level. 
2.3.3 Further, the DoYA submitted that the BE 2024-25 for the National Youth Corps was ₹75 
Crores.However, due to administrative reasons, the target number of NYV volunteers could not be 
deployed resulting in under-utilization of the budget allocation made under the scheme. Thus, the RE 
2024-25 was reduced to ₹ 18.25 Crores. Further, for 2025-26, it has been planned to deploy around 
13,000 NYV volunteers throughout the country for which enhanced allocation of Rs 65.00 crore shall 
be utilised for their training and for payment of monthly honorarium. These volunteers work as a 
bridge between the youth and the field officers of NYKS/MY Bharat and play an active role in the 
implementation of the programs of the Department. As of now, the volunteers are paid an honorarium 
of ₹ 5000/- each on monthly basis. There is no proposal for increasing the honorarium. 
2.3.4 The Committee notes with concern that there is a steady decrease in the RE of the 
National Service Scheme as compared to its BE for the last four financial years – the RE in 
2021-22 was 89.48% of the BE; in 2022-23 it was 87.91%, in 2023-24 it was 72.07% and in 2024-
25 it was 72.05%. The Committee recommends that the Department look into the reasons for 
the same and ensure that the enhanced budget for FY25-26 is utilized fully.  
2.3.5 The Committee notes that the National Youth Volunteers (NYVs) are the key 
implementers of this scheme since they work as a bridge between the youth and the field officers 
of the NYKS and MY Bharat. However, in the FY 2024-25, the Department was not able to 
reach the target number of NYVs and the scheme was implemented only in eight States and 
UTs. This must be avoided in the future.  
2.3.6 The Committee notes that during the EFC meeting for the continuation of RYSK scheme 
for the period from 2021-22 to 2025-26, all the seven schemes of RYSK including NYC were 
deliberated upon. The proposal of the Ministry for enhancing the honorarium of NYVs from Rs. 
5000/- to Rs. 15000/- was also discussed but not agreed to by the EFC. However, the Committee 
recommends that the Department continue to advocate for an increased honorarium of Rs. 
15,000 per month for NYVs. 
2.4  National Programme for Youth and Adolescent Development:  
2.4.1 National Programme for Youth and Adolescent Development (NPYAD) is an “Umbrella 
Scheme” of the Ministry under which financial assistance is provided to Government/ non-
Government organisations for taking up activities for youth and adolescent development. The 
assistance under NPYAD is provided under 5 major components, namely, 
a) Youth Leadership and Personality Development Training 
b) Promotion of National Integration (National Integration Camps, Inter-State Youth Exchange 
Programmes, Youth Festivals, multi-cultural activities, etc.) 
c) Promotion of Adventure; Tenzing Norgay National Adventure Awards 
d) Development and Empowerment of Adolescents (Life Skills Education, Counseling, Career 
Guidance, etc.) 
e) Technical and Resource Development (Research and Studies on Youth issues, 
Documentation, Seminars/ Workshops) 

12 
 
2.4.2 The DoYA has submitted that under the scheme, ₹ 65.00 crores has been allocated for BE 
2025-26. For 2024-25, the BE was ₹ 22.00 crores, the RE was ₹ 45.00 crores, and the expenditure was 
₹ 10.45 crores only. It may be observed that the reason for variation was given as the funds are 
required for the activities:- National Youth Festival, Grant to HMI, JIMWS, NYKS & NGOs for 
adventure/ scheme activities, conducting of Tenzing Norgay National Adventure Award (TNNAA) & 
National Youth Award (NYA) and North East Youth Festival.National Youth Festival (NYF) is 
organized in collaboration with one of the host State/UT. For FY 2024-25, NYF was restructured and 
called Viksit Bharat Young Leaders Dialogue (VBYLD). There was no host state this time and the 
expenses were borne by the department. As such the expenditure for the festival has been increased 
and thus provision for additional funds at RE stage was made for the NPYAD Scheme.

2.6 Youth Hostels 
2.6.1 The Committee was informed that the Youth Hostels are a joint venture of Central and State 
Government. Youth Hostels have been built to promote youth travel within the country by providing 
low cost budget accommodation and facilities to students and youth groups travelling on excursions or 
study tours. The aim of the scheme is to encourage youth travel to enable the youth to know more 
about the diversity of India’s culture and people. At present, 84 Youth Hostels have already been 
constructed across the country and one more Youth Hostel is under construction. The Ministry 
appoints the Managers of Youth Hostels on the recommendations of the respective Hostel 
Management Committee (HMC). The HMCs advertise the vacancy in local newspapers, collect 
applications from candidates, conduct interviews of the eligible candidates, and forward their 
recommendations to this Ministry for approval. The Committee was also informed that several State 
Governments are using the building of the Youth Hostels for activities other than youth hostelling. A 
number of requests for vacating the Youth Hostel premises have been made to the concerned State 
Government by the Department. 
 
2.6.2 Youth Hostel, a component of Rashtriya Yuva Sashaktikaran Karyakaram (RYSK), was 
allocated funds of ₹ 5.00 crores in BE 2025-26 while in RE 2024-25, budget allocated was also ₹ 5.00 
crores. Further, the DoYA informed the Committee that one Youth Hostel is under construction at 
Kota, Rajasthan. The work of construction has been assigned to the CPWD, Ajmer. Funds of ₹ 3.10 
Crore have been allocated as capital outlay in the FY 2024-25 and will be released to CPWD, Ajmer 
as and when demand is raised by them. An amount of ₹ 3.10 crore capital outlay has once again been 
provided for Youth Hostels in the budget of 2025-26. 
2.6.3 The Committee viewed that the scheme is a little faulty.  It gathered that the Central 
Government gives money to the State Government, they respectively share the cost of infrastructure.  
But, thereafter, the Youth Hostels are asked to sustain themselves on the charges that they collect from 
the persons who are staying in it.  This sustenance is not enough. In fact, The Department should also 
look at the maintenance aspect. The Committee espoused that youth hostels for girls is very important. 
If a single penny is not spent for its maintenance, by both the Governments, then this is not right. The 
institutions, thus set up in this mode, are not maintained for many years. The condition there is so bad 
that even if a youth goes there, he does not like to stay there. The Committee observed that Youth 
Hostel Management Committee are headed by District Magistrate/ Collectors if it is in District and by 
the Hon’ble Minister concerned for Youth Affairs if it is in State Capital. Hence it is headed by 
representative of State Government.  
2.6.3a The Department may make endeavour to impress upon the State/UT Govt. to formulate 
a plan for better utilization of these youth hostels. The fund allocation for these components is as 
under:

2.6.4 The Committee notes that the physical maintenance of 84 Youth Hostels will not cost 
much, thus, both the Central and State Government, should make allocations for their annual 
maintenance. The revenue expenditure under the Youth Hostel sub-scheme has two components 
i.e. ‘Honorarium to Managers & Wardens’ and ‘Repair/ Renovation of Youth Hostels’. As per 
the Youth Hostel Manual, the responsibility of the repair, maintenance, and improvement in the 
building of the Youth Hostels is with the State/UT Governments.  For alternations or major 
repairs to the building, if the State Government is unable to make available necessary funds, the 
Directorate of Youth Services & Sports of the State may refer it to Central Department for a 
grant.  The Committee notes that the Department informed the Committee that “some of the 
youth hostels are not in habitable conditions,” an observation which was corroborated by MPs. 
Accordingly, the Committee strongly recommends that funds should be provided by the 
Department for the renovation of youth hostels.  
2.6.5 The Committee was informed that several State Governments are using the buildings of 
the Youth Hostels for activities other than youth hostelling and that the Department has made 
numerous requests for vacation of these premises to the concerned State Government. The 
Committee notes this concern and recommends that the Department continue to take action for 
the same.  
2.6.6 The Committee notes that there are no youth hostels in NCT Delhi – although the 
Committee had specifically recommended it in all capitals. Similarly, the Committee notes that 
previous recommendations made by the Committee for hostels specifically for girl youth have 
not been accepted by the Department. It re-emphasizes the need for the same given the cultural 
sensitivities involved and the concerns around safety of female youth in these hostels.The 
Committee notes that there is acute shortage of youth hostels in the country, particularly in 
educational centres, which hurts the educational prospects of youth from low-income groups, 
girls, SCs, STs, OBCs, and EWS. The Committee, therefore, recommends that additional  
budgetbe made available for the construction of youth hotels in the four metropolitan cities, 
capital cities of each State, and centres of education for boys and girls separately to ensure the 
cheapest boarding facilities for the youth of the country. The Committee recommends that the 
Department seek additional funds from the Ministry of Finance for the same at RE 2025-26 
stage. 
2.6.7 The Committee recommends that the Department work more closely with the State 
Government officials in charge of youth hostels. Accordingly, the Youth Hostel Management 
Committees must have a representative from the State’s Commissioner for Youth affairs and 
Sports.

2.9 NATIONAL SERVICE SCHEME 
2.9.1 National Service Scheme (NSS) has the primary objective of developing the personality and 
character of student youth through voluntary community service. ‘Education through Service’ is the 
purpose of the NSS. The ideological orientation of the NSS is inspired by the ideals of Mahatma 
Gandhi. Very appropriately, the motto of NSS is “NOT ME, BUT YOU”. An NSS volunteer places 
the ‘community’ before ‘self’.  
2.9.2 NSS aims at developing the following qualities/ competencies among the volunteers: 
a) To understand the community in which the NSS volunteers work and to understand 
themselves in relation to their community; 
b) To identify the needs and problems of the community and involve themselves in 
problem-solving exercise; 
c) To develop among themselves a sense of social and civic responsibility; 
d) To utilize their knowledge in finding practical solutions to individual and community 
problems; 
e) To gain skills in mobilizing community participation; 
f) To acquire leadership qualities and democratic values; 
g) To develop capacity to meet emergencies and natural disasters; and  
h) To practice national integration and social harmony. 
2.9.3 NSS attempts to establish meaningful linkages between ‘Campus and Community’, ‘College 
and Village’ and ‘Knowledge and Action’.

2.9.5 The Department submitted that currently, the figure of youth volunteers stands at 39.87 
lakhs.  The NSS has a presence in over 33,000 institutions comprising 700 universities, 20,254 
colleges, 751 +2 councils and 11,761 Sr. Secondary Schools. The NSS provides opportunities to 
youth in Classes XI, XII and at various colleges and university departments to take part in 

22 
 
community service initiatives and programmes. So far, 7.4 crore youth have benefited from this 
programme.  The core programmes of the NSS are literacy, education, health, family welfare and 
nutrition, environment conservation, social service programme, programmes for empowerment of 
women, programmes connected with economic development and rescue and relief during 
calamities.   
2.9.6 The Department informed the Committee on the volunteer participation, the Department 
submitted that in volunteering for road safety programme, over 4,30,000 youths participated.  They 
helped the traffic police by working as traffic Marshalls at choke points.  Then, on 21stJune, 2024, 
there was the International Yoga Divas, that was celebrated pan India, in which over 43,00,000 
youths participated.  There was also the activity, ‘Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam’.  That was celebrated 
from June to August, 2024, in which more than 22,82,000 youths participated. It allows them an 
opportunity to participate in an important activity for the community.  In 2024, last year, the 
Programme, Swachhta Hi Seva, was celebrated in which more than 66,00,000 youths participated. 
The waste was collected. About 1,33,823 villages were covered. In addition, many community 
centres, school buildings, heritage sites, amritsarovars, gardens, parks and religious places were 
also covered. So, it was a very positive activity.  It gives the youth a chance to contribute positively.   
2.9.7 Essentially, The Department submitted that this kind of a platform provides access to 
opportunities to all to transcend the privileged few. It gives equal opportunities to all the youth.  
Experiential Learning Programme is learning by doing. It is a structured Programme.  Minimum 
duration is 15 days. Youths who participate in this are offered a certificate on completion.  Some of 
the ongoing programmes are there to help patients in hospitals, Digital Agriculture Mission and a 
few postal departments. The objective is to foster leadership, build an entrepreneurial team and to 
inculcate organizational skills among youths by engaging them in organizational settings.  Then 
there is a pilot project Seva Se Seekhen.  It was done in four hospitals of Delhi-NCR and PGI, 
Chandigarh.  Given the success of the pilot project, it was scaled up to 400 plus locations in 26 
States.  More than 51,000 patients have been assisted so far.  There are 474 hospitals where it is 
running and there are more than 3,700 volunteers.  
2.9.8 The Committee notes that the vacancies of NSS volunteers are around 50%. Hence, 
there is an urgent need to fill these vacancies especially in colleges and universities. The 
Department should develop an action plan to fill the same and share it with the Committee.  
2.9.9 The Committee notes that various states have taken initiative to reward and recognize 
the contributions of NSS volunteers, but that there is a wide variation in the policy adopted by 
different states. The Committee recommends the Department try to bridge this gap by 
developing and radiating a common framework for the same. In particular, the Committee 
recommends that the Department of Youth Affairs work with the Department of Higher 
Education to ensure that service hours undertaken by NSS volunteers are creditized in the 
Academic Bank of Credits accepted by HEIs.  
2.9.10 The Committee notes the proposal to transform the NSS into the National Service and 
Skill Development Scheme. It recommends that the transition should be expedited. It further 
recommends that the NSS take up communal harmony and drug abstention and de-addiction 
as major thrusts for its activities going forward. Like with the NYKS, the Committee 
recommends that all youth programs must begin with oath taking of the Preamble to the 
Constitution, and the recitation of the National Pledge.

volunteer schemes to track the tangible contributions made by volunteers under this scheme 
and understand how these programs can be improved in future years

OVERVIEW OF THE DEPARTMENT OF SPORTS 3.1 The Ministry of Youth Affairs & Sports was initially set up as the Department of Sports in 1982 at the time of the organization of the IX Asian Games in New Delhi.  Its name was changed to the Department of Youth Affairs & Sports during celebration of the International Youth Year, 1985.  It became a Ministry on 27th May, 2000.  Subsequently, the Ministry has been bifurcated in Department. of Youth Affairs and Department of Sports under two separate Secretaries w.e.f. 30th April,2008.   The specific subjects being dealt with by these two Departments are contained in the Order of the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961. 3.2 Sports promotion is primarily the responsibility of the various National Sports Federations which are autonomous.  The role of the Government is to create the infrastructure and promote capacity building for broad-basing sports as well as for achieving excellence in various competitive events at the national and international levels.  The Department schemes are geared towards achieving these objectives. Vision and Mission 3.3 Sports and games are crucial for holistic human development, serving not just as entertainment and physical exercise, but also fostering a spirit of healthy competition and community bonding. Athletic accomplishments on the global stage have long been a source of national pride.  3.4 The significance of sports for the nation has transcended from merely showcasing excellence on the global stage to playing a multifaceted role in contributing to the holistic growth of the country by promoting healthy lifestyles, driving economic activities, fostering community engagement, and providing opportunities for national pride through international achievements. Recognizing this multidimensional importance in nation-building, the Government of India has implemented several key schemes and initiatives through the Department of Sports, aimed at supporting athletes and stakeholders in reaching their full potential across disciplines. With flagship programs like Khelo India, the National Sports University, and the National Centre for Sports Science and Research, the aim is to develop India's sporting infrastructure and capabilities at par with major nations. While sports garnered attention for decades, it received dedicated push after hosting the 1982 Asian Games, leading to the National Sports Policies of 1984 and 2001 which outlined an organized framework for 

26 
 
development and promotion of sports, with the twin pillars of "Broad-basing" and "Achieving Excellence" reflecting the commitment to fostering a vigorous sporting culture and elite talent. As modern sports have become highly competitive, the use of advanced infrastructure, equipment, and scientific support has transformed the international sporting landscape. Recognizing the growing demands for such state-of-the-art resources, the Government of India has also undertaken several initiatives to assist athletes by providing training, exposure to international competitions, and access to scientific backing and cutting-edge equipment. This comprehensive support aims to equip Indian sportspersons with the tools necessary to excel on the world stage. Proposed National Sports Policy (NSP), 2025: 3.5 In terms of the National Sports Policy, 2001, the Central Government, in conjunction with the State Government, the Olympic Association (IOA) and the National Sports Federation will concertedly pursue the twin objectives of "Broad-basing" of Sports and "Achieving Excellence in Sports at the National and International levels". Sports activities, in which the country has potential strength and competitive advantage, need to be vigorously promoted. Towards this end, Sports and Physical Education would be integrated more effectively with the Education Curriculum. 3.6 While the broad-basing of Sports will, primarily remain a responsibility of the State Governments, the Union Government will actively supplement their efforts in this direction and for taping the latent talent, including in the rural and tribal areas. The Union Government and the Sports Authority of India (SAI), in association with the Indian Olympic Association (IOA) and the National Sports Federations, will focus specific attention on the objective of achieving excellence at the National and International levels. 3.7 Various sports disciplines will be prioritized on the basis of proven potential, popularity and international performance. Particular emphasis will be placed on the development of such priority disciplines and the prioritization reviewed, from time to time. The IOA and the State Governments would also accord higher priority to such disciplines. In planning the development of various disciplines, the genetic and geographical variations within the country would be taken into account so that in areas of potential, in particular disciplines, timely steps may be taken to harness the existing and emerging talent. Centers of excellence will be set up to identify and train outstanding sportspersons including sports academies where young and talented sports persons will be groomed to achieve higher levels of performance in the international sports arena. 3.8 The Department of Sports is in the way of finalizing the National Sports Policy (NSP), 2025. The draft policy was circulated to various stake holders for their comments. The comments received from various stake holders such as various Departments/Ministries of Central Government, various National Sports Federations 

27 
 
and general public have been incorporated. NSP 2025 has been submitted to Cabinet Secretariat for the approval of the Cabinet.  3.9 DEPARTMENT OF SPORTS – ORGANOGRAM:  (a) Sports Authority of India (SAI) (i) 12 Regional Centres (RCs)  24 National Centres of Excellence (NCOEs) and 69 SAI Training Centres (STCs (ii) Academic Centres  Netaji Subhash Institute of Sports (NSNIS), Patiala  Lakshmibai National College of Physical Education (LNCPE), Trivandrum (iii) 5 Stadias (b) National Anti-Doping Agency (NADA) (c) National Dope Testing Laboratory (NDTL) (d) National Sports University (NSU) (e) Lakshmibai National Institute of Physical Education (LNIPE) (i) Main Campus (Gwalior) (ii) Guwahati Campus

5.4  KHELO INDIA

– National Programme for Development of Sports’ or Khelo India Scheme was implemented with 
effect from the Financial Year 2016-17 and was formulated by merging the existing erstwhile 
schemes of Rajiv Gandhi Khel Abhiyan (RGKA), Urban Sports Infrastructure Scheme (USIS), and 
National Sports Talent Search Scheme (NSTSS). Taking from the experience gained in 
implementing the Scheme during the year 2016-17 and on the basis of consultations with major 
stakeholders, especially the State Governments and of inputs received from them, the Khelo India

2025-26 with outlay of Rs. 3790.50 cr. The basic objectives, vision and structure of the extant 
Khelo India Scheme have been retained. However, on the basis of the experience of this Ministry 
while implementing the extant Scheme as well as the evaluation/recommendations of the 3rd Party

stated that the National Sports University has been set up in the country to promote sports education 

41 
 
in the areas of sports sciences, sports technology, sports management and sports coaching besides 
functioning as the national training centre for select sports disciplines by adopting best international 
practices, thereby promoting sporting excellence in the country.  The Committee observed that in 
the past three years the scheme has consistently failed to utilize the approved budget. For instance 
in FY 23, budget utilization was only 60%. For FY24, it was 87.2%.The utilization of funds under 
the Khelo India Scheme is dependent upon the receipt of Utilization Certificates against the projects 
sanctioned. Since, ‘sports’ is a State subject; the State is to be the driving force in this matter. 
However, the Department has pursued an untiring follow-up policy. To complete the projects in 
time, of constant monitoring of the utilization certificates and completion certificates. Since, the 
projects of the scheme are majorly in completion phase, rapid consumption of the budget is 
foreseen during the leftover scheme cycle. Additionally, the switch from CNA to TSA and the 
remapping of the States, their training, education and handholding etc. was a time-consuming 
process. In spite of the above, as on date, the Department has been able to release Rs. 684.00 crore 
out of the BE of Rs.900 crore in current FY due to taking up of the remapping exercise on mission 
mode.  
5.4.9 The Committee notes that funds are allocated Scheme-wise and not State-wise in this 
Ministry. The Khelo India Scheme is a demand-driven scheme. The proposals received from 
the State/UT Governments and other eligible entities are considered for financial support, 
subject to their completeness, technical feasibility and availability of funds under the Scheme 
in line with the twin objectives of mass participation and promotion of excellence in sports to 
infuse sports culture in the country. Further the Detailed Project Reports (DPRs) received 
from the States are meticulously studied and the States are guided in respect of the 
shortcoming.  Hence, the Committee recommends that the Department should constantly 
monitor the utilization certificates and completion certificates. The Committee noted that so 
far, a total of 321 projects worth Rs 3080 Crores have been sanctioned under Khelo India 
Scheme, of which over 200 are complete.  
5.4.10 The Committee notes that budget utilization in Khelo India needs to be improved and 
that it was only ~60% in FY23 and 87.2% in FY24. The Committee recommends the 
Department work more closely with State Governments to achieve the same. Further, specific 
provisions must be made to support the promotion and development of Hockey. 
5.4.11 The Committee noted that the development of sports in the Northeast must be given 
special attention and focus. Due to the higher costs faced in this region, additional funds 
should be made available to NCOEs in this region, in collaboration with Ministry for DoNER 
and other agencies. 
5.4.12 The Committee noted that the Khelo India Games being organized by the Department 
of Sports are enabling talented young sportspersons to get experience of international 
standard events. A total of 16 editions of these Games have been hosted so far, where more 
than 50,000 athletes have participated, transforming the sports competition landscape in 
India. The Committee recommends that the Khelo India Games be held annually so as to 
ensure maximum participation of sportspersons in these games. The Committee further 
recommends that the name and eligibility of the Khelo India University games may be shifted 
solely to the age of the participant, to ensure a level playing field for all sportspersons who 
have not be enrolled in HEIs.  

42 
 
5.4.13 The Committee recommends that the disbursement of funds under Khelo India be 
directed towards investment in sportspersons, coaching, nutrition and health support, and 
investments in field-of-play over large-scale infrastructure projects like stadiums.

5.8 FIT INDIA 
5.8.1 Fit India Movement is a nation-wide movement in India to encourage people to remain 
healthy and fit by including physical activities and sports in their daily lives. The movement was 
launched by Prime Minister of India Narendra Modi at Indira Gandhi Stadium in New Delhi on 29 
August 2019 (National Sports Day). Fit India was founded by Shri Suparno Satpathy in 1993.  As 
per the union directive, states and union territories can request funds to procure listed fitness items 
for children studying in government schools. The equipment purchased from the grants are to be 
maintained in workable condition by the authorities concerned. It is also mandated to keep a record 
of working, reparable and damaged beyond repair equipment. The schools are also allowed to 
include their traditional and regional games.

5.10 NATIONAL ANTI-DOPING AGENCY 
5.10.1   The National Anti-Doping Agency (NADA) is the apex body in India responsible for 
promoting, coordinating and monitoring the doping control program in sports. Its mandate is to 
ensure that all sports activities in the country are free from doping practices, aligning with the 
international code established by the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA). 
5.10.2  The primary functions of NADA are as follows: 
i. Doping Control: Conduct in-competition and out-of-competition testing of athletes. Collect 
and analyze samples in accredited laboratories. 
ii. Results Management: Handle the process of identifying violations and determining 
sanctions. Ensure compliance with international standards for testing and results. 
iii. Anti-Doping Education Awareness: Organize workshops, seminars, and campaigns to 
spread awareness about anti-doping rules and the dangers of performance-enhancing drugs. 
Disseminate educational materials to athletes, coaches, and support staff. 
iv. Regulation and Enforcement: Formulate and implement anti-doping rules and regulations in 
India. Monitor compliance with anti-doping code of WADA. 
 
5.10.3  The key challenges faced by NADA are as follows - 
the National Anti-Doping Agency (NADA) faces several challenges in its efforts to maintain 
doping-free environment in sports. These challenges arise from various factors, including the 
evolving nature of doping practices. Many athletes, especially at the grassroots level, are unaware 
of banned substances and inadvertent doping risks through contaminated supplements. Every efforts 
are being made to reach the athletes for anti-doping education awareness at the grass root level i.e 
school/college etc.  
5.10.4  The Committee was informed that NADA has taken the following measures to 
ensure the accuracy and integrity of its testing procedures.These measures are designed to adhere to 
international standards and guidelines set by the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA). The Details 
are as under: 
i. Compliance with WADA Code. 
ii. Doping Control Officers (DCOs) and chaperones are thoroughly trained and certified 
to handle sample collection, ensuring standardized and professional procedure 
iii. A strict chain of custody is maintained to prevent tampering or mismanagement of 
samples 
iv. Samples are collected under standardized conditions, with athletes observed by 
trained personnel to prevent sample adulteration or substitution. 
v. Sample collection kits are tamper-proof and sealed in the athlete's presence. 
vi. Athletes are educated about the testing process to ensure they understand their rights, 
responsibilities, and the importance of compliance. 
5.10.5  By implementing above measures, NADA strives to ensure that its testing procedures are 
accurate, fair, thereby upholding the integrity of sports and protecting clean athletes. 
5.10.6  The National Anti-Doping Agency (NADA) plays a crucial role in educating athletes, 
coaches, and support staff about anti-doping rules to promote fair play and compliance. The details 
of such measures are as under:  
i. NADA conducts workshops, seminars, and training programs across various regions 
and sports disciplines. These sessions are tailored for athletes, coaches, medical staff, 
and other support personnel. 

52 
 
ii. NADA runs campaigns to promote a doping-free culture, emphasizing the importance 
of ethical sportsmanship. 
iii. NADA offers e-learning modules and resources accessible through its official website. 
iv. NADA encourages the use of the Anti-Doping Education and Learning (ADEL) 
platform for global anti-doping education. 
v. NADA publishes materials such as the Anti-Doping Rulebook, TUE guidelines, and 
supplement advisories. 
vi. These materials are often translated into regional languages to ensure broader reach. 
vii. NADA disseminates the updated WADA Prohibited List annually. 
viii. Athletes are educated about the risks of contaminated or unverified supplements and 
encouraged to consult experts before use. 
ix. Athletes and medical staff are informed about the process of applying for TUEs for 
medications containing prohibited substances through workshops. 
x. NADA partners with national sports federations, state associations, and educational 
institutions to organize joint awareness initiatives. 
xi. NADA leverages social media platforms to disseminate information quickly and 
effectively. 
5.10.7  The National Anti-Doping Agency (NADA) collaborates with other anti-doping agencies 
and international organizations to strengthen its efforts in ensuring fair play and clean sports. These 
collaborations allow NADA to align with global standards, share resources, and combat doping 
effectively.  The initiative taken in this regard, are as under: 
(i) Partnership with the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) 
(ii) NADA through regional coordination works with RADOs in South Asia to harmonize anti-
doping efforts and share expertise. 
(iii) NADA participates in international awareness campaigns like Play True Day, promoting 
clean sports globally. 
5.10.8  NADA coordinates with WADA and other agencies to align its TUE processes with 
global standards, ensuring fairness in granting exemptions. As a member, NADA benefits from 
shared best practices, policies, and anti-doping strategies among NADOs worldwide. NADA’s staff 
and Doping Control Officers (DCOs) receive training from WADA and other NADOs on advanced 
testing and investigation techniques. 
5.10.9   The increase in Anti-Doping Rule Violations (ADRVs) from 123 in 2022 to 249 in 
2024 is primarily attributed to the expansion of the testing programme and the result is as under: 
 2022: 4,260 tests conducted → 123 violations (2.88% violation rate) 
 2024: 7,466 tests conducted → 249 violations (3.33% violation rate) 
5.10.10  The reason for increase in cases of anti doping rules violations can be attributed to 
the followings:  
(i) The number of tests increased by 75% (from 4,260 to 7,466) in two years. 
(ii) Continued expansion of dope testing is key to maintaining clean sport for fair play. 
(iii) Use of advanced analytical techniques and targeted testing has led to higher detection 
rates.

invariably impacts the performance of Department and its organizations. These vacancies have 
increased the workload on the existing staff and in order to deal with the shortage of staff 
contractual staffs have been engaged.

5.11.9  The Committee was briefed that the Manipur crisis that began on May 3, 2023, led to 
significant disruptions across multiple sectors, with the State Government implementing frequent 
curfews to maintain law and order. The outbreak of violence in Manipur, including curfews and 
highway blockades, temporarily disrupted the construction of the National Sports University's 
permanent campus, leading to delays. However, from April 2024, construction had resumed without 
further interruptions.  Some students were temporarily relocated to LNIPE, Gwalior and LNIPE, 
Guwahati to ensure continuation of their academic programs, and examinations were also 
conducted for them at these locations. 
5.11.10 Stating about the impact of the law and order situation, The Department informed 
that the situation created numerous operational challenges, including intermittent suspension of 
mobile internet and broadband services, which hampered essential office functions like e-office 
systems, email communications, and attendance tracking. The crisis particularly impacted the sports 
sector, with athletes facing difficulties in booking air tickets for competitions and those without 
flight entitlements being forced to travel by air due to security concerns, resulting in substantial 
financial burden. The conflict caused severe logistical issues, including delayed delivery of sports 
equipment due to highway blockades, while essential commodity prices surged dramatically. The 
situation necessitated the temporary transfer of some staff members to other centers. However, 
these temporary relocation did not affect the functioning of the centre. The crisis led to several 
athletes withdrawing from NCOE Imphal, including participants from various sports such as 
football, judo, hockey, fencing, and weightlifting. Additionally, multiple staff members and athletes 
from SAI STC IMPHAL were temporarily displaced by the conflict, with some seeking shelter in 
relief camps, including MTS staff and athletes from wrestling, boxing, sepaktakraw, and 
gymnastics disciplines, particularly affecting those from areas like Sugnu, Pallel, Moreh, and 
Kangpokpi.

that the Budget Estimate for 2024-25 was kept at Rs. 91.90 crore in view of the uncertainty around

construction work was carried out at reasonably good pace, the R.E was increased to Rs. 189.09 
crore to meet the fund requirement for the construction of NSU new campus. The assigned budget 
under the creation of capital head for the current F.Y . has already been fully utilized for the

5.12  PENSION TO MERITORIOUS SPORTS PERSONS 
5.12.1  The Committee notes that the Department has provisioned for post-retirement support 
for ex-sportspersons who have brought laurels to the country, and that over 850 
sportspersons have been awarded lifelong pension ranging up to Rs. 20,000/- per month. The 
Committee observes that the career of sports persons and their pensions should be made 
lucrative so that the required talent is attracted and retained properly. Accordingly, the 
Committee recommends that the pension due to meritorious sportspersons be not less than 
the pension accorded to a retired Class 1 Officer. 
5.13  TARGET OLYMPIC PODIUM SCHEME 
5.13.1   The Committee evinced interest in the planning and strategy that is being worked out 
on to ensure spectacular performance of sportspersons in US Olympics, 2028 and Australia 
Olympics 2032.  The Committee understood that under the Target Olympic Podium Scheme, two 
types of athletes get continuous support. The two Groups are - Development Group and Core 
Group. Development Group consists of athletes who are younger and who are going ahead for the 
next Olympic cycle. The Development Group Scheme is devised in such a way that the athletes 
keep on training and growing through the time and reach their peak when they reach the Olympics. 
Once a kid qualifies for the Development Group of top athletes, it is not necessary that he or she 
will continue forever. They are very strictly monitored by experts. The parameters are at par with 
international format of training. The process is not fixed. It is quite a challenge for an athlete to 
continue in the scheme and it is considered very prestigious. 
5.14  PANDIT DEENDAYAL UPADHYAY NATIONAL WELFARE FUND FOR 
SPORTSPERSONS: 
5.14.1   The Committee was informed that the aim of the Pandit Deendayal Upadhyay 
National Welfare Fund for Sportspersons is to provide suitable assistance to the meritorious and 
outstanding sportspersons of yesteryear who had brought glory to the country in international field 
who are now living in indigent circumstances. 
The key objectives of the scheme are as follows: 
1. To provide suitable assistance to sportspersons injured during the period of their training for 
competitions and also during the competitions, depending on the nature of the injury. 
2. To provide suitable assistance to sportspersons for medical treatment. 
3. To provide suitable assistance to promote welfare of sportspersons generally in order to 
alleviate distress among them and their dependents in indigent circumstances. 
4. To provide assistance to sportspersons living in indigent circumstances for training, 
procurement for sports equipment, participation in national and international sports events 
etc.

5.16.1   The Committee notes that the National Games are typically organized by the

different states. The Committee recommends the Department try to bridge this gap by 
developing and radiating a common framework for the same. In particular, the 
Committee recommends that the Department of Youth Affairs work with the Department 
of Higher Education to ensure that service hours undertaken by NSS volunteers are 
creditized in the Academic Bank of Credits accepted by HEIs.  
(Para 2.9.9) 
28. The Committee notes the proposal to transform the NSS into the National Service and 
Skill Development Scheme. It recommends that the transition should be expedited. It 
further recommends that the NSS take up communal harmony and drug abstention and 
de-addiction as major thrusts for its activities going forward. Like with the NYKS, the 
Committee recommends that all youth programs must begin with oath taking of the 
Preamble to the Constitution, and the recitation of the National Pledge. 
(Para 2.9.10) 
29. The Committee recommends that there should be a regular impact assessment of 
volunteer schemes to track the tangible contributions made by volunteers under this 
scheme and understand how these programs can be improved in future years 
(Para 2.9.11) 
30. The Committee observed that for the FY 2024-25 the utilization of funds as on 31.01.25 is 
just Rs. 16 Crores while the RE for the year was Rs. 23.50 crores.  This is a notable under 
utilisation of funds.  However, the reason quoted while seeking the funds for BE 2025-26 
are disbursement of salaries and recruitment of Teaching and non-teaching staff. The 
Committee notes that the RGNIYD has been entrusted with the responsibility for training, 
documentation, research and evaluation and extension for all youth related activities in 
the country.  The Institute should be more pro-active in its utilisation of funds to deliver 
on its mission.  
(Para 2.10.14) 
31. The Committee was informed that all 5 positions for Professor in RGNIYD are currently 
vacant. The Committee was further informed that previous attempts to fill these positions 
were unsuccessful since no suitable applications were received. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry should look into the reasons for the same and take suitable 
corrective action if required, including possibly revisiting existing compensation, and 
working more closely with Universities for a wider dissemination of job advertisements. 
(Para 2.10.15) 
32. The Committee appreciates the Schemes which provide incentives and special cash awards 
to the sportspersons in recognition of their talents and the laurels they bought to the 
country, including the National Sports Awards, Cash Incentives, post-retirement pension 
etc.  The Govt. of India also provides a quota to sportspersons in jobs (upto 5%). Besides 
this, for Welfare, scheme for financial assistance to sportspersons with poor financial 

66 
 
condition is also operative.  The Committee however recommends that more be done to 
recognize our sportspersons. The prize money sportspersons win in prestigious 
competitions may be declared tax-exempt. 
(Para 5.1.5) 
33. The Committee notes that the Department of Sports is making an effort to provide 
financial assistance not only at the institutional level but also at the individual level.  It 
appreciated the efforts that the investments are not in all category of events / sports for 
sending the teams abroad for training, participating in international events, conducting 
international events in India, national championship events and for procuring sports 
equipment. Financial assistance is also extended through SAI for organizing coaching 
camps, for preparing national teams and for engaging the services of foreign coaches but 
also to provide comprehensive support to athletes with disabilities, covering aspects like 
training, competition exposure, medical support, travel, and financial assistance to ensure 
that India’s athletes are well-prepared for major events like the Paralympics Games, 
World Championships, and other international competitions.  The Committee 
recommends that the Department continue its initiatives and provide further resources to 
athletes and institutions under this scheme. 
(Para 5.3.10) 
34. The Committee recommends that the Department should integrate their strategy for 
talent hunt in all the games and sports with the National Sports Policy and that it should 
be synergized with the games at the school, district, state and national level. It should be 
continuous and ongoing process on yearly basis at all levels, so that sports talent is 
adequately identified and recognized. The Committee notes that it is heartening that SAI 
has deputed High Performance Analyst (HPA) Nutritionist at each NCOE to take care of 
the dieting and nutrition requirement of athletes. However, itrecommended that the 
Department give additional focus to the nutritional components of sports persons training 
in the SAI Training Centers (STCs), Extension Centers of STCs, and National Sports 
Talent Contest centers as well. The Committee recommended that places like Haryana, 
Manipur, Punjab, etc. which are famous for particular sports, need to be invested in to 
further develop the sports ecosystem in these states.  
(Para 5.3.11) 
35. The Committee recommends that education and sports need to be synchronized.  Special 
schools need to be established to promote such talents without compromising on school / 
college education.  The Committee noted that successful examples of sports education in 
foreign countries should be studied for adaptation in India as well.  Sport integrated 
learning, as envisioned in the NEP, should be promoted.  The collaboration of SAI, private 
players, the Ministry of Education, and State Governments should be materialized 
through a policy and at the ground level a sports-school curricula should be evolved.  The 
National Code for Good Governance in Sports should be paradigm for formulating the 
above policy, including CSR funds from some international brands and curricula.  This 
would bring about transparency and accountability in this field. 
(Para 5.3.12)  
36. The Committee noted that while the budget of Department of Sports has increased 
substantially in the last ten years, there is a need to further augment the financial 
resources for sports.  The Committee recommends that the Department attempt to 
maximize utilization of the budget to seek greater allocations in the coming years.  

67 
 
(Para 5.3.13) 
37. The Committee recommends that young sportspersons should be supported in their 
academic journeys so as to not have to be forced to choose between the two. Accordingly, 
the Committee recommends that all NCOEs and SAI regional centers establish residential 
sports schools with curriculum and school structure developed to specifically support 
sportspersons. 
(Para 5.3.14) 
38. The Committee notes that funds are allocated Scheme-wise and not State-wise in this 
Ministry. The Khelo India Scheme is a demand-driven scheme. The proposals received 
from the State/UT Governments and other eligible entities are considered for financial 
support, subject to their completeness, technical feasibility and availability of funds under 
the Scheme in line with the twin objectives of mass participation and promotion of 
excellence in sports to infuse sports culture in the country. Further the Detailed Project 
Reports (DPRs) received from the States are meticulously studied and the States are 
guided in respect of the shortcoming.  Hence, the Committee recommends that the 
Department should constantly monitor the utilization certificates and completion 
certificates. The Committee noted that so far, a total of 321 projects worth Rs 3080 Crores 
have been sanctioned under Khelo India Scheme, of which over 200 are complete.  
(Para 5.4.9) 
39. The Committee notes that budget utilization in Khelo India needs to be improved and that 
it was only ~60% in FY23 and 87.2% in FY24. The Committee recommends the 
Department work more closely with State Governments to achieve the same. Further, 
specific provisions must be made to support the promotion and development of Hockey. 
(Para 5.4.10) 
40. The Committee noted that the development of sports in the Northeast must be given 
special attention and focus. Due to the higher costs faced in this region, additional funds 
should be made available to NCOEs in this region, in collaboration with Ministry for 
DoNER and other agencies. 
(Para 5.4.11) 
41. The Committee noted that the Khelo India Games being organized by theDepartment of 
Sports are enabling talented young sportspersons to get experience of international 
standard events. A total of 16 editions of these Games have been hosted so far, where more 
than 50,000 athletes have participated, transforming the sports competition landscape in 
India. The Committee recommends that the Khelo India Games be held annually so as to 
ensure maximum participation of sportspersons in these games. The Committee further 
recommends that the name and eligibility of the Khelo India University games may be 
shifted solely to the age of the participant, to ensure a level playing field for all 
sportspersons who any not be enrolled in HEIs.  
(Para 5.4.12) 
42. The Committee recommends that the disbursement of funds under Khelo India be 
directed towards investment in sportspersons, coaching, nutrition and health support, and 
investments in field-of-play over large-scale infrastructure projects like stadiums. 
(Para 5.4.13) 
43. The Committee understood that enhanced infrastructure for J&K is provided to create 
better prospects for sportspersons. The Committee recommends that in J&K, the 

68 
 
improvement of sports infrastructure and the regular happening of sports events in 
Jammu and Kashmir has made it an emerging hub of sports. Be it cricket, martial arts, 
volleyball, athletics and other sports, regular competitions are being organised in the 
Union Territory under the ‘Khelo India’ programme. This has encouraged many players 
to qualify for national and international sports events. Hence, the organization of Sports 
events and activities is being promoted as a economic and cultural activity also.  
(Para 5.5.2) 
44. After going through the financial data submitted by the Ministry, the Committee observed 
that under the scheme of SAI there is an increase in need for funds due to establishment 
expenditure and to balance out to the expenditure, the amount was adjusted from the 
internal revenue. It recommends that the funds allocated should be expended only within 
its limits. The Committee hopes that proper procedure followed for adjusting the amount 
within the allocated budget of the Ministry. It was surprised to learn that in spite of SAIs’ 
demand for rising expenditure, only Rs. 830.00 crores was allocated in the BE 2025-26. 
The Committee would like to direct the Department of Sports to justify its expenditure vis-
à-vis BE 2025-26. 
(Para 5.6.17) 
45. The Committee observed from the data given above, that the recruitment situation in SAI 
is really needs attention. The staff position in Administrative cadre, Rajbhasha, Engineers 
& Sports Science (regular) Group A and B, Coaching Cadre, contractual personnel need 
to be filled up as urgently as possible. The Committee notes that such vacancies inevitably 
compromise the functioning of the institution.  
(Para 5.6.18) 
46. The Committee notes that another major issue that really hurts young sportspersons is 
that of over-age children competing in lower age groups. The Committee recommends that 
the Department consider solutions to this issue.  
(Para 5.6.19) 
47. The Committee recommended that all SAI regional centers must have adequate hostel 
capacity to provide residential facilities for all sportspersons. The Department is 
recommended to provide funds for the same. 
(Para 5.6.20) 
48. The Committee was informed that “As per the Recruitment Rules for the Coaching 
Cadre, a total of 1,524 posts have been sanctioned across all positions within the Coaching 
Cadre, including HPC, Coach, Senior Coach, Assistant Coach, and Chief Coach. Out of 
these 1,524 sanctioned posts, 685 are designated for contractual or deputation 
engagement. However, against these 685 posts, 307 coaches were working in the FY2024.” 
The Committee recommends that this trend of contractualising coaching positions must be 
halted.  
(Para 5.6.21) 
49. The Committee notes that the current sports talent scouting infrastructure for the country 
includes the 67 STCs (SAI Training Centers), 26 STC Extension Centers, and 68 NSTC 
(National Sports Talent Contest) centers across the country. The Committee recommends 
that this infrastructure be expanded over time with the goal of at least one talent scouting 
center in each district of the country, with the goal of scouting for sports talent between 
the age of 8 years and 14 years. The talent so scouted should be supported through 

69 
 
enrolment in the NCOEs, where the amenities extended to them should be expanded to 
eventually provide sports training cum residential facilities cum schooling. The 
sportspersons at NCOEs should have the facility for education cum sports training, along 
with the best of the coaching facilities, nutrition support, sports medicine, and mental 
counselling as part of the training program. The screening should be dynamic, and 
sportspersons must be held to high standards to retain their spot in the NCOEs. 
(Para 5.6.22) 
50. The Committee notes that a number of excellent sports persons are left out in villages and 
other remote areas who can excel in sports because they don't have adequate resources to 
pursue their games. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Department of Sports 
and SAI to conduct rallies along the lines of recruitment rallies of Army to identify such 
sportspersons in their early ages and to groom them with adequate training and financial 
aid. This will help the country to excel other countries in field of sports. 
(Para 5.6.23) 
51. The Committee recommends that the increase in allocation of funds should be spent on 
strengthening the organization by appointing new manpower in all the categories of posts 
like Groups A, B and C and in providing proper representation of all classes of the society.  
(Para 5.7.8) 
51. The Committee notes the numerous programs undertaken through the Fit India 
Movement, as part of Khelo India. The Committee also notes that the ASMITA 
initiative launched under the Khelo India scheme has made an impact in promoting 
women participation in sports across India. The Committee appreciates the initiative 
which covers 20 disciplines now and recommends that the Department further enhance 
the initiative.  The Committee recommends that the Department continue to focus its 
efforts on inclusion, i.e., organize programs for women, persons with disabilities, and 
other underrepresented groups.  
(Para 5.8.2) 
52. The Committee notes that the Department of Sports has prioritized promotion of para-
sports in all spheres through cash incentives, National Sports Awards, dedicated 
training facilities, and support under TOPS scheme. This has resulted in historic wins 
in international events, including 29 medals in the Paris 2024 Paralympics. The 
Committee appreciates the same.  
(Para 5.8.3) 
53. The Committee notes that India ranks second in doping in the world, which is an 
unfortunate development. However, the Committee appreciates that the crucial role 
played by NADA in guiding and regulating sportspersons to ensure fair play, integrity 
and adherence to anti-doping rules. The Committee notes that the shortage of staff in 
the Department of Sports and the NADA may impact its performance.  Therefore, the 
Committee recommends that the vacant positions in all categories of posts should 
immediately be filled in. 
(Para 5.10.18) 
54. The Committee notes and appreciates that the Department and NADA have 
successfully expanded the scale of dope testing by 75% in recent years, from 4,260 tests 
in 2022 to 7.466 tests in 2024 
(Para 5.10.19)  

70 
 
55. The Committee noted that the National Sports University offers a Masters in Physical 
Education course for the duration of two years, with the capacity of thirty seats. There 
is also a Bachelors in Physical Education with fifty seats, and a Master of Science in 
Sports & Coaching course with twenty seats. The Committee recommends that the 
number of seats available under these programs be increased. The Committee also 
recommends that the University be accompanied by a sports school to provide 
educational and residential facilities to sportspersons below the age of 18 years. 
Further, the Committee appreciates the progress in the completion of building NSU’s 
permanent campus in spite of the current disturbances in the state of Manipur. 
(Para 5.11.13) 
56.  The Committee notes that the National Sports University in Manipur is the only 
institution of its kind in the country and was established by an Act of Parliament in 2018. 
It has been running from a temporary facility at Khuman Lampak in Imphal while 
construction activities for the permanent campus at Koutruk are ongoing. The Committee 
notes that the University does not currently have a regular Vice-Chancellor or the 
required faculty. The Committee recommends that the construction of the campus be 
expedited, and that a permanent, full-time Vice Chancellor be appointed so that the 
recruitment of required faculty members may also occur. 
(Para 5.11.14) 
57. The Committee notes that the Department has provisioned for post-retirement support for 
ex-sportspersons who have brought laurels to the country, and that over 850 sportspersons 
have been awarded lifelong pension ranging up to Rs. 20,000/- per month. The Committee 
observes that the career of sports persons and their pensions should be made lucrative so 
that the required talent is attracted and retained properly. Accordingly, the Committee 
recommends that the pension due to meritorious sportspersons be not less than the 
pension accorded to a retired Class 1 Officer. 
(Para 5.12.1) 
58. The Committee recommends that the Department take proactive steps to train high 
quality coaches within the country. Furthermore, the Committee recommends that the 
Department institute a protocol that medical professionals should compulsorily 
accompany sports persons in all Games overseas. 
(Para 5.15.1) 
59. The Committee notes that the National Games are typically organized by the Indian 
Olympic Association (IOA) biennially, but that they weren’t organized between 2015 
and 2022, partly due to the COVID-19 pandemic. The Committee recommends that 
the Department work more closely with the Indian Olympic Association to ensure that 
the same is not repeated in the future. The Committee also recommends that the 
Department consider supporting the IOA in organizing the National Games annually. 
The Department may assist the IOA with identifying cities with the requisite sporting 
infrastructure and host the games there so as to avoid having to incur high expenses on 
capital expansion. 
(Para 5.16.1)

CHAPTER-I

Recommendation  
1. The Committee has observed the contamination of arsenic, fluoride and the presence of other 
heavy metals in ground and drinking water across multiple states. This contamination is contributing to 
severe health issues such as cancer, skin diseases, cardiovascular disease, and diabetes among the 
inhabitants in affected regions and States. Additionally, the Committee notes that substantial research 
dedicated to eradicating arsenic, fluoride, and other heavy metals from ground and drinking water in these 
affected areas is urgently needed to address the issue. Taking note of the magnitude of the issue, the 
Committee strongly recommends that the Department of Science and Technology, Department of Health 
Research, and Department of Higher Education, including various esteemed institutions like IITs should 
prioritize and fund comprehensive research initiatives aimed at eliminating arsenic, fluoride, and other 
heavy metals detrimental to health from ground and drinking water within the affected regions and states 
upon a mapping of such territories. This proactive step will not only address the immediate health hazards 
but also pave the way for sustainable, innovative solutions towards effective waste water management 
and saline water treatment practices. 
(Para 6.4 of the 358th Report of the Committee)

Enablers' as parameters for excellence.  The guidelines provide guidance to HEIs to achieve excellence in 
their identified areas. Further, these lay down a framework for steering the HEIs towards self-
sustainability.

enriches the country's heritage but also offers viable solutions to contemporary challenges in healthcare, 
agriculture, and sustainability and this holistic approach towards development is imperative for India's 
progress and cultural preservation. In view of this, the Committee recommends prioritizing research in 
India's traditional knowledge systems due to their immense significance on multiple fronts such as Vedic 
mathematics, heritage preservation as it plays a pivotal role in preserving and documenting the ancient 
wisdom and practices inherent in traditional knowledge systems, validating the efficacy of traditional 
medical systems like Ayurveda and Yoga, sustainable practices in respect of agricultural methods, 
ecological wisdom, and natural resource management.

To expand the innovation and incubation ecosystem in the country for the translation of

The ICAR is recommending soil test based balanced and integrated nutrient management through 
conjunctive use of both inorganic and organic sources (manure, bio-fertilizers etc.) of plant nutrients to

groundwater.  In addition, split application and placement of fertilizers, use of slow releasing N-fertilizers 
and nitrification inhibitors, growing leguminous crops and use of Resource Conservation Technologies 
(RCTs) are also advocated.  However, imbalanced use of chemical fertilizers coupled with low addition 
of organic matter over years may cause multi-nutrient deficiencies vis-à-vis decline in soil health. 
Long term studies conducted by ICAR indicated that bio fertilizers can improve crop yields by 10-
25% and supplement costly chemical fertilizers (N, P) by nearly 20-25% in most of the cases when used 
along with chemical fertilizers. When biofertilizers are applied along with compost @ 5t/ha or 
vermicompost @ 2 tonne/ha, fertilizer saving is almost 50%.  Further, ICAR has developed improved and

approach through formulation of a blueprint to bolster the research scenario in India and the following 
points be examined in light of current policies while developing the proposed blueprint:

recognizing research contributions, developing schemes that reward quality publications, patents, and 
impactful research outcomes.

among departments and institutions and establishing more interdisciplinary research centers to tackle 
complex challenges requiring diverse expertise.

encourage joint research projects, student exchange programs, and access to international funding 
opportunities.

standards.

Recommendation  
1. The Committee recommends that the Department of Higher Education, UGC, AICTE and 
Department of Science and Technology must take a proactive stance in identifying key national priorities, 
emerging frontiers, and strategic research areas and imperatively allocate substantial funding to these 
crucial research projects. Moreover, the Committee emphasizes the need for adequate funding towards 
research endeavors aimed at identifying scientific and practical solutions for addressing societal, 
developmental, financial, and techno-economic challenges, aligning with the objectives outlined in the 
Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF). The Committee is of the view that this strategic

Action Taken 
Department of Higher Education informed that NEP 2020 envisages the promotion of quality 
research within the Higher Education System. Research and innovation are essential aspects of enhancing 
quality education in Higher Education Institutions. 
The progress of India as a nation depends on its ability to foster innovation, research, and 
development across various fields. One crucial component of this is the support and encouragement of 
individuals pursuing Ph.D.  Doctoral research is the most significant catalyst for innovations and to 
accelerate the overall development of a country. Strengthening of innovation infrastructure is one of the 
priorities of nations to compete for a knowledge-driven market. India having the largest young population 
in the world has the highest prospect of establishing herself as a leading country in the knowledge 
division market, provided there is continuous growth in the magnitude of providing higher education of 
high standards.

establishment of Research and Development Cell (RDC) in universities and colleges with a vision: -

● To encourage collaboration across industry, government, community- based organizations, and 
agencies at the local, national, and international levels.  
● To facilitate greater access to research through mobilization of resources and funding.

(HEIs) will enable the attainment of targets of Atma-Nirbhar Bharat and is expected to play a pivotal role 
in catalysing the multidisciplinary/ trans-disciplinary and translational research culture mandated in NEP 
2020.

and symposia.

5. The Committee notes that substantial physical infrastructure, encompassing laboratories, 
computational resources, and other facilities, coupled with robust institutional and administrative support, 
are indispensable for advancing science and engineering research. The operational expenses incurred in 
maintaining these essential facilities and cutting-edge research equipment are considerable. Internationally 
renowned universities cover these costs, including infrastructure development and maintenance, through 
overheads or indirect costs on research grants. The Committee, therefore, stresses that it is imperative by 
the concerned Ministries/ Departments to reconsider the overheads provided on public-funded research 
projects as the current rate falls significantly short of meeting the actual operational expenses which 
impedes the progress and affordability of research initiatives. In light of this, the Committee strongly 
recommends that funding agencies for scientific research, such as the Department of Science and 
Technology, Department of Biotechnology, Department of Higher Education, etc. should allocate 
additional funds for the development and maintenance of physical infrastructure, including laboratories, 
computational resources, equipment and machineries in particular and other facilities, for all publicly 
funded research projects in various scientific disciplines. This supplementary allocation will help the 
institutions like IITs, Central Universities, and Higher Education Institutes to bolster their infrastructure 
and sustain high-quality research endeavours effectively.
