CHAPTER-III 
RECOMMENDATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF THE GOVERNMENT 
HAVE NOT BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE 
OVERALL ASSESSMENT OF THE DEMANDS FOR GRANTS (2025-26) OF THE 
DEPARTMENT OF SCHOOL EDUCATION & LITERACY (DoSE&L) 
Recommendation 
1. The Committee takes note of the recommendation of NEP 2020 which unequivocally 
endorses and envisions a substantial increase in public investment in education by both the 
Central Government and all State Governments to reach 6% of GDP. However, the Committee is 
constrained to note that the total expenditure on education (including all Central Ministries and 
all States/UTs) as percentage of GDP stands at 4.12% for the year 2021-22 which is far lower 
than recommendation of NEP 2020. The Committee also notes that SAARC countries like Bhutan 
and Maldives are spending 7.47% and 4.67% of their GDP respectively in 2022 as against 4.12 % 
spending on Education by India. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Education and Department of 
School Education and Literacy should make sincere efforts to increase the spending on education 
in the country to 6% of the GDP as endorsed and recommended by NEP 2020.The Ministry of 
Education should sincerely seek additional funds from Ministry of Finance to make feasible 
spending on education at 6% of GDP and thereby, strengthening and augmenting the public 
education system from school education to higher education truly world class and accessible to 
all sections of the society. 
(Para 2.9 ibid) 
2. The Committee taking note of the figures furnished at Line Graph/Chart 1 above, observes 
that public spending as percentage of GDP on education has not been consistent. During 2014-
15, 2015-16 and 2016-17 total expenditure on education by Centre and States as percentage of 
GDP has been 4.07%, 4.20% and 4.24% respectively. However, it has decreased to 3.87%, 3.90% 
and 4.04% of GDP during 2017-18, 2018-19 and 2019-20 respectively. Further, it has increased 
to 4.36% of GDP during 2020-21 and again declined to 4.12 during 2021-22. Similarly, total 
spending on education as percentage of GDP has also declined from 1.07%, 1.04% and 1.09% 
during 2014-15, 2015-16 and 2016-17 respectively to 0.97%, 0.96%, 1.01%, 1.04% and 1.02% of 
GDP during 2017-18, 2018-19, 2019-20, 2020-21 and 2021-22 respectively. 
 The Committee recommends that the Central Government should increase its share as 
percentage of GDP spending on education and to maintain consistent trends in expenditure on 
education as envisaged in the NEP, 2020, which is essential for economical growth, social 
development and global competitiveness. 
(Para 2.10 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 National Education Policy, 2020 (NEP 2020) unequivocally endorses and envisions a 
substantial increase in public investment in education by both the Central Government and all 
State Governments. To achieve the objectives of NEP 2020, the Government of India has taken 
several initiatives, including a consistent increase in budget allocation to the Ministry of 
Education from Rs. 93,224.31 Cr in 2021-22 to Rs. 1,21,118 Cr in 2024-25. 

83 
 
As per ‘Analysis of Budgeted Expenditure on Education 2019-20 to 2021-22’ published in 
December 2024, the total expenditure on education (including all Central Ministries and all 
States/UTs) as percentage of GDP stands at 4.12% for the year 2021-22. This is higher than that 
of China and Russia, albeit lower than the USA and Brazil. (- Source: 
https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SE.XPD.TOTL.GD.ZS?locations=IN)Centre’s share has 
shown an increasing trend over the years and gone up from 0.51% in 2000-01 to 1.02% in the year 
2021-22. 
 
Comments of the Committee 
The Committee notes with appreciation that there is gradual increase in Centre and States 
expenditure in education which stood at 4.12% of GDP in 2021-22. However, there is a long way 
to go before it achieves the target of 6% of GDP. Given that the nominal GDP of the country at 
current prices is around 360 lakh crores which is likely to further increase in future, public 
investment and expenditure in education needs to be at least doubled from the current budget 
allocation of Rs 121118 crore in BE 2024-25 to achieve the target. The Committee therefore 
recommends the Department to argue its case assiduously before the Ministry of Finance for 
enhanced allocation for the Ministry. The Committee notes the reply of the Department that our 
spending in education as a percentage of DGP is higher than Russia and China. So far as Russia is 
concerned, as its population may be about 1/10 of India, its per capita investment or expenditure 
in education may still be much higher than us. The Committee, therefore, reiterates that the 
Department must draw up a time-bound, outcome-linked roadmap to progressively raise 
education expenditure to 6% of GDP, with clearly defined annual milestones. 
 
SAMAGRA SHIKSHA ABHIYAN (SSA) 
 
Recommendation 
3. The Committee observes that to achieve near-universal primary education, Government 
of India spent several years pursuing policies that focused on the goal and provided adequate 
resourcing to back it up. The Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan and the Right to Education Act, 2009 were 
notable interventions in this regard. While near-universal levels of primary education have been 
reached, there still remain 11.7 lakh children across the country who are Out of School (OoSc). 
The Committee is of the view that this is partly because there is no proper mechanism to ensure 
that these children are retained in school. Section 4 of the RTE Act, 2009 primarily focuses on a 
‘curative/rehabilitative approach’ in the form of bridge courses, etc., after the child has dropped 
out for several months – there is no protocol for timely preventive action by authorities to retain 
children in schools. This absence of a preventive protocol is incompatible with the concept of a 
Fundamental Right. 
(Para 3.4.4ibid) 
Action Taken 
A D O letter has been issued to Education Secretaries of all States/UTs vide no 10-
6/2025-IS-3 dated 15.07.2025 (Annexure - I) wherein they are advised to ensure that preventive 
measures and actions are adopted to retain the children in schools. States/UTs are also advised to 
share the preventive measures being taken in their respective States/UTs and to make suitable 
efforts for mainstreaming of Out of school Children at all levels, so that vision of universal 
quality education may be fulfilled. 
 

84 
 
Comments of the Committee 
The Committee is of the view that the figure of 11.7 lakh out of school children is considerably 
high. Such children have a constitutional as well as statutory right to have access to education and 
the state is obliged to provide the same. Therefore, the Committee recommends the 
Department to consider developing a national preventive protocol under RTE Rules, 
designating cluster-level Education Coordinators as attendance authorities to act within a 
predefined days of absence and involve Child Welfare Committees for chronic cases. 
Further, the Department should also consider making appropriate changes in centralized 
UDISE+ to integrate real-time OoSC tracking report, mandating monthly state reports and 
third-party audits. The Committee also recommends that the matter should be pursued with 
the states so that appropriate measures are taken in an expeditious manner for inclusion of 
such children in formal education system and inform the Committee accordingly. 
 
Recommendation  
4. The Committee is well aware that the subject of education finds mention in Concurrent 
List of the Indian Constitution. It is also aware that recruitment of teachers in schools is a 
continuous process. However, the Committee notes that this continuous process of recruitment of 
permanent/regular teachers has almost been stopped and recruitment of contractual teachers is 
being opted by the State/UT Governments during recent years which would have adverse impact 
on overall school education. The contractual appointments of teachers undermines the 
Constitutional provision reservation in Government jobs to SC, ST, OBC, EWS, PwD etc. Since, 
the funds under SSA are granted to State/UT Governments by the Union Government, it is 
imperative for the Department of School Education and Literacy to seek data from the State/UT 
Governments and maintain it centrally. Further, the Department should proactively monitor 
filling up of vacancies of teachers in SSA funded schools by respective State/UT Governments in a 
time bound manner in the best interest of school education and millions of children studying in 
these schools.  
(Para 3.4.30ibid) 
5. The Committee also recommends that vacancies of teaching and non-teaching staffs 
should be visualised in advance and advertisements for recruitment should be published well 
ahead of the occurring of vacancies in SSA funded schools of the State/UT Governments. The 
Committee further recommends that recruitment process and joining of teachers should be 
ensured in a time bound manner i.e. within six months from the date of advertisements for filling 
up of the vacancies. 
(Para 3.4.31ibid) 
6. The Committee recalls that the Department of School Education and Literacy had 
informed during examination of DFG 2023-24 that there were 9,86,565 vacancies of teachers 
against sanctioned strength of 62,71,380 at the State level out of which, 7,47,565 posts at 
elementary level. 1,46.334 at secondary level and 92,666 at higher secondary level were vacant, 
as on 31 December 2022. However, the Committee was informed by the Department during its 
meeting on 7th January, 2025, that there are 9,82,662 vacancies of teachers in schools of 
States/UTs funded under SSA which shows that the Department and the States/UTs Governments 
have not taken any cognizance of the recommendation of the Committee contained in its 349th 
Report on Demands for Grants 2023-24 pertaining to the Department of School Education & 
Literacy, in utter disregard to Parliamentary Procedures. The Committee recommends that the 
Department should take up the issue of recruitment of huge vacancies of teachers proactively and 
direct the stakeholders to expedite the recruitment process to fill up the vacancies of 

85 
 
permanent/regular teaching/non-teaching staffs in a time bound manner and latest by the end of 
current calendar year i.e. 2025. 
(Para 3.4.32ibid) 
Action Taken 
Education being a subject in the Concurrent List of the Constitution, an overwhelming 
majority of the schools in the country comes under the administrative control of States/UTs. 
Their recruitment, service conditions come under the administrative purview of the respective 
State/UT concerned. 
 Under Samagra Shiksha, financial support is provided to States/UTs towards the Salary of 
Teachers (HMs/Teachers), to ensure maintenance of PTR norms at the school level. Teachers 
will be recruited as per the terms and conditions of the respective States/UTs and their Salary 
Structure will be determined by the State norms for salaries. However, the financial support 
under Samagra Shiksha is subject to certain assessable outcomes. 
 All state/UTs are expected to have a permanent and professional cadre of subject-wise 
teachers. Ad hoc or temporary appointments of teachers need to be discouraged. Ad hoc or 
temporary appointments without following the regular recruitment process almost invariably 
result in poorly qualified teachers causing adverse impact on quality of education. To mitigate 
such concerns, a technology-based comprehensive teacher-requirement planning and forecasting 
exercise needs to be conducted by the States/UTs to assess expected subject-wise teacher 
vacancies and accordingly recruitment of qualified teachers. Recruitment methods and processes 
largely affect the selection of quality teachers. Apart from NCTE guidelines and Teacher 
Eligibility Tests (TETs), competitive selection examination with due care for consistency and 
sanctity is one of the major strategies to bring quality teachers. The recruitment can either be 
entrusted to State Public Service Commission (SPSC) or can be done by education department by 
establishing a central recruitment unit. 
 The progress regarding filling up of teacher vacancies through a competitive selection 
examination conducted by States/UTs on a mission mode, with due care for consistency and 
sanctity and after a technology based comprehensive teacher requirement planning and 
forecasting exercise, is periodically reviewed through regular meetings with States/UTs as well 
as through advisories. The Department vide letter dated 24th March, 2025 has shared the model 
recruitment rules for academic and non-academic posts in schools with States/UTs requesting 
them to update their existing recruitment rules appropriately. 
 It is submitted that the overall pupil-teacher ratio of the country is 25:1 across all levels, 
that is within the norms laid down under the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory 
Education (RTE) Act, 2009 as amended from time to time.  
The matter regarding progress of filling up of existing vacancies, time bound recruitment 
of teachers etc. is reviewed at the time of annual PAB meetings with States/UTs. This is also 
followed up during monthly review meetings with States/UTs. The data regarding vacancy of 
teachers, as received from States/UTs, is also uploaded in the PRABANDH portal 
(https://prabandh.education.gov.in/) for effective monitoring. 
 
Comments of the Committee 
The Committee notes that the Department has acknowledged the issues in principle. 
However, the absence of enforceable timelines, accountability mechanisms, and funding-
linked incentives has resulted in stagnation in teacher recruitment. The Committee feels 
that keeping such large numbers of posts vacant for years together denies the students 
quality education and therefore is an infraction of the spirit of RTE Act. Given the 

86 
 
magnitude of vacancies and their direct impact on learning outcomes, the Committee 
stresses that urgent action is needed in the larger national interest and for safeguarding the 
future of millions of school-going children. The Committee accordingly recommends that 
the Department should actively engage with the State Governments to sort out difficulties, 
if any, in filing up the vacancies as soon as possible.

(i) Immediate release of Pending SSA Funds to States like Kerala, Tamil Nadu and

Action Taken 
The Centrally sponsored Samagra Shiksha Scheme covers children with special needs 
(CwSN) from primary to senior secondary level across the country. The Scheme is regulated and 
governed by the provisions of the Right to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 for 
elementary education of all children including those with disabilities mentioned in the schedule 
of disabilities of the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPwD) Act, 2016.  
There is a dedicated inclusive education component for the education of children with 
special needs as an integral part of Samagra Shiksha. Through the component, children with 
special needs are provided support via specific student oriented interventions such as 
identification and assessment camps, provision of aids & appliances and assistive devices, 
financial support for special educators, transport & escort facility, scribe support, Braille books

teaching-learning materials etc. in order to appropriately address their unique educational 
requirements in general schools. Further, individualized support is also provided through 
therapeutic interventions at the block level.  
Samagra Shiksha also has provisions for Disabled friendly Toilets, Ramps and Ramps 
with Handrails for barrier free access to schools for all children. 
The subject ‘Education’ is in the List – III (Concurrent List) of the Seventh Schedule of 
the Constitution of India. 
It is stated that Samagra Shiksha scheme is aligned with National Education Policy, 2020 
(NEP 2020). Therefore, implementation of Samagra Shiksha is implementation of NEP 2020. 
Further, PM SHRI Schools are exemplar schools that showcase all initiatives of NEP 2020 and

Comments of the Committee  
The Committee notes that the funds due to Tamil Nadu, West Bengal, and Kerala

Recommendation 
9. The Committee also notes that many of the private schools recognized by Central Boards 
are not complying with the provisions of RTE Act, 2009. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that the Department should collect and compile the list of erring schools and ensure penal action 
against those schools for violation of Act passed by the Parliament. The Committee also notes 
that many of the private schools recognized by Central Boards are not complying with the 
provisions of RTE Act, 2009. In particular, implementation of Section 12(1)c of the RTE has been 
inadequate. For instance, during its study visit to Guwahati, the Committee observed that there 
are 5,725 private schools in Assam, but only about 11,000 children had taken admission in these 
schools through the RTE – indicating limited coverage of Section 12(1)C. There are also several 
reports about students who have successfully obtained admission in these schools struggling to 
access stationery, meals, uniform, and textbooks. The Committee, therefore, recommends the 
Department to conduct a comprehensive study of the RTE’s implementation in private schools 
and to develop a policy response to existing inadequacies, including collecting and compiling the 
list of errant schools and ensuring penal action against them for violation of Act passed by the 
Parliament. 
(Para 3.4.41ibid) 
Action Taken 
The Right to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009, mandates that all children 
between the age of 6 and 14 years have the right to free and compulsory education. RTE 
Entitlements is one of the major interventions across all levels of school education under the 
centrally sponsored Samagra Shiksha Scheme. The amount of reimbursement for implementing 
section 12(1)(c) of the RTE Act, 2009 is released under Centrally Sponsored Scheme of Samagra 
Shiksha. The States/UTs first make their expenditure from the State funds for expenditure 
towards reimbursement under section 12(1)(c) of the RTE Act, 2009. Thereafter, States/UTs 
claim the funds for reimbursement under 12(1)(c) of the RTE Act, 2009 from Centre in their 
respective Annual Work Plan and Budget (AWP&B). Based on their proposal, the Project 
Approval Board (PAB) in the Ministry of Education approves an estimate as per the 
programmatic and financial norms of the scheme. The release of Central share is subject to, 
amongst other things, the mandatory submission of the requisite documents such as utilization 
certificate, up-to date expenditure statement, and audit report, the release of commensurate state 
share by States and the availability of budgetary resources at the Budget Estimate/Revised 
Estimate stage. The Central share is released to State/UTs based on approved funding pattern and 
not intervention wise. 
 
Financial support is provided to States/UTs also for RTE entitlements comprising of free 
uniforms, free textbooks along with reimbursement towards expenditure incurred for 25% of 

90 
 
admissions under Section 12 (1) (c), RTE Act, special training for age-appropriate admission of 
out-of-school children at the elementary level, etc. 
State Government is the appropriate Government for the implementation of the Act within 
the schools in that State. With respect to Assam, it has been stated by the State of Assam that the 
implementation of Section 12(1 (c) of the RTE Act is under the examination of the Hon'ble 
Guwahati High Court vide an ongoing PIL 30/2023. As a step towards implementation, the 
Department has taken various steps for awareness and has from time to time issued guidelines. 
The State of Assam has framed an online portal which mandates schools to be registered in the 
portal to facilitate the eligible students to apply online and get admitted in the neighborhood 
registered school. 
Comments of the Committee 
The Committee is not convinced with the reply of the Department and recommends 
that the Department should analyse the recommendations of the Committee given in its 
Reports and accordingly formulate an action plan with focusing on the points given as 
under:- 
(i) The Department should make it mandatory for the Central/State Boards to audit all 
affiliated private schools annually for RTE compliance, including seat reservations, 
admissions, and entitlements. Publish a national dashboard of compliant/errant 
schools; 
(ii) The Department should commission a study by NCERT or NUEPA on RTE 
implementation in private schools (focusing on Section 12(1)(c)), covering 
admissions, entitlements, and dropout rates. This study should be completed at the 
earliest with policy guidelines based on findings; 
(iii) The Department should enhance Samagra Shiksha norms for real-time grievance 
redressal portals, mandatory school audits for entitlements, and compliance 
certification should be made essential  reimbursements; and 
(iv) Steps should be taken for annual training for private schools on RTE via Central 
Boards, coupled with public campaigns to encourage invitation of applications. 
 
Recommendation 
10. The Right to Education Act 2009 allows only three non-teaching duties to Government 
teachers i.e. census, election (only on polling and counting days) and in case of natural disaster. 
However, Government teachers across the country are being engaged in several non-teaching 
activities viz. conducting cattle census, election duties, pulse polio work, maintaining mid-day 
meal registers, ration card verification etc.. As per the report released in 2018, only 19.1 per 
cent of a teacher’s annual school hours is spent on teaching activities and the remaining part of 
the teacher’s time goes as 42.6 per cent in non-teaching core activities, 31.8 per cent in non-
teaching school-related activities and 6.5 per cent on other department activities. 
The Committee therefore, strongly recommends that the Department should issue strict 
guidelines at the earliest to the State Governments and autonomous bodies running schools of 
Central Government to stop engaging teachers in non-teaching activities except Census, election 
duties (only on polling and counting days) and in case of natural disaster as mandated by RTE 
Act, 2009. 
(Para 3.4.46ibid) 
Action Taken 
Section 27 of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009 states 
that “No teacher shall be deployed for any non-educational purposes other than the decennial 

91 
 
population census, disaster relief duties or duties relating to elections to the local authority or the 
State Legislatures or Parliament, as the case may be.” Also, NEP 2020 in para 5.12 emphasizes 
the need to prevent the large amounts of time spent by teachers in non-teaching activities and they 
are not to be engaged in work that is not directly related to teaching, in particular, strenuous 
administrative tasks and mid-day meal-related work, so that teachers fully concentrate on their 
teaching-learning duties.  
Education being a subject in the Concurrent List of the Constitution, a majority of the 
schools are under the administrative control of the respective States and Union Territories (UTs). 
The recruitment, service conditions and deployment of teachers come under the purview of the 
respective State/ Union Territory (UT) Governments. The Ministry of Education has issued 
guidelines to all States and UTs that emphasize that teachers should not be deployed for non-
educational duties other than those which are in accordance with the RTE Act, 2009. 
Comments of the Committee 
The Committee notes that Ministry of Education has issued guidelines to all States and 
UTs that emphasize teachers should not be deployed for non-educational duties other than 
those which are in accordance with the RTE Act, 2009. However, in actual practice, these 
guidelines are not followed. The Committee therefore recommends that proper guidelines 
should be framed and monitored through digital dashboard by integrating into the existing 
UDISE+ (Unified District Information System for Education) portal. States should also 
report the average time teachers spend on non-academic tasks. Further, a dedicated 
Grievance Redressal portal for Teachers should be developed where teachers can 
anonymously report being assigned duties that violate Section 27 of the RTE Act. 
 
Recommendation 
11. The Committee observes that UDISE report for 2023-2024 shows some concerning 
figures. The decline in enrollment of SC, ST, and OBC students versus 2022-2023 was 3.35% 
compared to overall decline in enrolment of 1.49%. In absolute terms, the number of SC students 
declined by 16.23 lakh, ST students by 5.14lakh, and OBC students by 38.53 lakh. Enrolment of 
girl students also fell by 29.61 lakhs, a decrease of 2.55%. The overall decline in enrolment may

UDISE+ data. However, the disproportionate impact on disadvantaged communities is deeply 
concerning and merits a full investigation by the School Education Department.

The Committee feels that while the data confirms the enrolment decline, the absence

12. The Committee notes that UDISE data from 2023-2024 shows that 90.4% of government 
schools have electricity connections. However, data from the Annual Status of Education Report 
(ASER) 2024 shows that only 90% of those schools which are designated as having electricity 
connection actually had functional connections that were active on the day of the ASER team’s 
visit. The Samagra Shiksha’s Financial Norms allow funds for payment of electricity bills and for 
electricity connections, but there is no clear provision for upgrading schools with existing 
electricity connections to ensure that these connections are active. The Committee recommends 
the provision of a separate budget for providing functional electricity connection in all schools. 
(Para 3.4.58ibid) 
Action Taken 
Education being a subject in the Concurrent List of the Constitution, and majority of the 
schools in the country comes under the administrative control of States/UTs. All infrastructure 
related works come under the purview of the respective State Governments.  
Samagra Shiksha Scheme supports creation of infrastructure and basic facilities for 
students in Government Schools.  
The department has given directions to States/UTs to ensure 100% coverage of electricity 
in all government schools in 2025-26 in the Project Approval Board (PAB) 2025-26.  Further to 
achieve the objective of 100% electricity coverage the Samagra Shiksha framework supports 
financial assistance and specific norms for solar panel electrification of schools, particularly in 
hilly areas, to promote renewable energy and improve access to electricity. 
Comments of the Committee 
The Committee is of the view that mere electricity connections on paper are 
meaningless in the absence of reliable and functional power supply. Given the centrality of 
electricity to modern schooling and NEP implementation, the Committee stresses that 
functional electrification must be treated as a core educational entitlement, supported by 
dedicated funding, rigorous monitoring, and clear accountability mechanisms. 
Recommendation 
13. The Committee notes that as per Samagra Shiksha financial norms for upper-primary 
grades, Rs. 500 per child per year is allotted to each school for a “Learning Enhancement 
Program” (LEP) which can be utilized for remedial or “catch up” programs so that children 
acquire the skills expected of them upon completion of primary grades. This amount is given 
keeping in mind only 25% of student strength of the school – however, data repeatedly shows 
that the proportion of children requiring remedial support is much higher than the 25% for 

93 
 
whom funds are sanctioned. The Committee recommends that the financial provision be 
enhanced to support remedial learning for upto 50% of the student strength. 
(Para 3.4.59ibid) 
Action Taken 
Learning Enhancement/Enrichment Programme (LEP) is provided under Samagra Shiksha 
to close the gap in achievement of learning outcomes. Learning Enhancement/Enrichment 
Programme envisages that each student is given the opportunities necessary for her to make 
meaningful progress in acquiring skills/competencies, through a process of continuous 
improvement in teaching and learning. 
The Samagra Shiksha – Framework for Implementation currently provides financial 
support for Learning Enhancement Programmes (LEP) or remedial teaching for a maximum 
of 25% of the total student strength of a class, including Children With Special Needs (CWSN).  
This support is granted after proper identification of weaker students based on an 
assessment conducted at the beginning or end of the academic year, with a unit cost of up to ₹500 
per student. This intervention is available for students from Class VI to XII. 
Further, the approvals for LEP for FY 2023-24, 2024-25 and 2025-26, are at (Annexure-
VII).It can be seen that the funds approved for the purpose within the 25% ceiling have not been 
fully utilized by several States/UTs. Average utilization rate of LEP fund during FY 2023-24 and 
2024-25 is 18.66% and 54.31 % respectively. The Samagra Shiksha scheme has a runover period 
till 2025-26 and the PAB approval of the Annual Plans of various States/UTs have already been 
accorded. However, the recommendation of the committee has been noted. 
Comments of the Committee 
The Committee notes with great concern that the average rate of utilization of LEP 
funds by the states during FY 2023-24 was 18.66% and during FY2024-25 was 54.31% 
which means that most of the states are not able to even fully utilize even Rs,500/- per child 
per year allotted under the program. This pathetic rate of utilization of earmarked amount 
must have been seriously jeopardising the learning enhancement of such students who have 
somehow lacked behind acquiring skills and competences commensurate to their age or 
class and now has to do a remedial catch-up. The Committee therefore recommends the 
Department to find the reasons for such poor fund utilization by the states and help them in 
achieving full utilization of their allotted amount. 
Recommendation 
14. The Committee notes that the Department of School Education and Literacy does not 
currently track state-level student academic IDs. It recommends that the Department do so and 
ensure the linking of these state IDs to the APAAR ID to ensure single unified data sets and 
interoperability. 
(Para 3.4.62ibid) 
Action Taken 
 States and UTs have been requested to provide details of State level student academic 
IDs.  
Comments of the Committee 
The Committee observes that merely seeking information from States/UTs is not going to 
address the structural fragmentation of student data systems. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that to realise the NEP 2020 vision of seamless, lifelong academic tracking and 
to strengthen dropout prevention and equity, the Department must move decisively from 

94 
 
information-gathering to standard-setting, integration, and enforcement. A unified, 
interoperable student academic ID ecosystem anchored in APAAR is essential for a 
modern, inclusive education system. The Committee accordingly reiterates its earlier 
recommendation that Department should ensure the linking of these state IDs to the APAAR 
ID to ensure single unified data sets and interoperability. 
Recommendation: 
15. The Committee recommends that the process to give UDISE+ codes to the 22,298 schools 
without these codes must be expedited and that all students in these schools must be given 
APAAR IDs at the earliest. Further, it recommends that no student who is unable to or selects not 
to furnish their Aadhaar should be denied their APAAR ID. 
(Para 3.4.63 ibid) 
Action Taken 
UDISE codes for all these 22,298 unrecognized schools already exists in UDISE+ portal. 
Further, the letter was also issued to States from Secretary DoSEL (Annexure-VIII) on this 
specifically to initiate recognition of these schools, as they continue to function as unrecognized 
institutions, despite the provision under the RTE Act, 2009, which allowed such unrecognized 
schools to continue only for a period of three years post its implementation. 
 
Comments of the Committee 
The Committee expresses is concern that there still exists 22,298 unrecognised 
schools for more than three years in violation of the provisions of the RTE Act. This in the 
opinion of the Committee is a very serious matter as an unsuspecting student may end 
finding that the school from which he got education is not recognised by the government. 
This may cause crisis particularly for students appearing for Board Examination. The 
Committee therefore is the view that the Department should pursue the matter with the 
State Governments so that running of unrecognised schools is fully stopped immediately.  
 
Recommendation 
16. The Committee recommends that DIKSHA portal should be linked to UDISE+, Aadhaar, 
and APAAR ID to enable granular tracking of the uptake of DIKSHA facilities. 
(Para 3.4.64ibid) 
Action Taken 
 Linking APAAR IDs to enable granular tracking of the uptake of DIKSHA facilities is 
currently work in progress. 
Comments of the Committee 
The Committee is of the opinion that linking DIKSHA with UDISE+, APAAR, and 
Aadhaar is not merely a technical exercise but a critical enabler of outcome-oriented digital 
education policy. The current response of the Department though indicates intent but lacks 
specificity and urgency. The Committee therefore urges the Department to finish the task of 
linking the DIKSHA portal with UDISE+, Aadhaar, and APAAR ID at the earliest in order to 
fully realise the potential of DIKSHA as a national digital public good for education. 
 
 

95 
 
Recommendation 
17. The Committee notes that single-teacher schools continue to exist despite years after the 
passage of the RTE. It notes that the RTE’s stipulated Pupil Teacher Ratio of 30:1 for primary 
schools and 35:1 for upper primary schools took the focus away from the importance of having 
one teacher per grade. Thus, the Committee unequivocally advocates for a new policy of 
requiring one teacher per grade. 
(Para 3.4.67ibid) 
Action Taken 
The number of single teacher schools in the country has reduced to 1,10,971 as per the 
UDISE+ 2023-24 report from 1,18,190 as per the UDISE+ 2022-23 report highlighting a 
reduction of 7,219 single-teacher schools.  
  In order to provide continuous professional development opportunities to the teachers, 
NISHTHA (National Initiative for School Heads’ and Teachers’ Holistic Advancement) program 
has been introduced by the National Council of Education, Research and Training (NCERT). It 
aligns with the NEP 2020’s focus on enhancing teacher competency, fostering innovative 
pedagogical practices, and integrating technology into education. The NISHTHA training 
programme is available on the DIKSHA portal. The pedagogical perspective being transacted in 
these training programmes enables teachers to handle multi-grade teaching scenario also. 
Comments of the Committee 
  The Committee notes with concern that there still exists 1,10,971 single teacher 
schools in the country. The Committee understands that such schools often exist in remote 
and rural areas. The Committee further notes that the Department has taken several 
training, pedagogical and technical interventions to enable the teachers to handle multi 
grade teaching scenario. The  Committee however observes that one teacher managing 
multiple grades simultaneously not only makes the single teacher overloaded with academic 
and administrative work but also result in closure of school operations in case the teacher 
falls ill or remains absent for any other reason. While acknowledging the significance of 
such schools in catering to the educational needs of students in remote and far-flung areas of 
the country, the Committee recommends that such schools should be converted into at least 
two teacher in a time bound manner. 
  
PRADHAN MANTRI POSHAN SHAKTI NIRMAN (PM POSHAN) SCHEME 
 
Recommendation 
18. The Committee notes that while PM POSHAN has contributed significantly to school 
enrollment and attendance, the scheme remains incomplete in coverage and lacks effective 
monitoring mechanisms to ensure meal quality etc.. Additionally, adolescent malnutrition 
continues to be a concern, as students in secondary and senior secondary schools are excluded 
from the program. Strengthening nutritional support will directly impact student performance 
and retention. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department of School Education 
and Literacy should take initiatives on the following: -      
         (Para 3.5.10ibid) 
Sub-points (iii), (iv), (v) in Chapter 1 
Sub-points (vi) in Chapter 4 
 

96 
 
(i) Expansion of PM POSHAN to Secondary Education: PM POSHAN coverage should 
be extended to students up to Class 12th (up to the age of 18 years), with a focus on 
preventing adolescent dropouts and addressing gender disparities in nutrition. This is 
a natural corollary of the Committee’s recommendation to extend the RTE until the 
age of 18. 
 
Action Taken 
 As such there is no plan to extend the Scheme to cover more age groups. However, some 
States & UTs provide hot cooked meals to students of 9th & 10thstandards from their own 
resources. 
 
Comments of the Committee  
The Committee feels that sudden stoppage of nutritional meal to students after class 
VIII, when most of them reach adolescence is like suddenly turning the tap off before 
the bucket is filled completely. Given that adolescence is a critical growth phase which 
requires increased nutritional intakes, proper nutrition during these years will go a long 
way in preventing a large number of long term health issues, reduce drop outs 
particularly amongst girls as the poor families are incentivised to keep their children in 
schools. The Committee therefore feels that there is a sustained need to integrate 
education with nutrition beyond class VIII. This is all the more needed as students have 
to prepare for 10th and 12th Board examinations which demands higher focus and 
cognitive performance.  The Committee therefore recommends the Department should 
increase the scope and coverage of the scheme to all the students up to class X then   
take it to class XII in the next five years. 
 
Recommendation 
(ii) Breakfast Inclusion: A national breakfast program should be introduced to combat 
morning hunger and enhance cognitive performance, particularly in rural and 
economically weaker sections. This has already been envisioned in the NEP but is yet 
to be implemented by the Department. 
 
Action Taken 
 Providing adequate food and nutrition (breakfast and midday meal) to students is a long term 
thrust area for financing under NEP 2020. At present, there is no provision of breakfast in the in 
the PM POSHAN Scheme. However, some States and UTs provide breakfast and additional food 
items such as milk, egg, fruits, chikki and ragi malt etc. 
 
Comments of the Committee  
The Committee notes that the Department in its ATN has submitted that presently 
there is no plan to include breakfast under PM Poshan or extend the Scheme to students 
beyond class VIII. The Committee in this connection observes that breakfast being the first 
meal of the day is very crucial for students as it provides the essential energy for focus, 
improves memory and concentration and boosts academic performance. The Committee 
therefore recommends the department to introduce at least light breakfast in particular in 
the morning shift schools. The Committee further recommends that the Central and the 
State governments should gradually increase their share so that scope is created for proving 
an additional light meal along with the regular meal to all the students.  

97 
 
 
Recommendation 
(vii) The Department should significantly hike the compensation paid to mid-day meal 
workers. 
Action Taken 
 Cook-cum-helpers (CCHs) are honorary workers who have come forward for rendering 
social services. As per guidelines of the Scheme, honorarium of Rs. 1000/- per month for 10 months 
in a year is prescribed for these CCHs in recognition of their services. The honorarium expenditure is 
shared between the Central Government and States and UTs as per the approved sharing pattern. The 
State Governments and UT Administrations have the authority to enhance the honorarium by 
providing additional funds from their own resources and many State Governments and UT 
Administrations have supplemented the honorarium by providing additional funds. 
 
Comments of the Committee 
The Committee observes that the honorarium of Rs. 1000/- per month of the CCHs 
has remained stagnant for almost two decades. The inflation and cost of living during this 
period has increased many folds. The Committee underscores that there is high work load 
on these CHHs as they are involved in procuring, cleaning and cooking and serving hot 
meals to the students which should take not less than 4 or 5 hrs of arduous daily work. Since 
the present honorarium is by and large far below the statutory minimum wages, the 
Committee recommends that the Department should give due to the noble job these CCHs 
are doing and increase their honorarium suitably so that they are also encouraged and 
incentivised to do their  work with total devotion. 
 
 
PM SHRI 
 
Recommendation 
19. The Committee notes that Aspirational schools are needed to reform the image of public 
schooling in popular perception but it distracts from the necessity of large-scale improvements in 
quality. PM-SHRI should therefore be extended to average schools also by relaxing the norms – 
the Ministry cannot afford to concentrate resources on improving the top performing schools 
alone. The first step in this regard would be to exclude the KVs and JNVs from the scheme since 
as schools run by the Union Government, they should automatically be resourced and organised 
along the lines of the NEP rather than needing additional support to do so. The Committee also 
recommends that Department should make assessment of functioning and performance of PM 
SHRI schools on the impact that PM-SHRI status has had on schools and apprise the Committee 
in this regard. 
(Para 3.6.8ibid) 
Action Taken 
A School Quality Assessment Framework (SQAF) has been developed as per 
recommendations of National Education Policy (NEP), 2020, indicating the level of proficiency to 
be achieved by each PM SHRI school. SQAF provides a structured tracking and monitoring 
system for PM SHRI schools. 

98 
 
SQAF is divided into six main domains, based on the six pillars of the PM SHRI Scheme: 
Curriculum, Pedagogy, and Assessment; Access and Infrastructure; Human Resources and School 
Leadership; Inclusive Practices and Gender Equity; Management, Monitoring, and Governance 
and Beneficiary Satisfaction. 
The PM SHRI schools are evaluated on a scale of four stages: Inceptive, Transient, Stable 
and Dynamic Evolving, reflecting their developmental stage in each standard. This incremental 
approach helps schools progressively improve their practices. An online platform has been 
developed to facilitate the assessment process. Out of 13076 PM SHRI schools selected, 12448 
have completed the self-assessment on the SQAF portal. 
Further, NITI Aayog is conducting an evaluation of the PM SHRI scheme through an 
independent agency, ConveGenius Insights Pvt. Ltd. After receipt of the report by the 
Department, the same will be submitted to the Parliamentary Standing Committee. 
Comments of the Committee 
The Committee takes note of the Department’s response regarding development of 
SQAF and ongoing evaluation by NITI Aayog. However, the Committee reiterates that 
assessment mechanisms alone do not address its core concern of resource concentration in 
select schools. The Committee therefore recommends that the Department should make a 
clear policy decision on extending PM-SHRI benefits to average government schools by 
suitably relaxing norms and reconsidering inclusion of KVs and JNVs. The Committee also 
expects the evaluation report to specifically highlight tangible improvements attributable to 
PM-SHRI status and their scalability across the wider public school system.

NEW INDIA LITERACY PROGRAMME/ UNDERSTANDING OF LIFELONG 
LEARNING FOR ALL IN SOCIETY (ULLAS)/ULLAS- NAV BHARAT 
SAAKSHARTAKARYAKRAM 
Recommendation 
21. In response to question of the Committee regarding the number of illiterates in the 
country, the Department informed the Committee that there are around 17-18 crore illiterates in 
the country. Accordingly, the Committee recommends that the Department should accelerate the 
process of literacy programmes like NILP/ULLAS to achieve full literacy target within the 
irreducible minimum time latest by 2029. The Committee further feels that any scheme without 
incentive cannot succeed and accordingly, recommends that volunteer teachers registered on 
ULLAS App should be incentivized to make the scheme successful and efficacious. 
(Para 3.8.5ibid) 
Action Taken 
 The scheme ULLAS-Nav Bharat SaakshartaKaryakram is designed to be implemented 
through volunteerism driven by ‘Kartavyabodh’. Under the current provisions of the scheme, there is 
no financial incentive for the Volunteer Teachers. However, they are being incentivised in other 
manner like credit for voluntary work, marks in School examinations, felicitations, providing 
certificates, etc.  The UGC, NCTE and AICTE have issued directions to their affiliated institutions to 
grant academic credits to students actively volunteering for ULLAS towards this nation building 
noble activity. 
Comments of the Committee 
The Committee takes note of the Department’s emphasis on volunteerism and non-
monetary incentives under ULLAS. However, given the magnitude of illiteracy and the 
ambitious target of full literacy by 2029, the Committee feels that moral incentives alone may 
not ensure sustained engagement. The Committee, therefore, recommends that modest, 
performance-linked financial or material incentives for volunteer teachers, along with a time-
bound action plan should be explored to accelerate coverage and measurable outcomes under 
the ULLAS programme.

Recommendation

optimum utilization of the allocated amount during 2025-26 for nurturing the exceptional 
potential of gifted and talented students across the nation. 
(Para 4.2.4ibid) 
Action Taken 
An Expert Committee was constituted in FY 2024-25 to formulate the guidelines of the 
DHRUV Scheme, with extensive deliberations being held throughout the FY. The guidelines 
formulated thereof are at an advanced stage of finalisation. Pilot for the scheme is likely to be 
initiated in the current FY leading to optimal utilisation of the entire budget for intensive nurturing of 
gifted children. 
 
Comments of the Committee 
The Committee takes note of the constitution of an Expert Committee and the advanced 
stage of finalisation of DHRUV guidelines. However, the Committee remains concerned over 
nil utilisation of funds in 2024-25 and the continued modest allocation despite sharp percentage 
increases. The Committee therefore recommends that the Department should finalise the 
guidelines without further delay. It should also strictly adhere to a clear, time-bound rollout of 
the scheme in 2025-26 and ensure front-loaded utilisation of funds. The Department should 
also review the adequacy of allocations based on pilot outcomes so that the objectives of 
nurturing gifted students are meaningfully achieved.

Recommendation 
23. The Committee observes that few private schools force students and their parents to 
purchase books, shoes, dresses etc. from specific stores recommended by those schools, on very 
higher prices. Moreover, these schools have no capping on fees and other charges collected from 
students. Private schools are running like commercial business instead of community service 
against the provisions of Clause 9.1.3 of Affiliation Bye Laws of the Board. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends the CBSE to monitor these malpractices in private schools affiliated to 
CBSE and ensure compliance of provisions of Clause 9.1.3 of Affiliation Bye Laws of the Board 
by these profit making schools. 
(Para 5.2.8ibid) 
Action Taken 
CBSE has laid down specific provisions for determination of fees charged by schools.  
Chapter 7 of Affiliation Bye Laws of the Board stipulates that Societies /Trust /Companies are 
required to run schools in accordance with the provisions contained in these Bye Laws, “the 

102 
 
School shall endeavor to charge fees to the extent the expenses for running the School are met. 
Schools shall follow the following norms in respect of the fees charged from pupils:”  
 No Society/Trust/Company/School shall charge capitation fee or accept donations for the 
purpose of admission for pupils.  
 Admission Fee and Fee charged under any other head are to be charged only as per the 
regulations of the Appropriate Government  
 Fees shall be charged under the heads prescribed by the Department of Education of the 
State/UTs  
 The acts and regulations of the Central and State/UT Governments enacted/framed in 
connection with regulation of fee in respect of the various categories of the schools 
situated in the state will be applicable to the school affiliated with CBSE also. 
 Fee revision of schools shall be subject to laws, regulation and directions of the 
Appropriate Government. 
 Fee shall not be revised without the express approval of the School Management 
Committee or the process prescribed by the Appropriate Government under any 
circumstances. 
Further, Clause 9.1.3 of Affiliation Bye-Laws of the Board stipulates that Society/ Trust/ 
Company shall ensure that the school is run as a community service and not as a business and that 
commercialization does not take place in the school in any manner whatsoever. Board vide 
Circular No. CBSE/AFF/CIRCULAR/2015/1393058 dated 21.06.2018 has issued advisory to 
schools regarding not to coerce parents/ students for buying the books, stationery, uniforms or any 
other items from the schools tuck shop or from any other specified vendors. 
Appropriate steps are being taken to ensure compliance of clause 9.1.3 of Affiliation Bye 
Laws of the Board by the Schools affiliated to the Board. 
 
Comments of the Committee 
The Committee observes that the mere existence of regulatory provisions is 
insufficient in the absence of effective enforcement and deterrence. Continued 
commercialization of school education erodes public trust and defeats the constitutional 
vision of education as a social good. The Committee, therefore, urges CBSE to shift from an 
advisory-based approach to a monitoring-driven, transparent and accountable regulatory 
regime to ensure strict compliance with Clause 9.1.3 of the Affiliation Bye Laws.

SAMAGRA SHIKSHA ABHIYAN (SSA) 
1. The Committee observes that States like Kerala, Tamil Nadu and West Bengal have 
demonstrated strong educational outcomes with a Gross Enrollment Ratio (GER), significantly 
above the national average. However, underfunding and delays in transfer of SSA funds have 
constrained further advancements in their school infrastructure, teacher training, and student 
support. These States have been compelled to use their own funds to pay salaries to teachers and 
resource personnel due to delays in release of central allocations. During FY 2024-25, States 
like Tamil Nadu was allocated ₹3,586 crores under SSA, with the Union Government's share 
expected to contribute ₹2,152 crores, but this amount has not been released despite repeated 
requests by the State Governments. The withholding of funds is severely impacting teachers’ 
salaries, RTE reimbursements, and transportation for students in remote areas. The Committee 
further observes that withholding the funds under SSA to States for not entering into MoU for 
separate schemes like PM SHRI is not justifiable. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
the Department of School Education and Literacy, Ministry of Education to ensure the following:
         
(Para 3.4.35ibid) 
Sub points (i), (ii), (iv), (v), (vi) and (viii) in chapter 1 
 (iii) The Department should establish clear, automated quarterly fund disbursal tied to 
school- year cycles, ensuring predictability for States in teachers’ salary payments and 
infrastructure upgradation. 
(vii) The Deparment should accelerate teacher recruitment in STEM (teachers 
specifically for Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathermatics subjects) and 
regional language subjects, addressing gaps in critical knowledge areas. 
 
Action Taken 
The Centrally sponsored Samagra Shiksha Scheme covers children with special needs 
(CwSN) from primary to senior secondary level across the country. The Scheme is regulated and 
governed by the provisions of the Right to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 for 
elementary education of all children including those with disabilities mentioned in the schedule 
of disabilities of the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPwD) Act, 2016.  
There is a dedicated inclusive education component for the education of children with 
special needs as an integral part of Samagra Shiksha. Through the component, children with 
special needs are provided support via specific student oriented interventions such as 
identification and assessment camps, provision of aids & appliances and assistive devices, 
financial support for special educators, transport & escort facility, scribe support, Braille books 
and large print books for children with visual impairment, stipend for girls with special needs and 
teaching-learning materials etc. in order to appropriately address their unique educational 
requirements in general schools. Further, individualized support is also provided through 
therapeutic interventions at the block level.  

109 
 
Samagra Shiksha also has provisions for Disabled friendly Toilets, Ramps and Ramps 
with Handrails for barrier free access to schools for all children. 
 
The subject ‘Education’ is in the List – III (Concurrent List) of the Seventh Schedule of 
the Constitution of India. 
It is stated that Samagra Shiksha scheme is aligned with National Education Policy, 2020 
(NEP 2020). Therefore, implementation of Samagra Shiksha is implementation of NEP 2020. 
Further, PM SHRI Schools are exemplar schools that showcase all initiatives of NEP 2020 and 
offer leadership to other schools in the neighbourhood. 
The Annual Work Plan & Budget (AWP&B) submitted by Tamil Nadu for FY 2025–26 
amounting to Rs. 3044.52 crore (with a proposed Central share of Rs. 1826.71 crore) has been 
duly approved by the Project Approval Board (PAB). 
The Annual Work Plan & Budget (AWP&B) submitted by West Bengal for FY 2025-26 
amounting to Rs. 3467.47 Crore (with a proposed Central share of Rs.1965.66 Crore) has been 
duly approved by the Project Approval Board (PAB). 
The Annual Work Plan & Budget (AWP&B) submitted by Kerala for FY 2025-26 
amounting to Rs. 761.08 Crore (with a proposed Central share of Rs.452.04 Crore) has been duly 
approved by the Project Approval Board (PAB). 
 However, just as the Statesare implementing Samagra Shiksha Scheme that is aligned 
with NEP 2020, it would be appropriate that the States come forward to implement and showcase 
all the initiatives of NEP 2020 including under PM SHRI Scheme in order to develop 
government schools of the State as exemplar schools to facilitate best school education services.  
The Ministry is regularly engaging with the State Governments of Tamil Nadu, West Bengal and 
Kerala to resolve the matter.  
     Samagra Shiksha implementation framework already provides for Decentralized Planning 
Process starting from the school level.  The States and Union Territories draw up Annual Work 
Plan and Budget (AWP&B) proposal based on their requirements and priority and guidelines 
issued by the Ministry of Education.   
The release of the central share is contingent upon the expenditure incurred by the 
respective State/UT against the previous releases. To ensure timely and effective utilization of 
funds, the Ministry regularly monitors the expenditure and implementation progress through 
PRABANDH Portal, physical review meetings with States/UTs etc. 
The Department also publishes the minutes of the meeting of the Project Approval Board 
for various Centrally Sponsored Schemes on its official website which are accessible to the 
public. The Annual report of the department is published which details the department's 
activities, initiatives, and progress in the field of school education. 
To ensure availability of digital learning, DIKSHA platform, 200 TV channels and 400 
Radio Stations as part of PM eVidya has been made available to all students across the country. 
Channels have been allotted to States/UTs for providing e-content in regional languages. 
Teachers are offered various training courses through NISHTHA platform including integrating 
technologies with Pedagogy.   
ICT and Digital Initiatives component of Samagra Shiksha covers Government and Aided 
Schools having classes VI to XII. Under this component financial assistance is provided for 
establishing ICT Lab and Smart Classrooms in schools.  
         As per PRABANDH Portal, till date, 1,42,745 ICT Labs and 1,31,548 Smart Classrooms 
have been sanctioned to States/ UTs. 
For digital learning coverage, the department in May 2025 has conducted a supplementary 
Project Approval Board (PAB) Meeting under Samagra Shiksha for the FY 2025-26 to approve

dedicated allocations for 100% saturation of ICT Labs, Smart classrooms and Integrated Science

        An advisory has been issued on 11th July 2022 by the Department of School Education and

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE -AT A GLANCE  
 
1. The Committee notes with appreciation that there is gradual increase in Centre and 
States expenditure in education which stood at 4.12% of GDP in 2021-22. However, there is 
a long way to go before it achieves the target of 6% of GDP. Given that the nominal GDP of 
the country at current prices is around 360 lakh crores which is likely to further increase in 
future, public investment and expenditure in education needs to be at least doubled from the 
current budget allocation of Rs 121118 crore in BE 2024-25 to achieve the target. The 
Committee therefore recommends the Department to argue its case assiduously before the 
Ministry of Finance for enhanced allocation for the Ministry. The Committee notes the reply 
of the Department that our spending in education as a percentage of DGP is higher than 
Russia and China. So far as Russia is concerned, as its population may be about 1/10 of 
India, its per capita investment or expenditure in education may still be much higher than 
us. The Committee, therefore, reiterates that the Department must draw up a time-bound, 
outcome-linked roadmap to progressively raise education expenditure to 6% of GDP, with 
clearly defined annual milestones. 
(Para 2.9& 2.10 ibid) 
2. The Committee is of the view that the figure of 11.7 lakh out of school children is 
considerably high. Such children have a constitutional as well as statutory right to have 
access to education and the state is obliged to provide the same. Therefore, the Committee 
recommends the Department to consider developing a national preventive protocol under 
RTE Rules, designating cluster-level Education Coordinators as attendance authorities to 
act within a predefined days of absence and involve Child Welfare Committees for chronic 
cases. Further, the Department should also consider making appropriate changes in 
centralized UDISE+ to integrate real-time OoSC tracking report, mandating monthly state 
reports and third-party audits. The Committee also recommends that the matter should be 
pursued with the states so that appropriate measures are taken in an expeditious manner for 
inclusion of such children in formal education system and inform the Committee 
accordingly. 
(Para 3.4.4 ibid) 
3. The Committee notes that the Department has acknowledged the issues in principle. 
However, the absence of enforceable timelines, accountability mechanisms, and funding-
linked incentives has resulted in stagnation in teacher recruitment. The Committee feels 
that keeping such large numbers of posts vacant for years together denies the students 
quality education and therefore is an infraction of the spirit of RTE Act. Given the 
magnitude of vacancies and their direct impact on learning outcomes, the Committee 
stresses that urgent action is needed in the larger national interest and for safeguarding the 
future of millions of school-going children. The Committee accordingly recommends that 
the Department should actively engage with the State Governments to sort out difficulties, 
if any, in filing up the vacancies as soon as possible.   
(Para 3.4.30, 3.4.31 & 3.4.32 ibid) 
 
4. The Committee notes that the funds due to Tamil Nadu, West Bengal, and Kerala 
have been duly approved by the Project Approval Board (PAB) of the Samagra Shiksha 
Abhiyan. The Committee appreciates that the Ministry is regularly engaging with the State 
Governments of Tamil Nadu, West Bengal, and Kerala to resolve the matter. The 
Committee recommends that the funds that have been approved may be released. 

112 
 
 
(Para 3.4.34 , 3.4.35 (i), (ii), (iv), (v) & (vi) ibid) 
 
5. The Committee is not convinced with the reply of the Department and recommends 
that the Department should analyse the recommendations of the Committee given in its 
Reports and accordingly formulate an action plan with focusing on the points given as 
under:- 
(i) The Department should make it mandatory for the Central/State Boards to audit all 
affiliated private schools annually for RTE compliance, including seat reservations, 
admissions, and entitlements. Publish a national dashboard of compliant/errant 
schools; 
(ii) The Department should commission a study by NCERT or NUEPA on RTE 
implementation in private schools (focusing on Section 12(1)(c)), covering 
admissions, entitlements, and dropout rates. This study should be completed at the 
earliest with policy guidelines based on findings; 
(iii) The Department should enhance Samagra Shiksha norms for real-time grievance 
redressal portals, mandatory school audits for entitlements, and compliance 
certification should be made essential  reimbursements; and 
(iv) Steps should be taken for annual training for private schools on RTE via Central 
Boards, coupled with public campaigns to encourage invitation of applications. 
(Para 3.4.41ibid) 
6. The Committee notes that Ministry of Education has issued guidelines to all States 
and UTs that emphasize teachers should not be deployed for non-educational duties other 
than those which are in accordance with the RTE Act, 2009. However, in actual practice, 
these guidelines are not followed. The Committee therefore recommends that proper 
guidelines should be framed and monitored through digital dashboard by integrating into 
the existing UDISE+ (Unified District Information System for Education) portal. States 
should also report the average time teachers spend on non-academic tasks. Further, a 
dedicated Grievance Redressal portal for Teachers should be developed where teachers can 
anonymously report being assigned duties that violate Section 27 of the RTE Act.  
(Para 3.4.46ibid) 
 
7. The Committee feels that while the data confirms the enrolment decline, the absence 
of analysis, investigation, and remedial action is a matter of serious concern. Given the 
constitutional commitment to social justice and inclusive education, the Committee is of the 
view that any decline disproportionately affecting disadvantaged communities should be 
addressed immediately. 
(Para 3.4.48ibid) 
8. The Committee is of the view that mere electricity connections on paper are 
meaningless in the absence of reliable and functional power supply. Given the centrality of 
electricity to modern schooling and NEP implementation, the Committee stresses that 
functional electrification must be treated as a core educational entitlement, supported by 
dedicated funding, rigorous monitoring, and clear accountability mechanisms. 
(Para 3.4.58ibid) 

113 
 
9. The Committee notes with great concern that the average rate of utilization of LEP 
funds by the states during FY 2023-24 was 18.66% and during FY2024-25 was 54.31% 
which means that most of the states are not able to even fully utilize even Rs,500/- per child 
per year allotted under the program. This pathetic rate of utilization of earmarked amount 
must have been seriously jeopardising the learning enhancement of such students who have 
somehow lacked behind acquiring skills and competences commensurate to their age or 
class and now has to do a remedial catch-up. The Committee therefore recommends the 
Department to find the reasons for such poor fund utilization by the states and help them in 
achieving full utilization of their allotted amount. 
(Para 3.4.59ibid) 
10. The Committee observes that merely seeking information from States/UTs is not 
going to address the structural fragmentation of student data systems. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that to realise the NEP 2020 vision of seamless, lifelong academic 
tracking and to strengthen dropout prevention and equity, the Department must move 
decisively from information-gathering to standard-setting, integration, and enforcement. A 
unified, interoperable student academic ID ecosystem anchored in APAAR is essential for a 
modern, inclusive education system. The Committee accordingly reiterates its earlier 
recommendation that Department should ensure the linking of these state IDs to the APAAR 
ID to ensure single unified data sets and interoperability. 
(Para 3.4.62ibid) 
 
11. The Committee expresses is concern that there still exists 22,298 unrecognised 
schools for more than three years in violation of the provisions of the RTE Act. This in the 
opinion of the Committee is a very serious matter as an unsuspecting student may end 
finding that the school from which he got education is not recognised by the government. 
This may cause crisis particularly for students appearing for Board Examination. The 
Committee therefore is the view that the Department should pursue the matter with the 
State Governments so that running of unrecognised schools is fully stopped immediately.  
(Para 3.4.63 ibid) 
 
12. The Committee is of the opinion that linking DIKSHA with UDISE+, APAAR, and 
Aadhaar is not merely a technical exercise but a critical enabler of outcome-oriented digital 
education policy. The current response of the Department though indicates intent but lacks 
specificity and urgency. The Committee therefore urges the Department to finish the task of 
linking the DIKSHA portal with UDISE+, Aadhaar, and APAAR ID at the earliest in order to 
fully realise the potential of DIKSHA as a national digital public good for education. 
(Para 3.4.64ibid) 
 
13. The Committee notes with concern that there still exists 1,10,971 single teacher 
schools in the country. The Committee understands that such schools often exist in remote 
and rural areas. The Committee further notes that the Department has taken several 
training, pedagogical and technical interventions to enable the teachers to handle multi 
grade teaching scenario. The  Committee however observes that one teacher managing 
multiple grades simultaneously not only makes the single teacher overloaded with academic 
and administrative work but also result in closure of school operations in case the teacher 
falls ill or remains absent for any other reason. While acknowledging the significance of 
such schools in catering to the educational needs of students in remote and far-flung areas 

114 
 
of the country, the Committee recommends that such schools should be converted into at 
least two teacher in a time bound manner. 
(Para 3.4.67ibid) 
 
14. The Committee feels that sudden stoppage of nutritional meal to students after class 
VIII, when most of them reach adolescence is like suddenly turning the tap off before the 
bucket is filled completely. Given that adolescence is a critical growth phase which requires 
increased nutritional intakes, proper nutrition during these years will go a long way in 
preventing a large number of long term health issues, reduce drop outs particularly 
amongst girls as the poor families are incentivised to keep their children in schools. The 
Committee therefore feels that there is a sustained need to integrate education with 
nutrition beyond class VIII. This is all the more needed as students have to prepare for 10th 
and 12th Board examinations which demands higher focus and cognitive performance.  The 
Committee therefore recommends the Department should increase the scope and coverage 
of the scheme to all the students up to class X then   take it to class XII in the next five 
years. 
(Para 3.5.10 (i) ibid) 
 
15. The Committee notes that the Department in its ATN has submitted that presently 
there is no plan to include breakfast under PM Poshan or extend the Scheme to students 
beyond class VIII. The Committee in this connection observes that breakfast being the first 
meal of the day is very crucial for students as it provides the essential energy for focus, 
improves memory and concentration and boosts academic performance. The Committee 
therefore recommends the department to introduce at least light breakfast in particular in 
the morning shift schools. The Committee further recommends that the Central and the 
State governments should gradually increase their share so that scope is created for proving 
an additional light meal along with the regular meal to all the students.  
(Para 3.5.10 (ii) ibid) 
 
16. The Committee observes that the honorarium of Rs. 1000/- per month of the CCHs 
has remained stagnant for almost two decades. The inflation and cost of living during this 
period has increased many folds. The Committee underscores that there is high work load 
on these CHHs as they are involved in procuring, cleaning and cooking and serving hot 
meals to the students which should take not less than 4 or 5 hrs of arduous daily work. Since 
the present honorarium is by and large far below the statutory minimum wages, the 
Committee recommends that the Department should give due to the noble job these CCHs 
are doing and increase their honorarium suitably so that they are also encouraged and 
incentivised to do their  work with total devotion. 
(Para 3.5.10 (vii) ibid) 
 
17. The Committee takes note of the Department’s response regarding development of 
SQAF and ongoing evaluation by NITI Aayog. However, the Committee reiterates that 
assessment mechanisms alone do not address its core concern of resource concentration in 
select schools. The Committee therefore recommends that the Department should make a 
clear policy decision on extending PM-SHRI benefits to average government schools by 
suitably relaxing norms and reconsidering inclusion of KVs and JNVs. The Committee also 
expects the evaluation report to specifically highlight tangible improvements attributable to 
PM-SHRI status and their scalability across the wider public school system. 

115 
 
(Para 3.6.8ibid) 
18. The Committee is deeply concerned at the fact that the six targeted states are unable 
to fully spend their approved funds consistently over the years since the Scheme started in 
2020. The Committee recommends that the Department should closely work with these 
states to find out reasons for such low expenditure and fix the bureaucratic bottlenecks or 
implementation hurdles, if any, faced by these states so that approved funds are properly 
utilised. The Committee feels that unless proactively addressed, the challenges faced by the 
states risks diluting the very transformative intent of the STARS scheme.  
(Para 3.7.6 ibid) 
19. The Committee takes note of the Department’s emphasis on volunteerism and non-
monetary incentives under ULLAS. However, given the magnitude of illiteracy and the 
ambitious target of full literacy by 2029, the Committee feels that moral incentives alone may 
not ensure sustained engagement. The Committee, therefore, recommends that modest, 
performance-linked financial or material incentives for volunteer teachers, along with a time-
bound action plan should be explored to accelerate coverage and measurable outcomes under 
the ULLAS programme. 
(Para 3.8.5ibid) 
20. The Committee takes note of the constitution of an Expert Committee and the advanced 
stage of finalisation of DHRUV guidelines. However, the Committee remains concerned over 
nil utilisation of funds in 2024-25 and the continued modest allocation despite sharp percentage 
increases. The Committee therefore recommends that the Department should finalise the 
guidelines without further delay. It should also strictly adhere to a clear, time-bound rollout of 
the scheme in 2025-26 and ensure front-loaded utilisation of funds. The Department should 
also review the adequacy of allocations based on pilot outcomes so that the objectives of 
nurturing gifted students are meaningfully achieved. 
(Para 4.2.4ibid) 
 
21. The Committee observes that the mere existence of regulatory provisions is 
insufficient in the absence of effective enforcement and deterrence. Continued 
commercialization of school education erodes public trust and defeats the constitutional 
vision of education as a social good. The Committee, therefore, urges CBSE to shift from an 
advisory-based approach to a monitoring-driven, transparent and accountable regulatory 
regime to ensure strict compliance with Clause 9.1.3 of the Affiliation Bye Laws. 
(Para 5.2.8ibid) 
 
22. The Committee while noting that the Ministry of Education (DoSE&L) has decided to 
take up the recruitment of KVS & NVS together and observes that procedural reforms without 
firm timelines and outcomes are insufficient to address the issue of vacancies in KVS. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that KVS should complete the whole recruitment process 
during the current year.  
(Para 5.3.9 & 5.3.11 ibid) 
 
23. The Committee appreciates that out of 163 KVs functioning from temporary 
buildings, land in 121 KVs has been transferred in favour of KVS wherein construction 
activities are at various levels. The Committee recommends the Department to complete the 
construction in a time bound manner during the ensuing financial year and inform the 

116 
 
Committee. The Committee further recommends that in respect of the remaining 42 KVs, 
the matter should be vigorously pursued with the sponsoring authorities for transfer of land 
in favour of KVS. 
(Para 5.3.13ibid) 
 
24. The Committee is not satisfied with the reply of the Department which has chosen 
not to give any clear replies to its recommendation. The Committee feels that the Members 
of Parliaments with their vast experience in public service will only provide significant 
inputs for proper administration of Kendriya Vidyalayas. The Committee therefore reiterates 
its earlier recommendation that the local Member of Parliament be added to the School 
Management Committee of the KendriyaVidyalayas falling within their constituency 
(Para 5.3.15ibid) 
25. The Committee notes that in the ATN wrt Para 5.3.11, the Ministry of Education has 
informed that it has decided to take up the recruitment of KVS & NVS together. The 
Committee is of the view that reliance on contractual teachers in schools like NVS for so long, 
is undesirable. The Committee, therefore, urges the Department to complete the whole process 
of recruitment during the year 2026 for the appointment of Teachers on regular basis in the 
NVS.  
(Para 5.4.9ibid) 
26. The Committee notes the reply of the Department that the process of filling up 
vacant posts through regular appointments shall be initiated once the revised Recruitment 
Rules are notified. It also notes that the draft Recruitment rules though have been prepared 
but are yet to be placed before the Competent Authority for compliance. Since the 
vacancies as per the revised  staff strength in NBB is almost 50%, the Committee urges the 
Department to complete all the necessary formalities for the notification of the Recruitment 
Rules followed by completion of the recruitment process during the year 2026.  
(Para 5.5.6 ibid) 
 
27. The Committee notes that while the Department has initiated Recruitment in mission 
mode and reduced vacancies from 63 to 37, progress remains insufficient. To fulfil NCTE’s 
statutory role in implementing NEP 2020 and teacher education programs, the Department 
should ensure withdrawal of the no-recruitment directive, fill all vacancies permanently, 
and institute regular monitoring. 
(Para 5.7.6 ibid)

REPORT 
 
The Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Education, 
Women, Children, Youth and Sports deals with the action taken by the Government on the 
Recommendations/Observations contained in its 366th Report on “Demand For Grants – 2025-
26”, which was presented to the Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on 2nd April, 
2025. 
2. The Action Taken Notes in respect of Recommendations/Observations contained in the 
above mentioned Report were received from the Department of Sports, Ministry of Youth 
Affairs and Sports vide their communication dated 6th June, 2025. These have been categorized 
as follows:  
 
Chapter I: Recommendations which have been accepted by the Government:  
Paras - 2.1.17, 2.2.9, 2.2.10, 2.2.11, 2.2.12, 2.2.13, 2.2.14, 2.3.4, 2.3.5, 2.3.6,

2.9.10, 2.9.11, 2.10.15, 5.3.10, 5.3.11, 5.3.12, 5.3.13, 5.4.9, 5.4.10, 5.4.11, 
5.4.12, 5.4.13, 5.5.2, 5.6.17, 5.6.22, 5.7.8, 5.8.2, 5.8.3, 5.10.18, 5.10.19, 
5.11.13, 5.11.14, 5.15.1, 5.16.1

accepted by the Committee:
