(Para 6.1.7)
54. The  Committee  also  notes  that  although  ₹ 46.00  crore  was  projected  for  2026 – 27,  only
₹ 40.00  crore  has  been  approved  at  the  BE  stage,  reflecting  partial  rationalization.  Given
the  importance  of  timely  and  credible  disbursement  of  incentives  to  maintain  athlete
morale,  the  Committee  recommends  that  the  Ministry  may  closely  monitor  the  pace  of
applications  and,  if  required,  seek  supplementary  grants  in  a  timely  manner  so  that  no
eligible sportsperson or coach faces delay in receipt of due incentives.
(Para 6.1.8)
55. The  Committee  also  note  the  substantial  increase  in  allocation  for  Pension  to  Meritorious
Sportspersons  from  ₹ 4.00  crore  to  ₹ 10.00  crore  in  2025 – 26  owing  to  an  increase  in  eligible
beneficiaries.  Considering  the  long-term  welfare  dimension  of  scheme,  the  Committee
recommends  that  the  Ministry  should  periodically  review  pension  rates  and  eligibility
criteria  to  ensure  adequacy  and  sustainability  along  with  strengthening  digital  processing
and  verification  systems  to  have  a  transparent  and  expeditious  disbursement  mechanism
under all sub-components of the Incentives to Sports Persons Scheme.
(Para 6.1.9)
56. The  Committee  notes  that  the  Pandit  Deendayal  Upadhyay  National  Welfare  Fund  for
Sportspersons  is  a  vital  welfare-oriented  intervention  aimed  at  providing  financial
assistance  to  former  and  active  sportspersons  facing  indigent  circumstances,  medical
emergencies,  disability,  or  distress  conditions.  While  observing  that  the  scheme  is
demand-driven  and  that  the  allocation  of  ₹ 2.00  crore  at  BE  2025 – 26  and  BE  2026 – 27  is
considered  adequate  by  the  Ministry,  the  Committee  further  notes  that  the  AE  in  2024 – 25
stood  at  ₹ 0.95  crore  and  the  RE  2025 – 26  was  reduced  to  ₹ 1.00  crore.  The  Committee
recommends  that  the  Ministry  should  undertake  wider  outreach  and  awareness  initiatives
in  coordination  with  National  Sports  Federations  and  State  Governments  to  ensure  that
eligible  beneficiaries  are  adequately  informed  about  the  scheme  and  are  able  to  access
timely assistance.
(Para 6.2.5)

105
57. The  Committee  observes  that  the  scheme  addresses  critical  aspects  of  post-retirement
security,  medical  support,  and  social  dignity  of  sportspersons  who  have  brought  laurels  to
the  nation.  Considering  the  welfare  and  humanitarian  character  of  the  Fund,  the
Committee  recommends  that  the  Ministry  should  periodically  review  the  quantum  of
assistance,  eligibility  norms,  and  processing  timelines  to  enhance  accountability,  and  also
develop  a  technology-enabled  monitoring  system  to  ensure  transparency,  expeditious
disposal of cases, and optimal utilization of allocated funds.
(Para 6.2.6)
58. The  Committee  notes  that  the  National  Sports  Development  Fund  (NSDF)  plays  an
important  role  in  mobilizing  extra-budgetary  resources  for  sports  promotion  through
contributions  from  Government,  Public  Sector  Undertakings,  corporates  under  CSR,
institutions  and  individuals,  and  in  extending  targeted  assistance  to  sportspersons,
academies  and  the  Sports  Authority  of  India  under  the  Target  Olympic  Podium  Scheme
(TOPS).  However,  the  Committee  observes  that  allocations  under  the  Fund  have
witnessed  fluctuations,  with  BE  2025 – 26  of  ₹ 18.00  crore  being  reduced  to  ₹ 12.00  crore  at
RE  stage  and  BE  2026 – 27  approved  at  ₹ 15.00  crore  against  projections  of  ₹ 18.00  crore.
The  Committee  recommends  that  the  Ministry  should  evolve  a  more  practical  resource
mobilization  strategy,  including  advance  engagement  with  CSR  contributors  and  multi-
year  commitment  frameworks,  so  as  to  reduce  fluctuations  in  allocations  and  ensure
continuity of high-performance preparation of athletes.
(Para 6.3.7)
59. The  Committee  observes  that  Government  contribution  to  the  NSDF  is  linked  to  25  per
cent  of  funds  received  from  PSUs  and  corporates  under  CSR,  and  that  the  budgetary
reductions  at  RE  stage  is  attributable  to  lower  CSR  receipts  during  the  year.  The
Committee  recommends  that  the  Ministry  should  explore  diversification  of  funding
sources,  including  greater  outreach  to  private  foundations,  philanthropic  institutions  and
high  net-worth  individuals,  and  consider  instituting  incentive  mechanisms  for  long-term
endowments  so  as  to  augment  the  corpus  and  enhance  financial  sustainability  of  the
Fund.
(Para 6.3.8)
60. The  Committee  notes  that  substantial  block  grants  amounting  to  ₹ 58.94  crore  have  been
released  during  the  last  three  financial  years  to  SAI  under  TOPS  for  training,
international  exposure,  sports  science  support  and  procurement  of  high-performance
equipment,  thereby  benefiting  elite  athletes  across  disciplines.  In  order  to  further
strengthen  transparency,  the  Committee  recommends  that  the  Ministry  should  develop
institute  a  structured  impact  assessment  mechanism  with  performance  indicators,
periodic  public  disclosure  of  utilization  details,  and  measurable  outcome  benchmarks
linked  to  international  results,  so  as  to  ensure  optimal  utilization  of  NSDF  resources  and
greater accountability in sports promotion activities.

106
(Para 6.3.9)
61. The  Committee  observes  that  while  the  allocation  under  the  Scheme  “ Assistance  to
National  Sports  Federations  (NSFs) ”  has  increased  from  ₹ 400.00  crore  in  BE  2025 – 26  to
₹ 425.00  crore  in  BE  2026 – 27,  the  actual  expenditure  in  previous  years  ₹ 272.86  crore  in
2022 – 23,  ₹ 321.58  crore  in  2023 – 24  and  ₹ 256.05  crore  in  2024 – 25  indicates  persistent
under-utilisation  of  funds.  At  the  same  time,  the  projections  for  2026 – 27  ( ₹ 626.21  crore)
are  substantially  higher  than  the  Budget  Estimates,  reflecting  a  resource  gap  in  the
context  of  preparations  for  major  international  sporting  events  such  as  the  Asian  Games
2026,  Para  Asian  Games  2026  and  Commonwealth  Games  2026,  as  well  as  proposed
hosting  commitments.  The  Committee,  therefore,  recommends  that  a  performance-linked
disbursement  framework  with  quarterly  utilisation  reviews  and  outcome-based
benchmarks  should  be  put  in  place  for  National  Sports  Federations,  so  as  to  ensure  timely
fund  absorption,  improved  accountability,  and  optimal  utilisation  of  enhanced  allocations
towards sports development and international event preparedness.
(Para 6.4.4)
62. The  Committee  notes  that  the  Scheme  of  Human  Resource  Development  in  Sports
(HRDS)  is  important  for  strengthening  the  technical  and  professional  ecosystem  of  sports
through  capacity  building  of  coaches,  sports  scientists,  technical  officials  and  support
personnel.  While  the  BE  for  2026 – 27  has  been  enhanced  to  ₹ 5.00  crore  from  ₹ 4.00  crore
in  BE  2025 – 26  ( ₹ 2.00  crore  at  RE  stage),  the  pattern  of  utilisation  is  not  encouraging,  due
to  fewer  proposals  which  indicates  structural  constraints  in  outreach  and  absorption
capacity.  The  Committee  also  notes  that  despite  the  inclusion  of  new  components  such  as
support  for  publications,  e-publications  and  sports-related  digital  applications,  the
projected  requirement  of  ₹ 10.00  crore  has  not  been  fully  matched  in  the  Budget  Estimates
for  FY  2026-27.  The  Committee,  therefore,  recommends  that  the  Ministry  should  project
its  demand  for  higher  allocations  at  the  RE  Stage.  Besides,  the  Ministry  should  undertake
proactive  awareness  and  outreach  measures  in  coordination  with  National  Sports
Federations,  Sports  Universities  and  training  institutions  to  increase  the  number  and
quality  of  proposals  under  the  Scheme,  including  measures  to  ensure  optimal  utilisation
of funds to strengthen of the human resource base in sports.
(Para 6.5.6)
63. The  Committee  notes  with  concern  the  significant  fluctuations  in  budgetary  allocations
under  the  National  Centre  of  Sports  Sciences  &  Research  (NCSSR),  wherein  the  Budget
Estimate  of  ₹ 10.00  crore  for  2025 – 26  was  substantially  enhanced  to  ₹ 78.64  crore  at  the
Revised  Estimate  stage,  despite  actual  expenditure  being  ₹ 5.00  crore  in  FY  2024 – 25.
While  such  an  increase  may  reflect  major  capital  or  project-based  interventions  aimed  at
strengthening  sports  science  infrastructure,  the  sharp  decline  to  ₹ 15.00  crore  in  BE
2026 – 27  against  projections  of  ₹ 27.50  crore  and  an  80.93  per  cent  decrease  over  RE
indicates  the  absence  of  a  stable  funding  framework.  Given  the  critical  importance  of
scientific  support,  injury  management,  nutrition,  psychology  and  performance  analytics
in  achieving  international  competitiveness,  the  Committee  recommends  that  the  Ministry
should  formulate  outcome-oriented  financial  plan  for  NCSSR  with  clearly  defined

107
research  priorities,  institutional  partnerships  and  performance  indicators,  so  as  to  ensure
consistency in funding, and constant integration of sports science into athlete preparation.
(Para 6.6.4)
64. The  Committee  appreciates  that  Khelo  India,  as  the  flagship  programme  of  the  Ministry,
continues  to  command  the  largest  share  of  resources  and  has  made  notable  progress  in
grassroots  sports  development  through  the  approval  of  344  infrastructure  projects,
notification  of  1067  Khelo  India  Centres  (KICs),  35  Khelo  India  State  Centres  of
Excellence  (KISCEs),  accreditation  of  322  academies,  and  identification  of  2905  Khelo
India  Athletes.  However,  the  Committee  observes  a  consistent  gap  between  Budget
Estimates  and  actual  expenditure  during  the  last  three  financial  years,  with  actual
expenditure  in  2024 – 25  at  ₹ 620.75  crore  against  BE  of  ₹ 900  crore  and  RE  of  ₹ 746.54
crore,  and  similar  moderation  visible  in  2025 – 26  and  2026 – 27  allocations  vis-à-vis
utilisation  pattern.  The  Committee,  therefore,  is  of  the  view  that  the  advance  planning
and  phased  fund  release  mechanisms  should  be  adopted  in  consultation  with  States/UTs
to  minimize  surrender  of  funds  and  ensure  timely  execution  of  sanctioned  infrastructure
and competition-related activities.
(Para 6.7.15)
65. The  Committee  further  observes  that  while  55  infrastructure  projects  amounting  to
₹ 679.46  crore  were  approved  during  the  last  three  years,  only  17  projects  ( ₹ 384.97  crore)
have  been  completed,  indicating  implementation  bottlenecks.  Given  that  the  Scheme  is
demand-driven  and  funds  are  released  scheme-wise  rather  than  state-wise,  disparities  in
project  readiness  may  affect  uniform  sports  development.  The  Committee  recommends
that  a  project  monitoring  dashboard  with  tracking  and  third-party  technical  audits
support  to  State  implementing  agencies  be  developed  to  expedite  completion  of
infrastructure projects and ensure optimal utilization of investments.
(Para 6.7.16)
66. The  Committee  appreciates  the  comprehensive  athlete  support  framework  under  the
Khelo  India  Talent  Identification  &  Development  (KITD)  vertical,  including  financial
assistance  of  ₹ 6.28  lakh  per  annum  per  athlete  and  expansion  of  multiple  editions  of  the
Khelo  India  Games  with  participation  of  over  61,000  athletes.  However,  to  ensure
constant  high  performance  and  measurable  outcomes,  the  Committee  recommends  that
periodic  performance  evaluation  of  Khelo  India  Athletes  and  accredited  academies  be
undertaken  through  clearly  defined  benchmarks  linked  to  national  and  international
medal  prospects,  with  better  coordination  between  Khelo  India  Centres,  State  Centres  of
Excellence and National Coaching Camps.
(Para 6.7.17)
67.
The  Committee  also  notes  the  integration  of  allied  initiatives  such  as  women ’s  leagues
across  34  disciplines,  promotion  of  indigenous  sports,  and  alignment  with  mass
participation  movements  like  Fit  India.  While  these  initiatives  contribute  to  social
inclusion,  gender  equity  and  community  engagement,  the  Committee  recommends  that  an
impact  assessment  framework  taking  into  account  participation  metrics,  and  socio-

108
economic  outreach  indicators  should  be  developed,  so  as  to  evaluate  long-term  outcomes
and monitor future budgetary allocations should be developed under the Scheme.
(Para 6.7.18)
68. The  Committee  notes  that  the  Scheme  for  Enhancement  of  Sports  Facility  in  Jammu  &
Kashmir  has  exhibited  considerable  budgetary  fluctuation,  with  no  expenditure  incurred
in  FY  2024 – 25.  On  the  other  hand,  the  Budget  Estimate  of  ₹ 20.00  crore  for  FY  2025 – 26
reduced  to  ₹ 2.00  crore  only  at  the  Revised  Estimate  stage,  and  the  allocation  for  FY
2026 – 27  fixed  at  ₹ 5.00  crore  against  projections  of  ₹ 8.00  crore.  Such  wide  variations  may
delay  in  project  finalization  and  implementation,  or  procedural  constraints  in  fund
release.  Considering  the  strategic  importance  of  strengthening  sports  infrastructure  in
Jammu  &  Kashmir  for  youth  engagement  and  integration  of  regional  talent  into  national
competitions,  the  Committee  recommends  that  a  time-bound,  project-specific
implementation  roadmap  with  clear  milestones,  streamlined  approval  processes  and
quarterly  monitoring  mechanisms  should  be  prepared,  so  as  to  ensure  timely  execution  of
sanctioned  works  and  avoid  cost  overruns  to  achieve  intended  sporting  outcomes  in  the
region.
(Para 6.8.3)
69. General  industrial  zones  often  lack  the  required  testing  labs  required  for  sports
equipment.  The  Committee  is  of  the  view  that  manufacturing  centres  in  exiting  industrial
hubs,  already  equipped  with  common  facilities  for  carbon  fiber  molding,  wood  seasoning,
and  synthetic  leather  processing  may  be  developed  for  successful  implementation  of
sports goods manufacturing schools. 
(Para 6.9.6)
70. The  Committee  may  recommend  that  the  Department  of  Sports  ensure  timely  declaration
of  National  Sports  Awards  every  year  through  a  fixed  annual  calendar.  Further,  the
selection  criteria,  evaluation  parameters  and  marks  awarded  by  the  selection  committee
may  be  placed  in  the  public  domain  after  the  awards  are  announced.  This  would  enhance
transparency,  credibility  and  public  confidence  in  the  award  selection  process  while
ensuring that deserving sportspersons and coaches are recognized without undue delay.
(Para 6.10.3)
71. The  Committee  may  also  recommend  that  the  Government  periodically  revise  the
quantum  of  cash  incentives  and  pension  provided  under  the  Scheme  of  Cash  Incentive  to
Medal  Winners  and  the  Sports  Fund  for  Pension  to  Meritorious  Sportspersons,  taking
into  account  inflation  and  rising  training  costs.  The  scope  of  the  pension  scheme  may  also
be  expanded  to  cover  a  larger  number  of  deserving  retired  sportspersons,  particularly
those  from  less-popular  sports  disciplines,  to  ensure  financial  security  and  encourage
greater participation in sports across the country.
(Para 6.10.4)

109
72. The  Committee  notes  that  the  Scheme  of  Cash  Incentive  to  Medal  Winners  in
International  Sports  Events  and  their  Coaches  has  played  a  vital  role  in  rewarding
excellence  and  motivating  sportspersons  to  achieve  higher  standards  at  global  platforms.
However,  in  view  of  the  evolving  competitive  landscape  and  rising  performance
benchmarks,  the  Committee  recommends  that  a  comprehensive  review  of  the  incentive
structure  should  be  undertaken  to  ensure  timely  disbursement,  rationalization  of  award
slabs  in  line  with  inflation  and  international  standards,  and  greater  transparency  in
eligibility  criteria,  particularly  with  regard  to  coaches  and  support  staff  who  contribute
significantly to medal-winning performances.
(Para 6.13.5)
73. The  Committee  further  observes  that  while  the  National  Sports  Awards  continue  to
recognize  outstanding  sportspersons  and  coaches  under  various  categories,  fluctuations  in
the  number  of  awardees  and  the  discontinuation  or  restructuring  of  certain  awards  call
for  greater  clarity  and  consistency.  The  Committee  recommends  that  the  Ministry
establish  a  stable,  well-publicized  selection  calendar  with  clearly  defined  evaluation
parameters,  digital  nomination  processes,  and  wider  stakeholder  consultation  so  as  to
preserve the prestige of the Awards and enhance their credibility and outreach.
(Para 6.13.6)
74. With  regard  to  the  Scheme  of  Sports  Fund  for  Pension  to  Meritorious  Sportspersons,  the
Committee  notes  a  declining  trend  in  allocation,  and  number  of  beneficiaries  over  the  last
five  years  despite  the  Scheme ’s  objective  of  providing  assured  post-retirement  financial
security.  The  Committee  recommends  to  review  eligibility  norms  and  pension  rates
periodically,  expand  the  beneficiary  base  where  warranted,  and  ensure  automatic  revision
mechanisms  linked  to  cost-of-living  criteria  so  that  former  sportspersons  who  have
brought laurels to the nation are not left in financial distress.
(Para 6.13.7)
75. The  Committee  also  notes  that  under  the  Pandit  Deendayal  Upadhyay  National  Welfare
Program  for  Sportspersons,  allocations  have  remained  constant  at  ₹ 2.00  crore  annually,
while  expenditure  has  shown  a  gradual  decline  in  recent  years.  Considering  that  the
Scheme  is  intended  to  provide  urgent  financial  assistance  for  medical  treatment,  injuries
and  other  exigencies  of  sports  persons/  their  family  members,  the  Committee  recommends
that  to  strengthen  awareness  among  eligible  beneficiaries,  simplify  application  procedures
through  an  online  portal,  and  create  a  fast-track  mechanism  for  medical  emergencies  to
ensure  that  deserving  sportspersons  receive  timely  support.  Further,  the  Committee  also
recommends  that  necessary  steps  should  be  taken  for  continuation  of  this  scheme  during
the next Financial Cycle ( i.e.  2026-2031)
(Para 6.13.8)

110
76. The  Committee  further  observes  that  the  various  talent  development  and  training
schemes  implemented  through  SAI  institutions — including  National  Centres  of  Excellence
(NCOEs),  SAI  Training  Centres  (STCs),  NSTC  and  Indigenous  Games  initiatives — have
detailed  induction,  retention  and  monitoring  criteria  based  on  scientific  assessment  and
performance  benchmarks.  While  these  frameworks  are  comprehensive,  the  Committee
recommends  that  a  unified  digital  athlete  management  system  be  developed  to  integrate
performance  data,  scientific  assessments,  training  diaries,  medical  records  and  academic
support  details  across  all  centres , thereby  enabling  real-time  monitoring,  minimizing
duplication,  preventing  age  fraud  and  doping-related  irregularities,  and  ensuring  a
transparent and merit-based development from grassroots to elite levels.
(Para 6.13.9)
77. The  Committee  notes  that  the  Autonomous  Bodies  under  the  Department  of
Sports — namely  the  Sports  Authority  of  India  (SAI),  National  Anti-Doping
Agency  (NADA),  National  Dope  Testing  Laboratory  (NDTL),  National  Sports
University  (NSU)  and  Lakshmibai  National  Institute  of  Physical  Education
(LNIPE) — play  a  pivotal  role  in  strengthening  training  infrastructure,  anti-
doping  mechanisms,  sports  education  and  scientific  support  systems.  While
the  overall  allocation  under  Other  Central  Sector  Expenditure  –  Autonomous
Bodies  has  increased  from  ₹ 1,603.73  crore  at  RE  2025 – 26  to  ₹ 1,777.90  crore  at
BE  2026 – 27,  there  is  a  considerable  variations  and  fluctuations  in  fund
allocations  between  Autonomous  Bodies  over  the  years.  The  Committee
recommends  that  a  performance-based  funding  framework  may  be  adopted
for  Autonomous  Bodies,  with  a  focus  to  measurable  outcomes  such  as  medal
performance,  research  output,  anti-doping  compliance  standards  and  athlete
outreach parameters.
(Para 7.3.5)
78. The  Committee  observes  variations  in  fund  allocations  to  a  few  institutions,
particularly  the  National  Sports  University  and  the  National  Dope  Testing
Laboratory,  with  significant  differences  between  Budget  Estimates  and
Revised  Estimates  in  successive  years.  Such  variations  may  affect  planning,
faculty  recruitment,  research  continuity  and  laboratory  accreditation
standards.  The  Committee,  therefore,  recommends  that  annual  budgetary
provisions  be  aligned  with  approved  long-term  development  plans  of  these
institutions,  with  funds  provisions  for  committed  liabilities  and  capital
projects, so as to ensure stability of such institutions.
(Para 7.3.6)
79. The  Committee  also  notes  the  central  role  of  the  Sports  Authority  of  India,
which  continues  to  receive  the  largest  share  of  funding  among  Autonomous
Bodies,  alongside  critical  institutions  such  as  NADA,  NDTL  etc.  In  view  of  the
increasing  emphasis  on  clean  and  scientific  training  of  sports,  the  Committee
recommends  that  greater  institutional  coordination  among  SAI,  NADA,
NDTL,  NSU  and  LNIPE  should  be  developed  through  a  inter-institutional

111
coordination  mechanism  for  data  sharing,  research  collaboration,  sports
science  integration  and  athlete  monitoring,  thereby  optimizing  resource
utilization and enhancing sports performance ecosystem of the country.
(Para7.3.7)
80. The  Committee  notes  that  the  Sports  Authority  of  India  (SAI)  continues  to  play  a  central
role  in  achieving  sporting  excellence  through  its  multi-tiered  talent  identification  and
training  framework  comprising  National  Centres  of  Excellence  (NCOEs),  SAI  Training
Centres  (STCs),  Extension  Centres  and  NSTC  schemes.  In  view  of  the  enhanced
allocation  of  ₹ 917.38  crore  in  BE  2026 – 27  as  compared  to  ₹ 880  crore  at  RE  2025 – 26,  the
Committee  recommends  that  SAI  should  formulate  performance  based  such  as  medal
conversion  rates,  athlete  progression  from  STCs  to  NCOEs,  and  other  performance
benchmarks  to  financial  allocations,  so  as  to  ensure  optimal  utilization  of  enhanced
budgetary support.
(Para 7.2.18)
81. The  Committee  observes  that  while  SAI  has  expanded  its  footprint  across  10  Regional
Centres  and  2  Academic  Institutions  with  187  operational  units  nationwide,  disparities  in
infrastructure  development  and  utilization  and  athlete  density  across  regions  remain  as
bottlenecks  for  balanced  sports  development.  The  Committee  recommends  that  a  region-
wise  capacity  and  performance  audit  be  undertaken  to  rationalize  disciplines  based  on
local  strengths,  optimize  coach  deployment,  and  ensure  equitable  access  to  high-quality
training facilities, particularly in tribal, rural and remote areas.
(Para 7.2.19)
82. The  Committee  appreciates  the  structured  talent  scouting  mechanism  under  Khelo  India,
TOPS  Development  Group  and  Long-Term  Athlete  Development  (LTAD)  framework,
supported  by  scientific  monitoring  and  multidisciplinary  teams.  However,  to  strengthen
transparency  and  long-term  athlete  tracking,  the  Committee  recommends  development  of
an  integrated  digital  athlete  performance  management  system  across  all  SAI  schemes,
taking  into  account  data  on  training  load,  injury  management,  competition  results  etc. ,
thereby  enabling  practical  decision-making  for  overall  development  of  Sports  in  the
country.
(Para 7.2.20)
83. The  Committee  takes  note  of  the  recruitment  of  coaches  under  regular  and  contractual
categories  and  recognizes  the  importance  of  qualified  human  resources  in  achieving  high
performance  standards.  The  Committee,  therefore,  recommends  to  expedite  the  filling  up
of  sanctioned  vacancies  through  a  time-bound  recruitment  calendar,  thereby  enhancing
continuous  professional  development  of  coaches  through  international  certifications  and
exposure.
(Para 7.2.21)

112
84. The  Committee  acknowledges  the  measures  adopted  by  SAI  to  ensure  safety  and  welfare
of  athletes,  including  constitution  of  Internal  Complaints  Committees,  24×7  toll-free
helplines  and  hostel  security  arrangements.  While  these  initiatives  are  commendable,  the
Committee  is  of  the  view  that  periodic  independent  safety  audits  of  SAI  centres ,
mandatory  gender-sensitization  and  safeguarding  workshops  for  all  staff  and  trainees,
should  be  considered,  so  as  to  create  a  secure  and  sporting  environment  across  all  SAI
establishments.
(Para 7.2.22)
85. The  Committee  notes  that  the  Lakshmibai  National  Institute  of  Physical  Education
(LNIPE),  Gwalior,  is  dedicated  to  higher  education,  research  and  specialization  in
physical  education  and  sports  sciences  and  plays  a  crucial  role  in  strengthening  the
academic  and  professional  foundation  of  the  sports  ecosystem  in  the  country.  While  the
enhanced  allocation  of  ₹ 87.50  crore  in  BE  2026 – 27  over  ₹ 79.96  crore  at  RE  2025 – 26  is
primarily  attributable  to  salary  revisions,  pension  liabilities,  filling  up  of  posts  and
anticipated  construction  activities  at  both  Gwalior  and  NERC  campuses,  the  Committee
is  of  the  view  that  a  comprehensive  academic  and  infrastructure  development  plan  should
be  prepared  with  clearly  defined  research  priorities,  faculty  recruitment  plans  etc.  so  as  to
ensure  that  higher  allocations  translates  into  tangible  improvements  in  teaching  quality,
research output and institutional excellence in physical education and sports sciences.
(Para 7.3.3)
86. The  Committee  notes  with  appreciation  that  the  Fit  India  Movement  has  evolved  into  a
nationwide  behavioural  transformation  initiative,  with  extensive  outreach  through
programmes  such  as  Sundays  on  Cycle,  Fit  India  Freedom  Run,  National  Sports  Day
celebrations,  International  Yoga  Day  activities,  Fit  India  Carnivals,  Cycling  Clubs  and
the  Fit  India  Mobile  App.  The  large-scale  participation  across  districts,  educational
institutions  and  rural  areas  reflects  commendable  public  engagement  and  policy
convergence.  However,  in  order  to  ensure  sustained  impact  beyond  event-based
mobilization,  the  Committee  recommends  that  a  systematic  monitoring  and  evaluation
framework  with  outcome  indicators  such  as  measurable  improvements  in  physical
activity  levels  in  schools  and  communities,  integration  of  physical  education  in  curricula,
utilisation  metrics  of  Fit  India  Zones  and  Cycling  Clubs,  and  behavioral  change  surveys
may  be  developed  so  that  the  Movement  transitions  from  mass  participation  campaigns  to
a fitness ecosystem with long-term public health and youth development goals.
(Para 7.4.3)
87. The  Committee  notes  with  satisfaction  that  the  National  Dope  Testing  Laboratory
(NDTL)  has  secured  continued  accreditation  from  WADA  and  NABL  under  ISO
17025:2017,  established  a  WADA-approved  Athlete  Passport  Management  Unit,  and
strengthened  its  Quality  Management  Systems,  research  collaborations  and

113
infrastructure  in  accordance  with  international  standards.  These  developments  signify
India ’s  growing  credibility  in  the  global  anti-doping  framework.  However,  considering
the  dynamic  nature  of  doping  methodologies  and  the  need  for  constant  technological
upgradation , the  Committee  recommends  that  the  Ministry  should  ensure  assured  and
dedicated  financial  support  for  periodic  modernization  of  analytical  equipment,
expansion  of  research  capabilities,  and  continuous  capacity  building  of  scientific
personnel,  so  that  NDTL  remains  at  par  with  leading  WADA-accredited  laboratories
worldwide.
(Para 7.5.5)
88. The  Committee  notes  a  sharp  decline  in  internal  revenue  generation  from  2024 – 25
onwards  due  to  the  waiver  of  Dope  Control  Testing  Fee  for  NADA,  which  constitutes  the
majority  of  sample  inflow.  While  the  waiver  may  serve  broader  policy  objectives,  the
resultant  reduction  in  institutional  revenue  generation  could  impact  long-term
operational  sustainability  and  research  activities.  The  Committee,  therefore,  recommends
that  a  calibrated  funding  mechanism — either  through  enhanced  budgetary  support  or
diversification  of  testing  services  including  regional  collaborations  and  specialised
research  assignments  should  be  developed  to  compensate  for  the  revenue  shortfall  and
ensure that the Laboratory ’s financial stability is not compromised.
(Para7.5.6)
89. The  Committee  notes  that  the  National  Anti-Doping  Agency  (NADA)  plays  a  crucial  role
in  maintaining  the  integrity  of  Indian  sports  through  testing,  results  management,
regulatory  enforcement  and  extensive  education  and  awareness  generation  initiatives.
While  the  Agency  has  instituted  robust  mechanisms  in  compliance  with  the  World  Anti-
Doping  Code,  including  trained  Doping  Control  Officers,  strict  chain-of-custody
procedures  and  dissemination  of  educational  materials  in  regional  languages,  the  data  on
Anti-Doping  Rule  Violations  (ADRVs)  indicates  fluctuating  trends  and  continuous
violations  in  recent  years.  The  Committee,  therefore,  recommends  that  NADA  should
take  targeted  initiatives,  sport-specific  and  grassroots-level  preventive  educational
programmes,  particularly  in  high-incidence  disciplines  and  vulnerable  regions,  with  a
focus  on  supplement  awareness,  inadvertent  doping  risks  and  planned  engagement
through federations and training academies. 
(Para 7.6.8)
90. The  Committee  notes  that  the  Budget  Estimates  for  both  NADA  and  the  National  Dope
Testing  Laboratory  (NDTL)  for  FY  2026 – 27  has  reduced  compared  to  the  Revised
Estimates  of  FY  2025 – 26,  even  though  anti-doping  monitoring  responsibilities  and
international  compliance  obligations  continue  to  expand  as  cases  of  Anti-Doping  Rule
violation  cases  continue  to  occur  as  evident  from  Table  no.  36.  Although  the  allocation  is
stated  to  be  adequate  at  the  BE  stage,  continues  testing,  technological  upgradation  and

114
expanded  outreach  require  stable  financial  support.  The  Committee  recommends  that  the
Ministry  closely  monitor  fund  utilisation  and  testing  coverage  during  the  financial  year
should  be  monitored  and  ensure  timely  augmentation  of  funds  at  the  Revised  Estimates
stage,  if  warranted,  so  that  financial  constraints  do  not  adversely  impact  testing  frequency
or international compliance commitments.
(Para 7.6.9)
91. The  Committee  notes  that  the  National  Sports  University  (NSU),  envisioned  as  a  premier
institution  for  sports  education,  research  and  training,  has  made  progress  in  launching
specialised  undergraduate,  postgraduate  and  doctoral  programmes  in  Sports  Coaching,
Sports  Sciences,  Sports  Psychology  and  Applied  Sports  Nutrition.  The  University ’s
collaborations  with  reputed  international  universities  and  national  research  institutions,
along  with  its  focus  on  innovation  and  integration  of  laboratory  research  into  real-time
sports  settings,  reflect  its  potential  to  emerge  as  a  centre  of  excellence.  However,  the
Committee  notes  that  the  University  continues  to  function  from  a  temporary  campus  at
Khuman  Lampak  Sports  Complex,  Imphal.  The  Committee,  therefore,  recommends  that
priority  to  the  expeditious  completion  and  operationalisation  of  the  permanent  campus
with  world-class  academic,  research  and  residential  infrastructure  should  be  accorded,  so
that  the  University  may  fully  realise  its  mandate  as  a  national  training  centre  and  global
hub for sports education and research.
(Para 7.7.5)
92. The  Committee  further  notes  that  while  NSU  has  developed  modern  laboratories,  sports
infrastructure  and  industry  partnerships,  the  intake  capacity  across  programmes  remains
relatively  modest  considering  the  national  demand  for  qualified  sports  scientists,  coaches
and  support  professionals.  In  order  to  strengthen  India ’s  sports  ecosystem  move  in  a
fruitful  manner,  the  Committee  recommends  that  a  phased  expansion  plan  for  increasing
student  intake,  diversifying  specialised  disciplines,  and  enhancing  faculty  strength,
alongside  sustainable  Operation  &  Maintenance  mechanisms  should  be  formulated  for
better  development  of  Sports  ecosystem  in  the  country.  Greater  integration  with  National
Centres  of  Excellence,  Khelo  India  Centres  and  sports  federations  may  also  be
institutionalised  to  ensure  that  academic  output  directly  contributes  to  athlete
performance enhancement and capacity building across the country.
(Para 7.7.6)
93. The  Committee  notes  that  the  overall  representation  of  Women  and  other  categories  in
the  Main  Secretariat  and  in  key  technical  and  scientific  institutions  such  as  NADA,  NDTL
and  NSU  including  SAI  is  not  encouraging.  The  Committee,  therefore,  recommends  that  a
comprehensive  recruitment  policy  may  be  formulated  with  measurable  targets  and
periodic  review  mechanisms  to  enhance  representation  of  women  and  other  categories  in
various fields required for development of Sports ecosystem in the country.
(Para 8.6)

115
94. The  Committee  further  observes  variations  in  representation  of  SC,  ST,  OBC  and
Persons  with  Disabilities  (PWD)  across  organisations , with  comparatively  low  PWD
representation  and  certain  shortfalls  in  reserved  categories  in  specific  bodies.  While
reservation  policies  are  stated  to  be  followed  as  per  Government  norms,  the  Committee
recommends  that  a  detailed  reservation  roster  audit  be  undertaken  across  all  institutions
under  the  Department  of  Sports  to  identify  backlog  vacancies,  if  any,  and  to  initiate
special  recruitment  drives  to  ensure  full  compliance  with  statutory  reservation  provisions
and inclusive workforce participation.
(Para 8.7)
95. The  Committee  notes  the  considerable  reliance  on  contractual  appointments  over  the  past
five  years,  particularly  in  SAI  and  NADA,  where  contractual  engagement  appears
significantly  higher  than  permanent  recruitment.  While  contractual  hiring  may  provide
operational  flexibility,  continuous  dependence  on  such  arrangements  may  affect
institutional  memory,  continuity  of  programmes  and  accountability  structures.  The
Committee  recommends  that  a  manpower  rationalisation  exercise  should  be  undertaken
to  assess  core  versus  project-based  requirements  and  progressively  regularise  essential
positions  through  sanctioned  permanent  posts,  thereby  ensuring  long-term  organisational
stability.
(Para 8.8)
96. The  Committee  also  observes  that  permanent  recruitment  in  several  institutions  such  as
NSU,  NDTL  and  LNIPE  has  been  limited  in  recent  years,  which  may  constrain  academic
expansion,  research  output  and  technical  efficiency.  The  Committee  recommends  that
recruitment  processes  be  streamlined  and  expedited  in  coordination  with  the  competent
authorities so that sanctioned posts are filled in a time-bound manner.
(Para 8.9)
97. The  Committee  notes  about  the  vacancy  position  at  LNIPE,  NERC,  Guwahati , including
the  vacant  Professor  post  and  two  Assistant  Professor  posts . Given  the  critical  role  of
faculty  in  maintaining  academic  excellence,  research  supervision  and  curriculum
development,  the  Committee  recommends  that  immediate  steps  be  taken  to  fill  these
vacancies  and  to  periodically  review  sanctioned  strength  in  light  of  expanding  academic
programmes and student intake.
(Para 8.10)
98. The  Committee  recommends  that  a  centralised  Human  Resource  Monitoring  and
Planning  Framework  within  the  Department  of  Sports  may  be  established,  incorporating
sanctioned  strength,  persons  in  position,  vacancies,  category-wise  representation,
contractual  engagements  and  recruitment  timelines  across  all  subordinate  bodies.  Such  a
structured  monitoring  mechanism  would  enhance  transparency,  facilitate  evidence-based

116
workforce  planning  and  ensure  optimal  deployment  of  human  resources  in  furtherance  of
the Department ’s expanding mandate and long-term strategic objectives.
(Para 8.11)

INTRODUCTION 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human 
Resource Development, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its 
behalf, do hereby present the Fourth· Report of the Committee on the National Health 
Programme s of the Department of Health (Ministry of Health & Family Welfare). 
The Committee considered various documents and papers received from the Department of 
Health and also heard its Secretary and other officials to elicit further information at its meetings 
held on the lOth & 11th June, 1993. 
The details of the working, targets, achievements, allocations and expe nditur e regarding 
major Nationa l Health Programmes of the Department viz. National Malaria Eradication 
Programme; Kala-azar; National Filaria Control Progr amme; Nationa l Lepr0sy Eradicat ion 
Programme; National Programme for Co'1trol of Blindness and National AIDS Control 
Programme were discussed by the Committee and have been included in the Report. 
The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its sitting held on the 16th December, 
1993.

An Overview 
1. 'Health is Wealth' is a well-known proverb and it is an axiomatic fact that only healthy 
citizens can make a nation prosperous and healthy. Health plays a vital role in the making of a 
nation great and strong. Development and maintenance of good health is not only a personal or 
an individual effort but a Welfare State also plays a very important role in it. 
2. It is expressly mentioned in our Constitution in Article 47, which relates to the Directive 
Principles of State Policy, that 'The State shall regard the raising of the level of nutrition and the 
standard of living of its people an~ the improvement of public health among its primary duties ... ' 
The improvement of health and ritilrition on national basis is the respon sibility of the Central 
Council of Health. Since the inception of planning process in 1952, various health programmes 
have been introduced in the country. In pursuance of its commitment, Government also 
formulated a national Policy on Health in 1983. 
3. But, the dimensions that health problems have acquired in our country are really complex 
and alarming. Majority of diseases people suffer from are poverty-related , while some have their 
origin in the utter Jack of cleanliness and awareness or consciousness towards health. Rapid 
increase in environmental pollution , increasing population, cropping up of new diseases like 
AIDS and cancer are some of the challenges that the nation is facing today. To fight on all these 
fronts simultaneously is, of course, a formidable task, particularly when the resources at hand are 
limited. 
4. As per World Bank estimates, in India only 1.3% of the Gross Domestic Product is spent 
on health which is perhaps the lowest amongst the developing countries. It is flabbergasting to 
f~rther note that the alloca tion has shown a gradual diminishing trend in the successive Five Y car 
Plans. For instance, 3.3% of the total outlay in the First Five Year Plan has come down to a 
dismal 2:74% during the Eighth Five Year Plan. In the face of the financial constraints foreign 
assistance was sought. Some traditional diseases like Leprosy, Tuberculosis, Malaria, Blindness, 
~tc. still persist affecting the majority of our population. In such a situation, it is to be seen if 
Government's commitment to attain the goal of health for all by 2000 A.D. could possibly be 
fulfilled. 
5. World Bank assistance to the scale of 100 to 200 million dollars per year has been cleared 
for Health sector throughout the Eighth Five Year Plan. The first project taken up under this 
project is the AIDS Control Programme. A<>sistance is also expected for Leprosy and Blindness 
Control Programmes. 
6. In an effort to fight the menace of major diseases Government is implementing various 
National Health Programmes. The Committee had detailed deliberations on some of them 
namely; National Malaria Eradication Programme; Kala-azar; National Filaria Control Prog­
ramme; National Leprosy Eradication Programme; National Programm e for Contro l of Blindness 
and the National AIDS Control Jirogramme . 

I. National Malaria Eradication Programme 
7. It is estimated that at the time of country's Independence in 1947, there were over 75 
million malaria cases and about one million deaths had occured due to it. For its control, a 
national strategy was formulated in the year 1953. DDT proved to be a very effective insecticide 
and a great success was achieved in controlling this disesase. Encouraged by this initial success, 
the National Malaria Control was renamed as 'National Malaria Eradication Programme ' in the 
year 1958. By the year 1965, the incidence of malaria witnessed a downward trend, with nil 
mortality rat e which was, in itself, a great achievement. But this success was short-lived as in the 
mid-seventies recurrence of malaria was visible. There was a sharp increase in the number of 
reported malaria cases to the tune of 6.47 million per year. The strategy was revised once again 
named Modified Plan of Operation (MPO) ·with the objective of elimination of mortality rate, 
effective control of malaria and maintaining the gains achieved so far in its eradication. The 
objectives were sought to be achieved by prompt case- detection through active and passive 
surveillance and vector control by residual insecticidal spraying. 
8. Since 1984, the incidence of malaria has stabi lized at around 2 million cases per year. It is 
reported that during the year 1991, there were 1.81 million positive cases of malaria and around 
400 deaths. During the year 1992, there were approximately 1.4 million reported malaria cases. 
Though tribals constitute only 8% of the total population, yet they account for over 30% of the 
malaria cases and 60% of the deaths on account of P. Falciparum. Similarly, there was a sharp 
increase in the number of cases detected in urban slums from 1,39,057 in 1989 to 2,11,890 in 
1991. Studies and surveys conducted in this regard have shown the presence of resistance to DDT 
and a combination of anti-malaria insecticides. 
9. There are Seven States in the country namely, Madhya Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, 
Gujarat, Maharashtra, Orissa and Rajasthan which are more vulnerable and most of the malaria 
deaths have occured there. According to the Annual Report of the Ministry of Health & Family 
Welfare for the year 1992-93, Malaria cases during the last five years indicated that in the year 
1988, ther( have been 1.85 million cases with 0.68 million P. Falciparum cases and 209 deaths. In 
1989, there were 2.05 malaria cases with 0.76 million P. Falciparum cases and 268 deaths, in 1990 
out of the 2.02 million malaria cases there have been 0.75 million P. Falciparum cases with 353 
deaths, in 1991 out of 2.11 million malaria cases there were 0.91 million P. Falciparum cases with 
421 deaths and in 1992, there were 1.42 million cases with 0.45 million P. Falciparum cases and 
246 deaths. 
10. The National Malaria Eradication Programme is being implemented as a centrally 
sponsored category-11 on a 50:50 cost sharing basis between the States and the Central 
Government. Under this Programme, the Central Government meet s the cost of entire quantity 
of DDT and partially of BHC and Malathion, antimalaria drugs like Chloroquine, Primaquine 
and Pyrenthamine, etc. The State Governments are expected to meet the expenditure on staff 
and other operational costs for successful implementation of the Programme. 
11. During his oral evidence tendered before the Committee , the Secretary, Department of 
Health , informed that malaria has taken an endemic turn because of the fact that the health 
infrastructure in the most affected States is'ex tremely weak. The Dcptt. has also reali sed that the 
tribal and hilly areas where malaria infection cases are high, have to be dealt with on a different 
footing from the rest of the country. Fifty per cent share of the States has to be reviewed and the 

Central Government is thinking to have the central scheme implemented by taking assistance 
from World Bank to fight this menance. Keeping this in view, it is proposed to intensify the 
efforts for the full containment of malaria during the Eighth Five Year Plan. Accordingly, major 
attention is proposed to be given to the tribal sub-plan areas of Seven States of Andhra Pradesh, 
Bihar, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Orissa and Rajasthan, the urban population and 
population living in the project areas and rest of the country. This control strategy is a balanced 
mixture of preventive and curative measures for elective spraying for vector control, larviciding 
and source reduction in urban areas and early detection and treatment. 
12. During his oral evidence tendered before the Committee, the Secretary, Department of 
Health, informed that they had achieved a great initial success in controlling malaria, but when 
the incidence reached a figure of 1,00,000 in the entire country in the seventies, they liad a 
rebound and the incidence rose to about 6.5 million. Thereafter, the programme was started in 
1977 and they were able to bring this figure down to 2 million in 1984. After that, this figure has 
more or less ramained stable. It means there has been n0 further improvement after 1984. This 
was due to a very high level of infection in the tribal areas of North-East. The migrant labour 
iorce from these areas going to different parts of the country also contributes to the spread of 
Malaria. A lot of on going construction activities contribute to the cause of stagnation of water 
and pollute environment leading to breeding of mosquitoes, hence the incidence of malaria. 
13. The Committee was informed that for this purpose, a sum of Rs. 86 corres was spent 
during the year 1991-92. In 1992-93, Rs. 65 crores were allocated for malaria control programme 
which also included other vector diseases like Kala-azar and Filaria. Now, this amount has been 
increased to Rs. 87 crores for procuring insecticides, larvicides and drugs. For the year 1993-94, a 
sum of Rs. 110 crores has been allotted. It is also proposed to provide 100% Central assistance to 
the North Eastern States and the tribal sub-plan areas. For the tribal areas, it is also proposed to 
mobilise resourc es from the World Bank as well. 
14. The Committee was informed that there was mainly three reasons for the resurgence of 
malaria, namely:-
(i) Administrative reasons-complacency shown by the administration after getting some 
initial success. 
(ii) Technical reasons-
(a) Mosquitoes became immune to many insecticides and the insecticides which were 
very effective in the past became ineffective; 
(b) the parasites have been irresistable to certain drugs; 
(c) New drugs were tried out which also contributed in non-effectiveness of the 
programme to some extent. 
(iii) Financial reasons- The programme was integrated into the Primary Health Centres after 
getting initial success in the sixties. The Primary Health Centres being very busy in their 
own programmes, could . not provide attention and time which was very necessary for 
controlling malaria. Even financial allocation required for filling up the posts which were 
available in the sub-centres for eradication of malaria remained unfilled; the supply of 
PLO, etc. was not available because of financial constraints. All these factors 
contributed to the failure of the programme. Even financial allocations were reduced. 

Kala-Azar 
15. Kala-azar is another deadly disease which has become a serious Public Health Problem in 
Bihar and West Bengal. It is observed that after its resurgence in Bihar in early 70s, the disease 
has spread over from 4 districts to adjoining areas and now 30 districts in Bihar and 9 districts in 
West Bengal are the most affected. This estimate is based on cases reported in Government 
hospitals only. Some cases go to private practitioners and thus remain unreported. The disease is 
on the increase and has assumed serious dimensions in the above two States. 
16. According to the estimates, there were 14079 Kala-azar cases in the year 1986 with 47 
deaths and in West-Bengal there were 3718 cases with 25 deaths in the same year. There has 
be~n a rap id increase both in its incidence as weB as deaths in Bihar. In the year 1989, there 
were 30903 cases with 477 deaths in Bihar and 3575 cases with 20 deaths in West Bengal. In t~e 
year 1992 there were 66959 Kala-azar cases in Bihar with 1266 deaths (provisional upto October). 
So there has been alarming increase, both in the incidence and the death cases in Bihar which 
requires immediate remedial steps. 
17. Organised control measures have been initiated to control Kala-azar. Upto 1990-91, 
financial assistance for its control was being provided by the Central Government out of the

20. The Central Government is providing insecticides and imported anti Kala-azar drug i.e. 
Pentamidine Isothionate to the West Bengal Government. The Central Government has also 
provided assistance to the Bihar Government in cash and kind during the last two years i.e. in

21. A budget provision of Rs. 1500.00 lakhs has been made to provide material assistance for

22. In addition UNICEF assistance of Rs. 15.55 lakh had been provided for 1990-91 to the

32. The Committee expresses its deep concern over the shortage of some effective and 
potent medicines to cure malaria particularly P. Falciparum and recommends that steps should be

techniques and no laxity be shown in this regard. The Committee also recommends that both

Programme should be given wide publicity through print and electronic media. Adequate supply 
of anti-filaria drugs in hospitals, dispensaries and in the open market be ensured apart from the 
usual spraying. 
II. National Leprosy Eradication Programme 
36. India has a very high rate of incidence of leprosy, which is widespread all over the 
country, and is one of the major health problems. 
37. The magnitude of the disease can be judged by the fact that as per the Ministry's Annual 
Report (1992-93), out of 10 million cases of leprosy in the world, 2.5 million are estimated to be 
found in India. The prevalance rate of leprosy exists above 5 per 1000 population in 201 districts 
out of 468 districts and about 15% of the leprosy sufferers arc children below 15 years of age. 
38. The leprosy control Programme, which was in existence since 1955, was given priority 
and redesignated as National Leprosy Eradication Programme in 1983. It is one of the centrally 
sponsored Health Schemes financed 100% by the Central government and implemented through 
State governments. 
39. During the course of his oral evidence tendered by the Secretary, Department of Health, 
the Committee was informed that the programme has been launched in 135 districts which are 
considered endemic i.e. where the prevalence rate is more than 5 per thousand. The Programme 
remains to be launched in 66 other districts which are in the same category. Then 

there are 77 other districts which are moderately endemic i.e. having a prevalance rate of 2 to 5 
per thousand. If these 143 districts are covered over and above 135 districts that are already 
covered then 95% of the leprosy patil·nts will be covered. 
40. The Committee was also informed that in the last 5-6 years, since the introduction of 
Multi-drug Therapy there has been a major breakthrough in bringing down the incidence of 
leprosy as out of estimated 4 million cases in 1981, the number has come down to 1.4 million by 
the end of february, 1993. Wherever the Multi-drug Therapy Programme has been in operation 
for more than 5 years, there is 80% reduction in incidence. 
41. The Secretary of the Health department stated that the programme has produced 
dramatic results and it is expected that leprosy would be eliminated from the country by the turn 
of the century, i.e. when the prevalence rate will be below 1 per 10,000 population. 
42. The Secretary of the department admitted that in an effort to cure more and more cases 
sufficient attention had not been paid to rehabilitation and reconstructive surgery and to help the 
patients lead a normal life after they are cured. 
43. Therefore, it is very necessary to have centres of reconstructive smgery and rehabilitation 
and a sustained health eduction campaign to make people understand that the patients who are 
cured or have undergone treatment for the disease arc absolutely safe and infection free. 
44. The Committee was informed that under the programme of major reconstructive surgery 
there is no plan to create new institutions instead under the world Bank project institutes where 
reconstructive surgery is available will be revamped and provided with equipments and appliances 
free of cost. 
45. These institutes will also be provided Rs. 250CY- for each major surgery and package of 
services which include full cost of operation service, OPD and total care of the patient. If an 
institute is not available within a district then the patient will be referred to any such institute 
established in a nearby district. In that case, the amount will be Rs. 250()1.. plus the 
reimbursement of travel expenses of the patient. 
46. It was informed that there are district Leprosy Officers in 105 districts in which Multi­
drug Therapy Programme has been taken up and also there is one doctor for every 4-5 lakhs of 
population. To ensure that the programme reaches every village there are village level workers 
for every 20,000 population who are supposed to go around and find out the cases and see that 
the services reach them for their treatment. 
47. The Secretary conceded that some posts of doctors are lying vacant in some districts and 
the State Governments have been urged to fill them up. 
48. There arc also District Leprosy Societies in all the districts where the programme has 
been taken-up. In the societies there are local representatives, members of Legislatures, 
panchayats etc. with whom various aspects of the programme are discussed. 
49. As regard role of Voluntary organisations it was informed that out of about 285 
voluntary organisations, 55 are receiving assistance from Central Government. The grants-in-aid 
are given under the Survey, Education and Treatment (S.E.T) Scheme and are released through 
the State Governments. 
50. The performance of the voluntary organisations are being closely monitored by the 
Central Government and also by the State Governments themselves. However, the Secretary 
admitted that it is possible that some voluntary organisations may not be performing upto the 
expectations but by and large they are doing commendable work. It was also informed that there

61. The Committee also recommends that some scheme be formulated for the poor patients

Committee is of the considered view that only doctors as District Leprosy Officer can properly

District Leprosy Officers. 
64. The Committee also recommends that wherever the post of District Leprosy Officer is 
vacant it should be immediately filled up and it should also be ensured that posts of District 
Leprosy Officers are not kept vacant for long durations. In case it is not possible to fill up the 
post for some reasons the alternative arrangements be made. 
65. The Committee feels that budget allocation of Rs. 35.00 crores for NLEP for the year

would lead to the reduction of the cost of Refampicin, which is a costly drug now. The 
Committee thinks that instead of the price of drugs being primarily within the purview of the 

Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, Health Ministry be also involved in this particularly in the 
case of basic drugs needed for national programmes.

70. The Secretary, Dcpa1tment of Health, Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, in his oral

71. The Committee takes it seriously that the achievement rate of cataract operations is

73. The Committee is surprised to find that no foolproof method has been adopted in

74. The Secretary , Department of Health informed the Committee that corneal blindness

76. The Committee feels that it is a very good step taken by Government in order to

National AIDS Control Programme 
78. Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS) has emerge d as one of the major 
public health problems in recent years. It is caused by human immuno deficiency virus (HIV). 
AIDS virus destroys the body's immune system i.e. strength to fight against disease. Hence 
the person becomes susceptible to all kinds of diseases and slowly and slowly goes down and 
dies. The virus spreads primarily through sexual intercourse, but can also be transmitted by 
sharing drug injecting needles, through transfusion of infected blood, and from infected 
mothers to their unborn and new born children. 
79. According to the World Health Organisation (WHO) estimate, there are about one 
million people infected with HIV in India. HIV infection in the country has been reported 
from as many as 23 States/Union Territories of which Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Delhi and 
Manipur have the highest incidence. 
80. The first HIV infection case in India was detected in Madras in 1986, in a survey 
conducted by the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR). Subsequently, the AIDS 
Control Programme was formulated in 1987, which has following components: (i) Surveillance; 
(ii) Safety of blood and blood products; and (iii) Health Education. 
81. A separate wing known as AIDS Control Organisation has been established in the 
Ministry of Health & Family Welfare from September/October, 1992, in order to co-ordinate 
the programme effectively. Since AIDS has no cure as of now, the thrust of the whole 
programme is on creation of awareness through information, communication and education for 
promotion of safe practices including safe sex, use of sterilised/disposable needles, use of 
uninfected blood and blood products etc. 
82. The Committee feels that proper and effective implementation of the National AIDS 
Control Programme is possible only when there exists essential infrastructure. In a country 
like India where a large number of population is illiterate, it is a challenging task to educate 
and arouse awareness to make them understand the causes of the disease and advise them on 
taking necessary precautions. In the absence of a vaccine, it is necessary to inform people as 
to how HIV is transmitted and educate them to protect themselves and their loved ones from 
the deadly disease. As the number of AIDS cases increase education aimed at preventing the 
syndrome becomes more important and imperative. 
83. During the course of his oral evidence tendered before the Committee, the Secretary, 
Department of Health informed that efforts are being made to educate people in order to 
control Sexually Transmitted Disease (STD) because it is one of the major factors for 
transmission of HIV infection. There are 332 STD clinics spread all over the country. Efforts 
are also being made to impart training to rural doctors so that they can identify the symptoms 
and refer the persons suffering from the disease to STD clinics. Alarming and rapid increase 
in IUV positive cases in our country has necessiated utmost and precautionary measure in the 
field of AIDS control. The Committee, therefore, recommends that it should be made 
mandatory to carry out HIV tests of persons who undergo normal blood tests in hospitals. It 
will in this way be easier to detect and screen out the AIDS cases. 
84. The Committee observes that services available in some of the STD clinics are not 
being properly utilised. The Committee recommends that efforts should be made to utilise the 
STD clinics fully for the treatment of the afflicted persons. 

85. The Committee feels the need tc launch a massive programme to promote public 
awareness and community support. So that myths and misconceptions about the disease could be 
obliterated. In this regard the Committee recommends that:-
(i) An advertisement campaign should be designed to reach large number of people with 
messages about prevention of AIDS. Television and radio spots may also be used. 
(ii) Leaflets should be published for distribution in various public forums and in health care 
facilities. Such material must contain latest medical information, reach new target popula­
tion, and should stress matters that survey results have indicated to be of special importance. 
This material may also be prepared in regional languages for distribution among local 
population. 
(iii) Forums should be set up and workshops, classes and seminars should be organised from time 
to time in different areas to enable members of the general public to interact with the 
experts. This will allay the fears and wrong notions which exist in society about the disease. 
(iv) Journalists and specialists should prepare articles to enhance readers' general knowledge and 
arouse awareness and understanding about AIDS. 
(v) The programme should be designed not only to inform the target population about the 
disease but also to motivate them to act on information they already possess. 
(vi) The programme should not rely entirely on printed and broadcast messages. Face to face 
education may also help people to clarify their misconceptions. More and more voluntary 
organisations may be encouraged to take up the challenging task of enlightening the people 
through the use of different media viz. drama, street plays, exhibitions and videos. 
(vii) W}lile educating people about the disease and its control, public sensibilities should be 
considered carefully . in order to make the programme acceptable to them. 
86. The Committee emphasises on the need to evolve broad AIDS Control Strategy covering 
all major aspects such as revamping of STD Control Programme, safe blood transfusion and 
streamlining infection control in hospitals. There should be a stricter enforcement of Screening of 
blood donors. Besides this, a responsible system of primary health care centres should also be 
established for providing psycho-social care to infected persons and to counter social ostracism 
against them. 
87. The Committee also stresses the need to encourage extensive grass-root participation of 
general public and voluntary organisations in the AIDS prevention and control programme. 
88. The indigenous systems of medicine contain a reservoir of wisdom which concerns public 
health. The Committee recommends that efforts may be made to revive and strengthen the 
traditional systems. Ayurveda and other indigenous systems of medicine may be encouraged to 
find treatment of the AIDS. 
89. Neem is found in abundance in India. Many International investigations and research 
studies have proved beyond doubt that it is very effective and safe in the cure of deadly diseases 
like AIDS and Cancer, etc. Therefore, the Committee recommends that concerted efforts should 
be made to harness the use of Neem and its products in the cure of AIDS and cancer in addition 
·to other such diseases. The Committee also recommends that more and more emphasis should be 
laid on research in this regard for which adequate funds should be provided. 
90. While the Committee agrees that proper precautionary measures should be taken to 
check the spread of HIV infection which might lead to AIDS, the Committee recommends for an 
indigenous study of AIDS cases in the country, for proper assessment of its extent, instead of 

relying on World Health Organisation report alone. The Committee fails to understand the 
reasons for the priority given to the anti-AIDS programme in the World Bank assisted scheme. 
While assistance is still to come for most of the other national programmes (e.g. Malaria 
Eradication Programme) and hardly any real increase in budgetary allocations has been made. 
The enormous quantum of World Bank assistance for the anti-AIDS programme seems to be 
totally lop-sided, to say the least. The Committee feels that instead of this lavishness, 
enhancement of allocation in basic health services like Anti-Malaria, Anti-Tuberculosrs Program­
mes, etc. would also have pre-empted spread of AIDS.

REPORT 
I. INTRODUCTION 
1.1. The Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare is instrumental and responsible 
for implementation of various programmes of national importance like family welfare, 
primary health care, prevention, control and eradication of major diseases which form the 
main plank of our development efforts. Apart from these, the Ministry also takes special 
care for preventing the spread of diseases assuming the dimension of epidemic. The 
Department of Health, under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, which is 
committed to achieve the goal of health for all by the year 2000 A.D. is responsible for 
evolving broad policies for the health sector and provides financial and technical assistance · 
to State Governments in critical areas through the implementation of important health 
programmes. 
1.2. Broadly, the objectives of the Department are to undertake National Health 
Programmes, to promote education, research and training in various medical disciplines, to 
prevent adu.Iteration of food as well as drugs, to provide primary health care at the door 
steps of the people, to take steps for better implementation of health care programmes for 
tribal and other weaker sections of the society and also to collaborate with member countries 
of United Nations and international agencies like WHO, UNICEF, etc. in matters relating 
to health promotion and development, etc. 
1.3. The Department finances a number of health programmes aimed at controlling 
Malaria, Leprosy, Blindness, AIDS, TB, Gunieawarm either on 100 per cent or on 50 per 
cent basis. The Department also finances wholly or substantially autonomous institutions 
engaged in patient care and or research such as All India Institute of Medical Sciences, 
Postgraduate Institute of Medical Education and Research , Chandigarh, All India Institute 
of Speech and Hearing, Mysore, Indian Council of Medical Research, New Delhi, National 
Institute of Mental Health and Neuro-Sciences, Bangalore etc. The Department also assists 
voluntary organisations and institutions substantially such as Indian Red Cross Society, New 
Delhi, Tuberculosis Centre, New Delhi, Lala Ram Swarup TB Hospital, Mehrauli, etc. 
1.4. The health infrastructure comprises of 2,385 Community Health Centres, 1,693 
Primary Health Centres and 1,31,900 Sub-centres. Some of the new programmes initiated 
·during the current financial year by the Department are Urban Hospital Waste 
Management, Setting up of National Illness Assistance Fund and National Blood Transfusion 
Council, Development of Public Private Partnership and Joint Sector Approach and 
Epidemiological Surveillance and Support System, etc. Pilot projects on Diabetes Control, 
Oral Health, Prevention of deafness and hearing impairment, micro nutrient, malnutrition, 
. medical rahabilitation and cardio-vascular diseases have also been initiated. 
1.5. The overall proportion of the Budget to the Health sector has not increased since 
the beginning of the first Plan. The Health Sector including Family Welfare has been getting 
only abo\tt 3 per cent of the total outlays through the successive Five-Year Plans. The 
Working Group for Health Financing set up by the Planning Commission for the 8th Five 
Year Plan had .recommended that the Health Sector allocation should not be less than 5% of 
the total outlay. The Fourth Conference of Central Council of Health and Family Welfart>. 
has recommended that the direct investment by the Government should be raised .to a 
minimum o(S per cent of the GDP and the total investment in health could go up to 10 per 
cent. The World Health Organisation (WHO) also recommended that the public health care 
expenditure should be at least 5 per cent of the GDP if equity and universal coverage is to 
be realised. However, as per the figures available, the total investment on health and family

1.8 The Committee feels that one of the important factors leading to rise in various 
diseases is the unhygienic conditions and lack of cleanliness all around in the public life. 
Conceding to this fact, the Secretary stated tha·t a Committee under the Convenorship of 
Shri M.S. Dayal, former Health Secretary, was constituted to examine this problem. The 
task of the Committee was to examine the ground situation and evolving Comprehensive · 
National Programme on Sanitation and Environmental Hygiene on the lines of a Technology 
Mission. The Committee submitted its report in July, 1995. The Department has further 
stated that the Committee of Secretaries discussed the matter and ·suggested that the . 
recommendations contained in the Dayal Committee Report pertaining to various Ministries/ 
Departments concerned with environment and sanitation may incorporate them in their 
respective 9th Plan proposals. The Committee desires that it should be given utmost priority 
in view of the deteriorating unhygienic conditions in public life. There is also an urgent need 
to educate people about civic sense and maintenance of cleanliness all around as unhygienic 
conditions are the root cause of many diseases especially the communicable disease. 
II. CENTRAL GOVERNMENT HEALTH SCHEME (CGHS) 
2.1 The Plan aliocation provided to the CGHS had been reduced from 7 crores in 
Budget Estimates for 1995-96 to Rs. 6.07 crores in RE 1995-96 and has further been slashed 
to Rs. 6 crores in BE 1996-97. When the Department was asked to explain the reasons for 
reduction the Department have stated that the CGHS was allocated Rs. 7 crores under BE 
.1995-96 (Plan). Due to non-implementation of disputed SIU Report of CGHS allopathic 
dispensaries the new proposals of CGHS were held up and not sanctioned by Ministry of 
Finance. Further, the approval for the 100 bedded hospital at Hyderabad which was included 
in the allocation for 1995-96 could not be obtained. Due to these reasons, the provision 
made for this purpose had to be surrendered/diverted for . other programmes, the 
Department added. The Committee is constrained to note that the Department could not 
• pursue the revision of SIU Report with Ministry of Finance. Revision of SIU Report is 
urgently needed for creation of new posts and opening of new CGHS dispensaries. Presently 
only a few cities in the country are covered and the Committee desires that all major cities 
should be covered at the earliest. Moreover, with the expansion of the metro cities, the 
coverage is not even and many pockets in these cities are not covered. Therefore, more 
dispensaries are required to be opened even in the cities where CGHS coverage is already 
there. For this. the Department would require additional funds. It is, therefore, necessary . 
that the Department should pursue the matter vigorously with the Ministry of Finance for 
the revision of SIU Report so that the allocation could be enhanced at the RE stage. The 
Committee has noted that the sanctioned strength of.C.G.H.S. ~s 7318 out of which 6822 are 
in position and 495 vacant posts are there. Posts abolished which are required to be revived 
are 166 and the requirement of staff for proposed expansion in 1996-97 is 130. The 
Department proposes to set-up five Allopathic new dispensaries and five new Homoepathic 
dispensaries, and the financial requirement for the expansion is Rs. 86 lakh per annum. The 
additional funds required for the existing dispensaries is Rs. 60 lakhs. The Planning 
Commission may consider meeting the additional ·requirements. The Committee, however, 
has examined the functioning of CGHS and submitted a separate detailed report on the 
functioning of CGHS (A Summary of recommendations is enclosed-Annexure I). Therefore, 
the Committee would not like to discuss the issues relating to CGHS at length :.il this stage.

(ii) National Leprosy Eradication Programme 
5.9. This programme is implemented with the aim to achieve elimination of leprosy by the 
year 2000 A.D. The Government of India have taken World Bank assistance of Rs. 302 crores 
for ensuring early detection and free Multi-Drug Therapy (MDT) services to all leprosy cases. 
The progress of the programme, the Committee was given to understand, has been remarkable. 
The prevalence of leprosy has been reduced from the level of 4 million estimated cases in 1981 
to 0.54 million on record by March, 1996. The prevalence rate of leprosy was 57 per 10,000 in 
1981 which has since been reduced to 5.8 per 10,000 population by now. A total of 6.53 million 
patients have been cured with MDT till March, 1996. The implementation of the programme, 
however, appears to be lacking the desired determination and seriousness as the funds allocated 
for the programme have not been utilized fully. For example, during 1995-96,· out of the total 
allqcation of Rs. 30 crores, only Rs. 64.8 crores could be utilized. Again during the current year, 
Rs. 74 crores only have been allocated. Explaning about the under utilisation of funds, the 
Department have stated that this was mainly due to non-finalisation of agreement for supply of 
additiof\al drugs and free supply drugs received from W.H.O. The M.D.T. Scheme was 
sanctioned in about 200 Districts, towards the end of the financial year 1994-95 and the Districts 
took time in establishing the infrastructure and recruiting staff. The Committee recommends 
that the programme should be implemented with added seriousness and be extended in all parts 
of the country. Funds allocated should be utilized fully._ There is also a need for intensified 
health education and public awareness compaigns to remove the social stigma attached with the 
disease. The Department, should take necessary steps in this direction.

that the Department should instruct all the States/Union Territories to ban the sale of 
uniodated salt meant for both human as well as animal consumptions. 
(viii) Prevention of Deafness · and Hearing Impairment Programme

production of an equal amount. It is, further, worsened by the continued social dependance 
of the deaf on the community. When the Secretary was asked to explain about the plans

project for treatment, research and prevention of deafness and hearing..Jmpairment diseases

the pilot project should be finalised at the earliest so that it may start implementation during

playing with the lives of innocent people. Theroe are vested inte~ests which are flourishing 
unchecked. There is no check and monitoring by the Government. The outlay for the

VII. NURSING SERVICES 
7. The Committee is of the view that the nursing services need to be strengthened 
further. There is a need for setting up more nursing schools and colleges particularly in rural 
and trib"l areas. · The Secretary during his oral evidence informed the Committee that in 
order to expand the nursing services and nursing education qualitatively and quantitatively in 
the country, State Governments were requested to send proposals. The Committee is, 
however, constrained to note that there is no encouraging response from the States. The 
Secretary has also informed the Committee that in view of lukewarm response from the 
States, a concept proposal has been prepared by the Nursing experts for upgradation of 
nursing services in qualitative and quantitative terms. The requisite data for preparing 
projects are being collected and the proposal will be crystalised in about 2-3 months time, 
the Committee was informed . The Committee desires that this proposal should be finalised 
at the earliest and it's implementation should be started during the current financial year 
itself. ' . • 
VIII. AVAILABILITY OF SPURIOUS DRUGS 
8. The Committee is disturbed to note that spurious drugs are freely available in the 
market without any check and monitoring. This has been posing a very serious problem 
resulting in grave health hazard and consequent deaths of innocent persons. The problem of 
manufacture and sale of spurious and fake drugs in man-made and it has to be curbed with a 
firm hand. The Committee is of the firm view that the matter needs to be examined at great 
length. We can't afford to be silent spectator to innocent lives being taken away by anti­
social elements fndulging in ~h e sale of spurious drugs. A comprehensive plan, the 
Committee recommends, should be prepared to check the menace of manufacture, sale and 
supply of spurious and fake drugs. There should be provision for stringent punishments 
against the persons found responsible for spurious drugs. At a time when there are already 
many diseases like AIDS, Malaria, Cancer, etc. afflicting the nation, the country cannot 
afford to have another man-made problem like the one of spurious drugs . The Committee 
also recommends that a legislation should be made to provide for rigorous punishment to 
those who indulge in manufacture, sale and supply of spurious and fake drugs.
