SUMMARY OF RECOMMENDATIONS I OBSERVATIONS OF 31ST REPORT 
1. Overcrowding 
Hospitals in or outside Delhi are extremely overcrowded with patients. This is mainly 
due to Jack of adequate medical care facilities and personnel at the PHCs', and the dist·rict 
and sub-district hospitals for providing primary and secondary level of treatment to patients. 
As a result of this, patients from all parts of the country directly approach the hospitals even 
for minor ailments instead of going to the PHCs or the district and sub-district hospitals. 
Another factor, particular to Delhi, is that some patients try to approach many hospitals, 
one after the other, for the same ailment for psychological satisfaction. (Para 4) 
This results in shortage of beds, resulting in two to three patients sharing the .same bed 
in many hospitals. The hospital authorities cannot increase the number of beds due to acute 
shortage of space. The solution to the problem is that the Government should pay 
immediate attention to improve and expand facilities for medical care at the primary and 
secondary ·levels so . that only those patients needing specialist care and attention, ·are 
referred to the tertiary level hospitals located in the Metro cities. The problem could be also 
tackled partly by setting up screening OPDs, with essential testing facilities slightly away 
from the· main hospitals. "Fhe Committee, therefore, recommends that overcrowding may be 
reduced by simultaneous improvement in: · 
(a) the levels of management efficiency in hospitals; 
(b) improvement in peripheral facilities in District and Sub-districts hospitals for 
primary and secondary treatment; and 
(c) organising a functionaf referral sys.tem. (Para 4. 7) 
There is a need to optimise all existing and available physical facilities to control 
overcrowding. The Committee would emphasise the necessity for opening more counters and 
creating space for patients attending OPDs. There is also a need for proper guidance and 
direction to patients approaching the OPDs so that patients dq not have ·to wander from one 
counter to another. This will, to some extent, ease congestion and overcrowding of patients 
at strategic points. There is also an urgent need to reduce the waiting time of the patients at 
various counters keeping in view the patients' convenience. The underlying idea behind this 
proposal should be that the patients visiting OPD do not have to spend more than half a day -
at the hospitals for purpose of consultation/treatment, etc. (Para 4.12) 
2. Referral Character 
The premier institutions like the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) and 
the Post Graduate Institute of Medical Education and Research were set up to promote high 
standards of medical care, training and research. These were originally marked as referral 
hospitals where patients would be referred by other hospitals for a specialised treatment of a 
high ordt!r. These hospital s were n~)t supposed to entertain new patients, with common 
disease:-., which cuuid be trea ted at the ordinary hospitals. In course of time, due to non-

patients to the metro cities. The premier instituti~ns like AIIMS and PGIMER have lost their 
referral character as they have to attend to all kinds of patients, irrespective of the nature of 
disease. This has prevented specialists to carry out research of the highest order as their 
attention is primarily focussed on the day to day medical problem of ordinary patients. (Para 5) 
The Committee was informed that there was a proposal under consideration with the 
Government to restore to AIIMS and PGIMER their referral character. The Committee would 
like to know the fate of the proposal. The Government should draw a time-bound programme 
to conyert these hospitals into purely referral hospitals and sort out all the related issues I 
problems of strengthening the peripheral medical facilities by providing them adequate finance 
and other resources. (Para 5.3) 
3. Computerisation 
There is an immediate need for providing computers in the hospitals for maintenance of 
patient - related records, and for better coordination between various departments /wings of 
the hospitals. (Para 6) 
4. Duplication of Facilities 
Duplication of specialist services in the hospitals results in non-optimal use of scarce 
resources. This requires proper co-ordination.and redesignation of the hospitals with specialised 
services .. There is a need for greater horizontalliaisoning among the specialists and to evolve a 
scheme for linking a group of smaller hospitals with one major hospital having specialists' 
expertise. For example, neuro-surgery facilities to deal with accident cases could be made 
available in one hospital and a group of smaller hospitals could make use of these services for 
entire region. (Para 7.1) 
Duplication of services, and facilities in hospitals, particularly in view of the constraints of 
space, beds and financial resources, results in wasteful expenditure and, thus, should be avoided 
as far as possible. Every hospital could specialise in a particular area I discipline so that the 
patients know which hospital they should approach for a particular disease/treatment 
(Para 7.2) 
5. Coordination amongst Hospitals 
Duplication of services I facilities cannot be altogether avoided unless there is a proper and 
efficient coordination between various hospitals there should be a close liaison and coordination 
among di.fferent hospitals for making available efficient specialist services to patients. For 
example, Safdarjung Hospital and AIIMS could work with greater coordination between them 
so as to reduce the burden on each other. (Para 8) 
6. More autonomy to Medical Superintendents 
Medical Superintendents of some hospitals have voiced concern about their dependence on 
the Ministry even for day-to -day works needing immediate attention. This results in avoidable 
delay, affecting the efficiency and quality of services rendered by the hospitals. (Para 9) 
The Committee recommends that the Medical Superintendents should'be given more 
autonomy to enable them to discharge their functions more efficiently. The Ministry may 
consider redesignating the posts of Merlical Superintendents of major hospitals as 'Directors' 
with all the concomitant powers. Such redesignation would not have any financial implication as 
the posts of Medical Superintendents of major hospitals have already been upgraded to that of 
Additoinal D.G. of Health. Services, whjch is equivalent to the rank of Additional Secretary to 
the Government of India. (Para 9.1)

7. Maintenance/Repair of Medical Equipment 
Maintenance of sophisticated and costly equipments is very crucial keeping_ in view the 
investments made in their procurement and also the patients' care and convenience. The 
Government should consider running of workshop in Delhi for this purpose where all the 
medical equipments and appliances could be serviced I repaired without delays. (Para 10) 
8. Strengthening of Blood Banks 
The Blood Banks in the Central Government hospitals have no modern facilities and 
equipments commensurate with the nature of services required today. There is an urgent 
need to look into this problem, keeping in view the detection of new and deadly diseases 
like AIDS etc. The Government should provide HIV tests facilities and modern blood banks 
in each hospital where fractionation of .blood into its different components can be done and 
the transfusion of blood is made foolproof. (Para 11) 
9. Poor Performance of Family Welfare 
The Committee found that the infrastructure provided in the Family Welfare Units in 
each hospital was not being put of op-vimum use. Near total Jack of motivation and 
dedication in the staff was also noticed. The Committee is surprised to note the indifferent 
and nonchalant attitude of the Ministry/hospitals in regard to such a high priority aspect of 
our socio-economic development. It, therefore, recommends that family welfare units 
provided in the Central Government hospitals be strengthened and activated immediately. 
(Para 12) 
10. Campaign against AIDS 
The Central Government hospitals, which are supposed to be role models in campaign 
against AIDS, do not appear to be serious about in. The Committee, therefore, feels that 
the Central Government hospitals should launch massive· campaign against the spread of this 
deadly disease. (Para 13) 
11. Establishing ·an epilepsy Centre 
Epilepsy in our country is being treated in Neurological centres of the major hospitals 
where the •facilities available for its treatment are inefficient and unorganised. The 
Committee feels that there is an imperative · need to establish an Epilepsy centre, to begin 
with, in New Delhi. Once this centre is developed, similar centres, either separate or 
branches thereof, should be set up in other parts of the country. (Para 14.1) 
12. Exposure of Doctors to latest Development 
With the advancement of medical science and technology, there is an urgent need for 
doctors/professors to keep pace with the latest medical innovations so as to pass on the 
benefit of these advancements to patient care. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
the Doctors and Faculty Members should be provided with adequate opportunities to 
undergo training, and refresher courses, from time to time, to improve the quality of 
services. Simultaneously, the technicians/para medical staff handling various sophisticated 
and modern medical equipments should also be given requisite training to facilitate efficient 
handling of these equipruents and bring precision in their work. (Para 15)

Cleanliness and hygienic conditions in various hospitals are of very poor standJr d. 
Choked sewage leaking water pipes, stinking toilets and heaps of garbage lying uncovered in 
various comers of the hospitals could be seen almost in every hospital. The Committee is 
deeply distressed to see such unhygienic conditions and the hospital authorities paying scant 
attention to such an important aspect of medical care. The hospital buildings, including the 
Operation Theatres and the wards, are no better in their upkeep and maintenance. (Para 16) 
One of the reasons cited for this state of affairs is that the CPWD, which is primarily 
responsible for the maintenance of the buildings, is not giving prompt and efficient services 
and they are also not under the direct administrative control of the hospital authorities. The 
hospitals should, therefore, either have their own engineering departments or the CPWD 
unit should be put under the direct administrative control of the respective Medical 
Superintendents to control and supervise the maintenance work. (Pa_ra 16.1) 
14. Shortage of Staff 
The shortage of staff particularly in Group 'C' and 'D' categories, in almost all the 
hospitals has been observed by the Committee. Similar was the position for many posts of 
faculty members and senior doctors which were lying vacant for years together. The problem 
was more prominent in JIPMER, Pondicherry, where no one is willing to go because of the 
distance factor. Similarly, in AIIPMER, Bombay, doctors are reluctant to join mainly 
because of acute shortage of residential accommodation. Unattractive pay-scales have also 
been cited as another reason for doctors not joining the Government institutes. Further, 
while the number of doctors over a period of time, has increased manifold, there is no 
corresponding increase in the staff of Group 'C' and 'D' categories. (Para 17) 
The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that shortage of staff in Group 'C' and 
'D' categories should be immediately made good and procedure of filling the higher level 
posts should be reviewed and streamlined to avoid delays in recruitments. (Para 17.2) 
15. Doctors on Prolonged Deputation 
The Committee deprecates the practice of doctonvprofessors going on deputation and 
coming back at the time of promotions, which is against the very ethics of medical 
profession. It, therefore, recommends that the Department should take a serious view in 
these cases and discourage such practices. (Para 18) 
16. Indiscipline in Hospitals 
Complaints of rude behaviour by Doctors and other staff in hospitals are a common 
feature. There is no cordial relationship between the hospital administration and the 
employees either. Irresponsible unionism is very much rampant amongst the employees, 
culminating, quite often, in 'Bandhs' and 'Strikes'. There is no effective grievance redressal 
machinery in the hospitals. While the genuine grievances of the employees should be 
redressed promptly, through the medium of JCMs or other grievance redressal machineries, 
indiscipline resulting in chaotic situations, causing inconvenience to patients, should be 
firmly dealt with. It would be useful to set up a mechanism similar to the JCM in 
Government establishm~nts, in each hospital to redress the grievances of the staff . The role 
and functions of hospital Management Boards ~!so need to be redefined in order to improve 
the effectiveness and cred:bility of these Boards. The services of outside experts in these 
Boards may also be utilised to improve the state of affairs. (Para 19)

17. Lack of Residential Accommodation 
Doctors and nurses are responsible for running the patient care services round the clock 
and are required to come to hospitals at odd hours at short notice. In case they are provided 
residential accommodation nearer the hospitals they would be able to discharge their duties 
more efficiently and promptly. The Committee; therefore, recommends that sufficient 
number of residential units for all categories of employees be provided in the hospital pools 
and the Department should also take up the matter with the Ministry of Urban Affairs and 
Employment to get adequate number of quarters earmarked for the hospital functionaries in 
the nearby Government colonies. There is also a strong-felt need to provide adequate 
hospital accommodation to the resident doctors and nurses, preferably within the campus of 
the hospital itself. Nurses should also be given priority in the Working Women's Hostels 
situated near the hospitals. (Para 20.4) 
The Committee is happy to learn that there is a proposal to construct Delhi Nurses 
Colony in Srinivaspuri for which the possession of land has been taken. There are proposals 
in hand to acquire two acres of land in Rohini. The Committee is, however, distressed to 
note ·that funds for the purpose were not provided by the Ministry of Finance last year and 
recommends that sufficient funds be allocated for this purpose. The Ministry of Health may 
also vigorously pursue the matter of allocation of land at suitable si..:es with the D.D.A. and 
N.O.I.D.A. for construction of residential quarters for the hospital employees. (Paras 20.1 
& 20.3) 
18. Separate CGHS Wings 
The CGHS Wings, presently earmarked and functioning in Safdarjung and Dr. Ram 
Manohar Lohia Hospitals, are not geared enough to cope with the needs of the CGHS 
beneficiaries. At times, the time taken in the CGHS wings is more than the time taken in 
the general OPD's. It is, therefore, recommeded that the procedures for consultation/tests 
etc. in the CGHS wings of the hospitals need to be thoroughly streamlined so as to provide 
prompt and efficient services. (Para 21) 
19. Senior Citizens 
There should be special arrangements in the hospitals for the senior citizens and the 
retired CGHS beneficiaries keeping in view their old age problems. (Para 22) 
20. Geriatrics 
'The Committee recommends that Government should take necessary steps to develop 
geriatrics as specialised subject, and provide sufficient number of specialists and 
infrastructure for opening Geriatric Clinics in all the Central Government hospitals. 
(Para 23) 
21. Provision for Poor Patients 
The Committee has noted that several major invasive procedures, e.g. cardiac surgery 
are far too expensive for the poor people. Therefore, it would suggest the Ministry must 
urgently explore all appropriate sources of funds to assist poor patients coming to AIIMS or 
other Central Government hospitals for specific life threatening illnesses. If a mechanism can 
be set up, such as a National Catastrophic lllness Assistance Fund, then resources can flow 
from all sources, induding private charities and international agencies and organisation. 
Besides, there can be many imaginative methods of requiring both government and private

22. Facilities for Visitors/Attendants 
The Committee feels that there is an urgent need to construct 'DharmashalaSISarais' by 
the Government, in association with charitable institutions, wh·o may be interested in this 
noble cause. Such institutions should ·be provided all necessary help in procuring land etc. on 
concessional rates by the Government. (Para 25.1) 
23. Budget 
The Committee noticed that there was a general complaint about the lack of adequate 
funds and in fact, it was cited as one of the reasons for several problems in the hospitals. The 
Committee is fully aware of the general resource crunch in the country. It, however, feels that 
in view of the need for improving quality and adequacy of medical care, the Government 
should explore the possibilities of generating-Sparing more resources for allocation to this 
sector. (Para 26.2) ·

I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human 
Resource Development, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its 
behalf, do hereby present this Fifth Report of the Committee on the Demands for Grants of the 
Department of Education, Ministry of Human Resource Development for the year, 1994-95. 
At its meeting held on 3rd March, 1994 the Committee decided to take up for consideration 
the Demands for Grants relating to the Department of Education , Ministry of Human Resource 
Development (Demand No. 47). 
The Committee considered the various documents and relevant papers received from the 
Deptt. of Education; Ministry of Human Resource Development and also heard the Secretary 
(Education) and other Officials of that Deptt. on the said Demands for Grants in its meeting held 
on 23rd & 24th March, 1994. 
The Committee considered the Draft Report in its sittings held on 29th and 31st March, 1994 
and adopted the same on 31st March, 1994.

AN OVERVIEW 
The Ministry of Human Resource Development was set up in 1985 with the objective of 
integrating efforts towards the development of human potential in the areas of Education, 
Women & Child Development, Art, Culture, Youth Affairs & Sports. The Department of 
Education is an important constituent of this Ministry. During 1993-94 a budget provision of 
Rs. 2159.33 crores was made available for education in the Central Sector. This was increased to 
Rs. 2192 crores in the Revised Estimate 1993-94. 
2. There are a large number of subordinate offices and autonomous organisations under the 
Department which are engaged in carrying out the activities and programmes of the Department. 
They include, among others, the Directorate of Adult Education, National Council of 
Educational Research & Training (NCERT), National Institute of Educational Planning & 
Administration (NIEPA), University Grants Commission (UGC), Indian Council of Social 
Science Research (ICSSR), Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan (KVS), the Navodaya Vidyalaya 
Samiti (NVS), the Central Board of Secondary Education, the National Book Trust, Indian 
Institutes of Technology and Regional Engineering Colleges. 
3. The National Policy on Education, 1986 has been instrumental in laying down the 
priorities in education at the national level. Elementary Education has been getting the highest 
priority in the educational sector, to accelerate the pace for achieving Universal Elementary 
Education by the end of this Century. The Operation Black Board scheme, launched in 1987-88, 
aims at bringing about significant improvement in the provision of facilities in primary schools. 
This is expected to improve retention of children in primary schools. 
4. The programme of Non-Formal Education aims at bringing education to working children, 
girls and children living in habitations which are not covered by formal schools. NFE is envisaged 
as an alternative strategy for formal education and plays a complementary role in achieving 
Universal Elementary Education by covering drop-outs or those who have not enrolled for one 
reason or the another. 
5. The Adult Education programme provides basic functional educational skills for those who 
could not avail the opportunities for education through formal and non-formal schools. The 
Technology Mission for Literacy, set up in 1988 with the aim of covering the total area, has 
achieved success in the southern, eastern and western regions and the focus has now shifted to 
the Hindi speaking States which have a low percentage of literacy. 
6. The Department is giving serious attention to achieving Education for All, and its 
endeavours towards this end found mention during the "Education for All Summit" of 9 populous 
countries of the world, held in 'New Delhi' in December, 1993. As a result of these endeavours, 
the resource allocation to education is expected to be increased from the existing 3.2% to 6% of 
the GNP from the 9th Plan. 
7. In the school education field, there are 796 Kendriya Vidyalayas, including three 
Vidyalayas in foreign countries. These are opened in areas with a sizeable concentration of 
Central Government employees. 
8. The Navodaya Vidyalayas scheme, launched in 1985, provides good quality education to 
talented children predominantly from rural areas. There are 321 Schools which are residential and 
offer education free of charge for all students. 
9. In the area of Vocational Education, a Centrally Sponsored Scheme was started in 1988 
with the main objective of providing diversification of educational opportunities to enhance 
individual employability. Vocational courses, mainly in the areas of Agriculture, Business & 
Commerce, Engineering & Technology, Health and Para Medical, Humanities and Home 
Science, are introduced at the +2 level in schools selected by the State Governments. So far, 

Vocational Sections have been sanctioned in 5,588 schools creating a capacity for diversification 
of 7.96 lakh students. 
10. The scheme of pre-vocational education has also been launched at the lower secondary 
stage in 1993-94 with the objective of imparting simple marketable skills to students in classes IX 
and X. 
11. The Department of Education has been seeking bilateral and multilateral assistance from 
international agencies so that additional resources may be available for educational programmes. 
Some new projects have been started in the last few years such as Mahila Samakhya Project in 
four States with the assistance of Netherlands; Andhra Pradesh Primary School Project with UK 
assistance; Lok Jumbish Project in Rajasthan with the assistance of SIDA; Shiksha Karmi Project 
in Rajasthan with the assistance of SIDA and Bihar Education Project with UNICEF assistance. 
12. In the Higher Education Sector, the University Grants Commission is concerned with 
promotion and coordination of university education and determination and maintenance of 
standards of teaching, examination and research in universities. The total number of Universities 
in 1993-94 was 189 with 7938 Colleges and a student enrolment of 48.05 Jakhs. A new Central 
University is also being set up in Tezpur to increase the facilities for higher education in the 
North-Eastern Region. 
13. In the Technical Education field, 5 Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs) have been 
established to provide instruction and research in some branches of Engineering and Technology, 
Science and Arts for advancement of learning. These Institutes are imparting education at the 
undergraduate, postgraduate and research level, in addition to sponsoring research and they are 
fully funded by the Central Government. One more liT is proposed to be set up in Assam. 
14. The Regional Engineering Colleges have been set up to enable the country to meet the 
growing requirement of trained technical manpower. There are 17 Regional Engineering Colleges 
which offer First Degree Programmes in Engineering and Technology, out of which 14 have 
facilities for postgraduate and Doctoral programmes and also conduct research. 
REPORT 
15. Human Resource Development is of paramount importance for the progress of the 
country and education is one of the most important components in this regard. Though we are 
committed to achieve the objective of Education for All (EFA) by 2000 but increasing population 
and limited resources at hand are the two obstacles in the way of achieving this goal. 
16. At present, Budget outlay for Education is 3.2% of the (Gross Domestic Product) GDP 
and the Department of Education has assured that from 9th Plan onwards the outlay will be 6% 
of the GDP. 
17. The Committee welcomes the decision of the Government that Education will get an 
allocation of 6% of GDP. The Committee also hopes that there would be reflection of this decision 
in the Budget Estimates of the year 1995-96 and of subsequent years. 
18. Revised Budget Estimates for 1993-94 of the Deptt. of Education is Rs. 2192 crores. There 
has been a 10% increase in the Budget Estimates for 1994-95 over the previous year at Rs. 2423.6 
crores, out of which Rs. 1548.3 crores have been provided for planned expenditure and the rest of 
Rs. 875.3 crores is earmarked for Non-Plan expenditure. 
19. Secondary and Physical Education have been allocated 24.3% of the Budget Estimates of 
Educationl Deptt. and 24.2% of the funds of the Deptt. have been provided for University and 
Higher Education. Elementary and Technical Education have been provided 21.6% and 18% 
respectively of the funds for 1994-95. 
20. The Secretary, Deptt. of Education, in his oral evidence before the Committee has stated 

that the major thrust of the budget is on Elementary Educatiofi) with the objective of achieving 
education for all by 2000, decentralisation of educational administration and review of all these 
programmes quarterly, by a group of Chief Ministers. 
Demands for Grants (1994-95) of the Department of Education 
21. Department of Education is running about a dozen schemes, but the Committee took up 
for consideration only some of the major ones, which have been stated in brief in the following 
paragraphs, alongwith the Committee's observations/recommendations thereon. 
I 
Elementary Education 
22. Article 45 of the Constitution of India provides for free and Compulsory Education for 
all children below the age of 14 years. It was expected that by the year 1995, India would achieve 
Universal Elementary Education. However, there is still 153 million children, as on March, 1991, 
in the age group of 6-14 who are yet to be covered under the scheme. They constitute 18 per 
cent of the total population of the country. The Committee hopes that by the end of this century 
this backlog will be covered and total universal Elementary Education will be achieved. 
23. The Revised Budget Estimate for 1993-94 for Elementary Education is Rs. 443.7 crores. 
In Budget Estimate for, 1994-95, has been given Rs. 523.86 crores for Elementary Education. 
24. While the Committee takes note of this increase in allocation for Elementary Education, it 
feels that in view of the rising prices, the increase in real terms, is not substantial. 
25. The Committee feels that the Deptt. may take steps to decentralise Elementary Education 
and take help of Panchayati Raj institutions for proper monitoring and implementation of the 
Scheme. 
Operation Blackboard 
26. In the Eighth Plan it has been provided that the Scheme would continue and a third 
teacher and a third room would be added to primary schools wherever enrollment exceeds 100 
students. Thirty per cent of such schools would be covered in the said plan. Besides these, 
Operation Blackboard would cover 10 per cent of upper primary schools during the last two years 
of the Plan.

29. The Committee feels that the question of increase in the weight of primary school bags

lessen the weight. Mechanism for ensuring minimum standards in schools in regard to teachers as

30. The Committee is not satisfied with the efforts made on the basis of last year's committee

31. The Committee feels that the scheme should first achieve the targets laid down earlier, 
that is they should fu-st cover all the single teacher schools before going in for three-teacher

efforts are required in this direction.

increase in allocation and also take steps to evaluate, from time to time, the existing methodology

38. In the year 1993-94 Revised Estimates, the Department of Education had provided 
Rs. 305.5 crores for plan and Rs. 256.7 crores for non-plan expenditure for Secondary and 
Physical Education. For 1994-95, the figures are Rs. 335 crores and Rs. 255.5 crores respectively. 
39. The Committee feels that secondary education in general is facing resource crunch 
therefore, suggests that sufficient funds may be allocated for its various schemes. 
Vocational Education 
40. Rs. 85 crores have been provided for the scheme in the Revised Estimates for 1993-94. For 
1994-95, the Budget Estimate has been increased to 88.46 crores. 
41. The National Policy on Education 1992 envisages well-planned programmes for 

Vocational Education for developing a healthy attitude among students. It is expected that about 
10% of higher secondary students would be directed to the vocational stream by 1995 and 25% 
by 2000 AD. 
42. The Committee feels that adequate funds be provided to implement the scheme and to 
achieve the fixed targets. 
Computer Education 
43. Computer education has been started in secondary schools keeping in view the recent 
chapges in the technology and its immense potentialities in day-to-day life. 
44. The Committee feels that the Budget allocation of Rs. 25 crores for 1994-95 is not 
sufficient as it is even less than that of last year's Revised Estimate (i.e. Rs. 26 crores). Therefore, 
more funds should be provided for computer education. 
45. The Committee also suggests that adequate infrastructural support for the upkeep and 
maintenance of computers should be provided and the scheme, should also be monitored 
effectively. 
Scholarships 
46. The Committee is unhappy over the curtailment of budget allocation under the head 
"Scholarships". Instead, the number of scholarships should have been increased to help the 
economically backward and meritorious students so that more and more students could complete 
secondary education and go for higher studies. 
47. The Committee feels that there should be more provision for loan scholarships for the 
benefit of needy students.

An Overview 
The Department of Youth Affairs & Sports is comparatively a new Depa ·tment which deals with 
the vital subject :>f youth and promotion of sports. Though both these subjects fall under the P!!rview 
of the States, yet Government of India has a very prominent role to play not only in terms of 
operating its own ~chemes but also for coordinating with State Governments and other agcnc1es. The 
Committee found that on youth side, though there are a large number of schemes, but bulk of the 
budget allocation is for the National Service Schemes (NSS) and Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan 
(NYt<S). National Scrvic.! Scheme (along ,.ith NCC) is the most important scheme fc; voiuntary 
participation by student community in a nation building. It is a low-cost scheme which aims at 
personality development of the students through their involvement in social service, literacy, health, 
and environment, etc. Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan, on the other hand, mainly mobilises rural 
youth and focuses on the activities of the Youth Clubs. Amongst other impo;tant schemes there are 
the schemes for National lnteiration and Adventures. There is some scope for streamlining the 
remaining schemes also. Among the new initiatives, taken in the current year is the preparatior for 
the establishment of Rajiv Gandhi National Institute for Youth Development. 
2. On the Sports side, it is observed that the Department has to coordinate with the State 
Governments as well as sports federations, which are autonomous bodies working for 54 different 
disciplines. The important scheme being operated by the Department are the schemes of Grants to 
Sports Federations, and 'Assistance for creation of Sports Infrastructure. While the development of 
infrastructure is essential, it is felt that there is a tendency to set up large stadia in big towEs and 
cities and since the resources with the Centre, as well as State Governments are limited, creation of 
play-fields and other facilities at the Tchsil level do not get the required attention . The Sports 
Authority of India (SAl) is the executive part of the Department and is main.y concerned with the 
broad-based sports, as well as grooming of talented children It is also responsible for organisation of 
National Camps for participation in major international events. The performance of Indian 
sportspersons at the Olympic Games has been undistinguished and it is necessary that all efforts arc 
made oy various concerned agencies to raise the requisite/International standards. In this connectiOn , 
the Committee welcomes the reported consensus of the State Governments about the introduction of 
Sports and Physical Education as a compulsory subject from sehoul level onwards. 
3 It is observed that the Plan provision for 1993-94 was Rs. 98.10 crores including Rs. 37.19 
crores for Youth and Rs. 60.66 crores for Sports. Whereas. this year, Plan provision is Rs. 94 00 
crores only Rs. 4.10 crores less than the previous year Plan provision. The provision for 1993-94 
includes addition of Rs. 13.10 crores earmarked for preparation for the Asian Games . It is felt that 
Department consists of two important parts 1.e. Yout 1 and Sports, therefore, decrease in the 
allocation will go against thl!ir interest. Therefore, the Committee recommends that allocations may 
accordingly be increased.

5. The National Service Scheme was started in the year 1969, and now it has spread over to 159 
universities; 7,000 colleges and other educational institutions. 
The objective of this programme is to involve the students in nation-building activities to inculcate in 
them a sense of responsibility towards society. 
6. Budgetary provisions made under the scheme for the current year show a diminishing trend 
whereas the targets set are high. As per the performance budget (1994-95), of the Deptt. it is 
proposed to increase, this year, the number of N.S.S. volunteers to 12 Jakhs from 11.16 Jakhs last 
year; to commemorate its Silver Jubilee Year by focussing on five thrust areas. But, the non-plan 
provision has been reduced from Rs. 485.00 lakhs to Rs. 480.00 lakhs. The Committee is of the view 
that both plan and non-plan provisions be increased not only to meet the targets set but also to make 
this scheme result oriented and more effective. 
7. Secruary, Department of Youth Affairs & Sports has during the course of his oral evidence, 
averred that the attitude of State Governments has not been very co-operative as they did not release 
their share of grants for this purpose. This adversely affects the progress of the scheme. The 
Committee is of the view that Government should evolve some mechanism to tackle this problem. The 
CJ mmittee recommends that an evaluation of the scheme should also be done il! order to streamline its 
functioning and strengthen its network. 
8. Coverage of schools, as compared to colleges and Universities under the NSS Scheme, has been 
far from satisfactory. Even after 25 years, a sizeable number of youth remains uncovered. Therefore, 
the Committee is of the view that a time bound programme should be framed for this purpose. 
Nehru Yuva Kendra Scheme 
9. Nehru Yuva Kendra Scheme, started in 1972~73 with a view to formulating and implementing 
programmes for rural and non-student youth, has considerably expanded its network throughout the 
country. To activate and strengthen it, the NYK Sang:1 •f.:~n r::tme into being in 1986-87 as an 
autonomous organisation. In order to evaluat e the programme~ of Nehru Yuva Kendras, four 
Information Development and Resource Agencies {IDAR As) lla',. ~x~cn set up, one each in West 
Bengal, U.P., Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra.

bare Rs. 108.00 lakhs. Whereas there has been an addition of about 16.18 Kendras during the year 
1993-94.

13. Under this scheme, financial assistance is extended to Voluntary Organisations for 
undertaking and implementing youth programmes such as involving youth in social reconstruction, 
imparting vocational trai1ing in agro-based vocations, such as tailoriilg and embroider) etc , for 
promoting self-employment anenius among the youths of the country. 
14. Though it is a very good scheme, but a look at the expenditure in the year 1992-93 shows a 
considerable downward trend in the utilisation of the sanctioned funds. Out of a total of Rs. 56.50 
lakhs. only Rs. 41.50 lakhs could be spent during the said year. Therefore, Government should take 
·.om~.. ~rrang.:ments to ensure proper utilisation of the budget allocations. 
15. The performance budget of the Department has lauded this scheme by saymg that the 
u:-, ~ 1ln1!ss of this programme may be measured from the large number of proposals the Departm ent is 
r~cciving. but strangely there is a cut in the provision. The amount meant for non-plan expenditure 
under this scheme was done away with from the year 1993-94 and after that there has been an 
allocation of Rs. 55.00 lakhs for the last two years. During 1994-95 projections have been made to 
-:over 20,000 youth but the static allocation docs not hold much hope. 
Promotion of Adventurous Activities 
16. Under this scheme, assistance is extended to individuals, groups, institutions ard voluntary 
organisations to develop among the youth a spirit of adventure, challenge and endurance by providing 
them opportunities to undertake mountainerring, trekking, raft expeditions, study of flora and fauna 
in forests and deserts, etc. and such other activities. 
17. During the year 19992-93 (upto November) 132 voluntary organisations, educational institutions 
and mviduduals were benefited under this scheme, whereas in the year 1993-84 (upto mid Decem ber) 
the number of beneficiaries came down to 108 (as per the performance budget, 1994-95). The 
background note supplied by the Department gives a figure of 122 beneficiaries Similarly the number 
of youth covered under this programme has declined from 8,455 during the year 1992-93 to 5,600, 

(as per the performance budget) and 6,336 youth during 1993-94. (according to the background note, 
P.7) 
18. In spite of of the fact that three National Adventure Awards on the pattern of Arjuna Awards 
have been introduced this year, but no Non-plan provision has been made. The Committee would like 
to know the factors leading to decline in the number of beneficieries and also to discontinuation of 
provision for non-plan expenditure. The Committee recommends that efforts should be made to involve

Scouting and Guiding 
19. There arc two organisatiions functioning under this scheme, one is the Bharat Scouts and 
Guides meant for the students and the other All India Boy Scouts, which caters to the needs on non­
student youth in the age group of 14-17 years. For the former, the Department provides funds for 
both administrative activities and related expenses, but not to the latter. This is not tenable, in view of 
the fact that non-student youth deserves more and more care and assistance. Therefore, the Committee 
opines that the Department should try to expand the network of All India Boy Sco11ts and involve more 
and more youth in this programme and start extending assistance for the activities related expenditure 
of All India Boy Scouts also. 
20. According to the performance Budget (1994-95), it is proposed to cover 80,000 b()ys and girls 
during this year but taking into account the diminishing allocation it appears to be a difficult task. 
Plan provision continues to be static at Rs. 92.00 lakhs during the last two years. On the Contrary, 
the non-plan provision of Rs. 12.00 lakhs has been done away with. In thes(; circumstan:es, it is 
doubtful whether the target of adding 80,000 boys and girls to this scheme could be achieved. 
21. The Committee is sceptical about th~ claims of targets being achieved year after year and, 
thcrefGre, recommends strongly that a mechanism be evolved through which this number could be 
verified. An evaluation of thi'i scheme may also be undertaken in the near future. 
National Service Volunteer Scheme 
22. Kational Service Volunteer Scheme aims at engaging graduates below 25 years of age, in 
nation-building activities for a period of one/two years on a full time b .. sis on agross payment of Rs. 
700 per month. Though 17 years have elapsed since its incep;ion, this programme has nc~ been able 
to catch the attention of the youth in the rural .. .rcas of country as a result of which youth from rural 
areas are not able to p~rticipatc in it. The Committee, therefore, recommends that a publicity

youth has not been spclt out in any of the documents supplied by the Department. In the case of y'>uth 
!wiling from backwards and tribals areas, suitable relaxations must be given at the time of selection. 
23. During the year 1993-94 proj ctions have bee:-~ made to cover 3,300 youths under tht; 
programme and for this year also the target remains the same. But the cut in non-plan provision of 
around Rs. 10.50 lakhs may hamper the achic11ment of the target. 
Exchange of Delegations of Youth at International level 
24. l\othing much is known about tl is scheme, except that youth delegations are exchanged under 
various Cultural Exchange Programme. What are the criteria for selecting youths, how they are 
selected for this prognm1me, who were d1e persons sent abroad under this scheme last year, whert they 
went, what were the achievments, whe1 her any advertisement was given in the nati,mal news~)apers to 
this effect is not known. The Commit tee recommends that these details should be spelt out in the 
documents of the Department so that there is transparency in this scheme. An increase in tha allocation 
of Rs. 1400 lakhs suggests that more ): rogrammes will be taken up under this scheme but not details 
are ll\ ailable. 
Exhibition for Youth 
25. This scheme is, to some extent, : duplication of the scheme of National Integration Programme 
which is undertaken by the same Of! anisations like National Service Scheme (NSS) Nehru Yuva 

Kendra Sangthan (NYKS) and educational institutions etc. therefore it may be clubed with these 
programmes. During the year 1992-93 a sum of about Rs. 10 lakhs was sanctioned for 32 exhibitions

was sa .. ctioncd for only 25 exhibitions, till December, 1993, as against the target of 150 exhibitions. 
This year an ambitious target of 100 exhibitions has been set but the total allocations for the scheme 
show no increase. The Committee recommmends that this should be looked into. 
Youth Hostels 
The idea behind building youth hostels is to enable youth to experience the diversities of their 
country aud facilitate them to have a glimpse of the glories of the past - a process which promotes 
national integration. But, it is surpising to note that some of the centres of historical and cultural 
importanc:: like Patna, Nalanda, Rajgir, Bodgaya, Panipat, Banaras, Ajmer, Khajuraho etc. have not 
been found suitable for construction of such hostels. The distribution of such hostels is also not 
equitable. J\.lany of the Stutes have been neglected. Therefore, the Committee recommends, that to the

27. In the Department's note it has been admitted that only 37 youth hostels have so far been set up 
whereas the performance budget gives a figure of 34 hostels. As regard the youth hostels under 
construction, the former presents a figure of 31 whereas the latter of 29. The Committee is not in the

28. The Commit tee recommends that the final decision regarding transfer of scheme to the States 
should be expedited. 
29. It is astonishing to note that a drlstic cut was made in the Budget estimates for the year 1993-
94 in regard to this scheme, as against the B.E. & R.E. provisions for the year 1992-93. A substantial 
decrease has also been made in the B.E. for the year 1994-95, almost a reduction of Rs. 58 lakhs as

National Discipline Scheme & National Fitness Corps 
30. When the scheme of National Discipline scheme (1'-.TDS) has become a non-entity long ago and 
its instructors have been absorbed in State Government services, it appears to be stranges as to why 
the t'cpartmcnt of Yo11th Affairs & Sports is bearing the expenditure under this Scheme. The

31. According t"l the background note supplied by the Department, a separate scheme, called

Assistance tu Youth Clubs 
32. This scheme was started with a view to giving impetus to the youth movement in the country 
and to involve the youth in constructive activities which is being implemented by Nehru Yuva 
Kcndras and state Govts. and U.T. Administrations. It is, undt.mbt,dly, a well conceiv( i scheme

33. During the years 1992-93 only 3, youth clubs could be assist~d and during 1993,94 with the help

Programme of Training of Youth 
34. This scheme appears to be duplication of the scheme of assistance to voluntary organisations as it 
also aims at imparting vocational education of different kinds to the youth. Therefore, the Committee

Rajiv Gandhi National Institute of Youth Development 
35. National Institute of Youth Development, named after late Shri Rajiv Gandhi, was launched as

36. A centre is proposed to be opened for information, sports, and training, etc. for the rural youth

almost one-third of the total amount is spent on establishment and miscellaneous items and a little

39. The Committee recommends that adequate funds be harnessed for sports promotion and 

development activities and also some mechanism should be evolved to make various sports schemes 
result-oriented. Some accountability should also be ensured in this regard so that in case of poor 
performance at the sports events the weak points may be identified and rectified. Year, after year, 
Government comes out with assurances that the country's performance in international sports events 
woul1 improve in future, but nothing happens. The Secretary, Department of Youth Affairs and 
Sports, in his oral evidence tendered blofore the Committl'~ has conceded that performance in sports 
has not been upto the mark for the last many years and expressed his firm resolve to make honest and 
sincere efforts, to draw up programmes by which performance could be improved. 
40. The Committee also expresses its deep concern over the constitution of the generaVgoverning 
body of SAl in which more and more bureaucrats are represented rather than the Sports persons and 
experts. The Committee recommends that professionals be given more representation iu the general 
governing body of SAl. 
The Committee notes with concern the reduction in budget allocation of SAl. As compared to 
the Revised Estimates for the year 1993-94 Plan and Non-Plan alloc:Jtion this year has come down to 
Rs. 3913.00 lakhs from Rs. 4,380.00 lakhs. 
41. Sports Authority of India is ruuning various s .. hemcs and programmes to identify persons in 
different disciplines and trnin them to achieve excellence both at national and international levels 
some of which arc as follows:-
(a) Nationa l Spurts Talent Contest (NSTC) Scheme 
42. The main objectiv~ of the scheme is to identify promising school children in :he age group of 
8-12 years and to provide them with opportunit ies to develop them to be a talented sports p.:!rsons. 
For this, children arc required to undergo various tests awl once thC) qualify they arc reared in SAl 
adoplctl schools which hav~ coaching and specia: infra structure facilities. 
43. But the progre ss made in this scheme, as underlined In the performance budgets of the years 
1993-94 and 1994-95, shows that it is almost negligible. During the year 1993-94 the number of adopted 
children was 1300 and the number as sho\vn in the performllnce Budget for 1994-95 remains the same. 
The number of adopted schoo ls vary from 68 (as in the performance Budget, 1994-95) to 58 (Brief back 
ground note on SAl). Whether the selection team visits the schools or selections are made at a 
particular place where school children are required to cQme and participants is nowhere mentioned. 
The Committee recommends that the network under this programme should be considerably expanded 
in rural, backward and remote areas where there is no consciousness and facilities for sports do not 
exist. 
44. The disciplines such as Badminton, Basketball, Gymnastics, Hockey, Table Tennis and 
Volleyball, chosen for the contest are such in which mostly children with affluent family background 
may excel. The Committee recommend s that traditional and indigenous games like Kabaddr and 
Khokho etc., may also be included in the Jist of disciplines under this scheme. 
(b) Sports Project Development Area (SPDA) Scheme 
45. This scheme aims at providing basic sports facilities to the rural children between the age of 
9-14 years at a centre having linkage with regional centres of SAl whicij covers about 80 to 100 
Development blocks. The progress of this scheme is very slow as out of 78 sanctioned centres only 34 
centres have so far been constituted. Even those centres which have been set up are not working 
satisfactorily . Therefore, the cummitte e urges upon the Government to take necessary corrective steps 
in this regard and also recommends that some sort of surveillance committees be constit uted to look 
after the functioning of these centres. The Committee recommends that effective steps should be taken 
to open all the sanctioned centres and make even distribution of the centres. The allocation has come 
down from Rs.280.00 lakhs during 1993-94 to Rs.250.00 lakhs this year. This decrease in allocation as 
compared to last year may affect the progress and, therefore, the amount should be appropriately 
enhanced. 
There has b~en und er-utilisation of the resources also during the year 1993-94, as around Rs.20 
lakhs remained unutili sed. 

(c) Sports IIo~tel Scheme 
46. The progress of this scheme also appears to be tardy. As against the target of establishing one 
hostel in every Stat< only 18 hostels have so far been constructed. Some States like U.P., Punjab and M.P., 
which have vast potentialities for producing sportsmen, do not have such hostels. Therefore, the 
Committee recomends that construction of youth hostels may be expedited. 
47. Apart from the Sports Authority of India development and promotion of sports is undertaken by 
vajous other or~anisations and bodies. National Sports Federations are such bodies which are getting 
financial assistance for furthering various sports disciplines. For this purpose, sports federations 
undertake such activities as conducting national championships, organising coaching camps, purchasing 
sports equipment, participating in International Tournaments, etc. During the year 1993-94 a total of 
Rs.l480.00 lakhs for plan and Rs80.00 lakhs for non-plan expenditure (which include an additional 
allocation of Rs.1080.00 lakhs for the preparation of Indian Contingent for Asian games)' was given to 
sports :ederations. But, the poor performance of teams in international level games has shown that all is 
not going well with the sports federations. Therefore, the Committee recomends that while doling out such 
huge amounts norms and conditions fixed therefor should be strictly adhered to. There should also be some 
mechanism for monitoring to find out whether the amount is being properly utilised or not. There must also 
be a supervisory body to see that the sports federations functions smoothly. 
48. The Secretary, Department of Youth Affairs & Sports during the course of his oral evidence 
tenderd before the Committee stated that since sports is a State subject no proper check upon sports 
federations could be kept. He further added that plans are also being formulated to ensure that these 
federations are run properly. The Committee strongly recommends that all-out effort should be made by 
Government to tone up the functioning and performance of the Sports Federations. 
Grants for Creation of Sports Infrastructure 
49. This scheme is important for expanding the sports infrastructure in the country. For this purpose 
~:!1ancial assistance is extended to State Governments, Union Territory Administrations, local bodies and 
registered voluntary organisations. 
50. The Committee is unhappy to no~c that more and more sports infrastructure is being 
concentrated in large cities and towns, and small cities ~nd towns arc neglected. The Commitee, therefore, 
rccor:uncnds that efforts should be made to ensure that spor ts infrastructure is spread all over the country 
properly utilised. The Committed deplores that the SAl and the Department of sports have no plans for 
purposeful and regular utilisation of the infrastructure already created. They have also no plans to 
construct multipurpose ! !adia in towns and cities which could be utilised for sports during the day and as 
open air theatres for cultural programmes in the evening and "night. 
General ObservationS! Recommendatio11s 
T!lc Committee made some general recommendations which are as follows: 
(a) Efforts should be made to set up hostels for youths on the lines of working women's hostels in major 
cities and towns. (b) Physical educatio n may be integrated in school curriculum and it should be made 
compulsory. Writte11 examinations on physical education may also be conducted as is being done in 
Maharashtra. Provisi<-.ts should be made to have at least one physical education teacher for every 150 boys 
·•nd girls. Effortc should also be made to provide play grounds in every school. (c) Government should also 
make arrangements to provide sports opportunities to the aged persons. (d) The year 1994 is being 
celebrated as SAARC year for the youth. The Committee, in this connection suggests that all out efforts 
should be made to make it successful, and to awake and mobilise the youth of the country. (e) Government 
has taken some measures to give incentives to the outstanding sports persons. Recently, a new scheme of 
incentive to meritorious sports persons has been introduced under which life long pension would be given to 
them who have won me:lals in important hternational events, but these are not adequate and sufficient. 
Still, a large number of promising sports persons are facing lot of hardships. Therefore, the Committee 
recommends that adequate steps should be taken to give encouragement to the outstanding sports persons 
by providing tht:m jobs and also extending financial assistance . 
(f) Corporate and Private Sector is doing commendabl e job in furthering the cause of sports by 

organising and holding tournaments for various disciplines and maintaining sports teams etc. Therefor , 
the Committee recommends that private and corporate sectors may be encouraged to come forward in 
the promotion of sports. •

REPORT 
Women and Children, who represent more than 50% of our population, constitute the two 
vulnerable segments of our society without whose upliftment real development cannot take place. 
Although total Budget Estimates for 1994-95 in the Central Plan outlay for women and child 
development show an increase of Rs. 96 crores as compared to Budget Estimates for 1993-94, the 
increase, as explained by Secretary (Women & Child Development), in her ora! evidence tendered 
before the Committee, is mainly on account of World Bank assistance of Rs. 38 crores to ICDS and 
an increase in sanction for Mahila Samridhi Yojna. On all other schemes increase in allocations for 
1994-95 is only marginal. It is a matter of concern for the Committee that in the SAARC Decade of 
Girl Child and condition of women, there has not been adequate increase in the Budget allocations.

3. The Committee feels that gender inequality is one of the problems all over the world. Actual 
development cannot take place unless the Govt. takes initiative to remove this bias and guarantees 
equal status to women as enshrined in our Constitution. Committee is of the view that all out efforts 
should be made for greater involvement of women in the national development process by raising their 
status - social, economic, legal and political - at par with that of man. The Department of Women 
and Child Development has started a number of schemes for the development and welfare of women 
and children The Committee has deliberated only on some of the points relating to Demands for Grants 
(1994-95) which are enumerated in the following paragraphs along with the Committee's observations 
and recommendations. 
Women Welfare and Development 
(i) Rashtriya Mahila Kosh 
4. Rashtriya Mahila Kosh was set up in March, 1993 under the Registration of Societies Act, 
1869. With the main aim to help the poorest of the poor and assist women who are unable to utilize 
formal banking facilities but are in need of credit. For the purpose, a Corpus of Rs. 31 crores was 
sanctioned, to be utilised in a phased manner. 
5. The Committee observes that as against Rs. 31 crores sanctioned last year for this scheme, only 
a token amount of Rs. one lakh has been earmarked this year. It feels that unless 

schemes for the utilisation of sanctioned money are formulated well in time, setting up of such 
funds becomes infructuous. Therefore, it recommends that Department should, ensure that schemes 
are framed for prop er utilisation of the funds without delay. 
(ii) National Commission for Women and Commissioner for Women's Rights 
6. The Nation al Commission for Women was set up as a nodal agency to monitor the 
enforcement of lega l status of women, to review the existing legislation and suggest amendments 
and to liaise with the concerned Ministries, State Governments and NGOs, in order to create 
awareness and spread literacy. For this purpose, an amount of Rs. 1.75 crores in RE was 
provided in 1993-94, which has been increased to Rs. 2 crores in the Budget Estimates for 1994-
95. 
7. The Committee notes that there is substantial increase in the Budget provisions for the 
National Commission for Women for 1994-95, as compared to 1993-94. Govt. should ensur e full 
utilisation of the budg et of Rs. 2 crores by the Commission. 
8. The Committee recommends that Govt. should fulfil the assurance given to th e Parliament 
by creat ing the post of Commissioner for Women 's Rights and all consultations and other 
formalities be completed as early as possible. 
(iii) Hostels for working Women 
9. To protect young working women in urban areas from exposure to undesirable and anti­
social elements, financial assistance to the extent of 50% of the cost of land and 70% of the 
cost of building construct ion is provided to Voluntary Organisations. In 1993-94 Rs. 7.00 crores 
were provided which has bee n increased to Rs. 7.75 crores in the Budget for 1994-95. This 
year's target is to provide assistance to 60 hostles which would benefit about 3000 working 
women.

11. The Committe e is of the view that though there is acute shortage of working Women' s 
Hostels in the country, the Department could not achieve the physical targets during 1993-94, but 
ambit ious targets have been flXed for 1994-95. The Committee desires that effective steps should 
be taken by the Depar tment to achieve the targets set for 1994-95. 
12. As frequent complaints are received about mismanagement of the hostels rece1vmg grants 
and assistance from the Government the Committee is of the view that there is need for evolving 
some system of monitoring so as to control any sort of irregularities in these hostels. For this 
purpose, the Committee recommends that a Government representative be included on the Board 
of Management of each of such hostels. 
13. The Committee eA.presses its concern over the inadequacy of hostels for working women 
and recommends that , taking into consideration the importance of these hostels, Government 
should encourage construction of more such hostels not only through grants but also by allotment 
of land where ever necessary. 

(iv) Education for prevention of atrocities against Women 
14. The programme was sta rted in 1982 with the aim of creating public opinion against exploita tion 
of women and atrocities against them. This objective is sought to be achieved mainly through 
programmes, publicity and research work , as well as holdin g meetings, conferences, seminars , 
exhibitions, etc. 
15. Financial assistance extended in 1993-94 for this purpose was Rs. 35.00 lakhs and the same 
amount has been allocated during 1994-95. 
16. The Committee expresses its concern over the increasing numbers of cases of atrocities against 
women an d recommends that Govt. should conduct some review of these publicity programmes to find 
out whet her these are sufficient to create a significant impact on the public mind. 
17. The Committee recommends that the amount sanctioned for the year 1993-94 for legal aid in 
cases of atrocities against women should be increased. 
18. The Committee was informed of training and other awareness generation programmes 
undertaken by the Department. Production of legal literacy manuals in regi ona l languages and gender 
sensitization are part of this programmes. The Committee feels that such programmes should be 
extended to the grass root level also. 
(v) Indira Mahila Y ojna 
19. Indira Mahila Yojna, as originally conceived in 1991 and included in the President's Address of 
the year, has four basic components: (i) Awareness generation (ii) Income generat ion (iii) Convergence 
of inter-sectoral services; and (iv) Integration of field cadres of all related departments in the country. 
20. The Committee expresses its deep concern over the fact that though the scheme was announced 
in the President's Address in 1991, till this date it has not been operationalised. 
21. The Committee was informed by the Department that the original draft scheme for Indira 
Mahila Yojna contained components of awareness generation, income generation, integr ated system of 
delivery, inter-sectoral services and integration of field cadres of concerned Departm en ts, with an 
allotment of Rs. 1785 crorcs for the Eighth Plan. The concerned Departments could not, however, 
come to a consensus on integration of cadres and transfer of schemes from one Ministry to the other. 
Subsequently, there was a revised scheme to cover 200 blocks, with income generation and awareness 
generation components (Rs. 78 crores for the remainder of the 8th Plan.) But this also is yet to be 
approved by the Planning Commission. The Provision of Rs. 8 crores in the 1994-95 Budget may go into 
the World Bank-aided ICDS project, if the approval does not come in time. 
The Committee feels that such a big scheme should be implemented only when proper assessment of 
financial and infrastructural implications is made. Duplication of efforts should be avoided. whether a 
single-window delivery system would benefit women, in immensely varied circumstances, has also to be 
assessed. 
(vi) Mahila Samridhi Yojna 
22. This is a new scheme launched on 2nd October, 1993 to promote thrift, self-relia nce and certain 
amount of economic independence among rural women. It is implemented by the Depar t· of Posts 
through the network of 1.32 lakh post offices in rural areas. An amount of Rs. 10.5 cror cs \',as initially 
sanctioned for the scheme which has been increased to Rs. 19.89 crores in the Budgetar y orovis ions for 
1994-95. 
23. The Committee notes that significant increase in allocations for Mahila Samridhi Yojna has been 
made this year. The Comm.ittee, however, recommends that there should be proper monitoring to see 
that these funds are properly utilised. 
24. The Committee is of the view that various programmes under the Mahila Samridhi Yojna are 
implemented keeping in view the welfare of rural women, whereas poor women in urban areas , who are 
also in need of assistance, are not covered under it. The Committee recommends that requiremen ts of 
needy urban women belonging to the weaker sections of society should also be kept in mind while framing 
and implementing schemes for women's welfare. 

25. Committee also feels that there is not sufficient awareness among the rural people regarding 
the benefits of Mahila Samridhi Yojna. Secondly, the postmasters in the villages are not fully info.-med 
and trained about the scheme, and there is also dearth of forms. The need is, therefore, to train 
postmasters about the functioning of the scheme and to make the forms available so as to avoid 
inconvenience to the needy. 
26. There should also be a monthly review of the progress made under the scheme so as to take 
corrective measures wherever necessary. 
Nutrition and Child Development 
27. The Committee expresses its concern over the sharp decli~e in the Plan Budget estimates 
under the Head 2235 for Child Welfare. As against. Rs. 43.35 crores in 1993-94, it has gone down to 
Rs. 20.17 crores in 1994-95 and recommends restoration of the last year allocations. 
(i) Integrated Child Development Services (/CDS) 
28. The main thrust of ICDS programme is on the provision of Anganwadis in every village and 
urban slum areas. Generally, there is one Anganwadi for a population of 1000 in rural areas and 
urban slum areas and of about 700 in tribal area~, which is run by an Anganwadi worker, a female 
voluntary worker and a helper. By the end of 1993, 3120 ICDS projects were sanctioned which 
benefited about 1.94 crorc children and women. For the year 1994-95 an outlay of Rs. 426.00 crores 
has been approved for the ICDS and 200 new projects are likely to start. 
The Committee feels that a large portion of the increased outlay is likely to be absorbed in the 
increased honorarium to Anganwadi workers. Therefore, the Committee feels that the amount available 
for the projected expansion of the scheme to cover new areas seems to be insufficient. Of 5239 blocks, 
2119 block remains to be covered. At the rate of 200 projects per year, it will take another 10 years for 
all blocks to be covered. Thus is too slow. To expedite the process, any shortfall in the projected 
expansion by the end of the 8th Plan should be properly estimated and additional allocations made. 
29. The relative success of the ICDS scheme in improving child health and lowering IMR is due 
to its decentralized and popular structure. probably because of this, ICDS is being increasingly seen 
as an umberlla organisation within which other schemes could be incorporated. Thus, early childhood 
education is now a part of ICDS_. There is a new scheme for adolescent girls, creches and day care 
centres arc sought to be made a part of ICDS. Indira Mahila Yojana, in its revised form, will become 
a component of ICDS. Separate allocations have been proposed for these schemes, but the National 
Creche Fund has only been notified. Allocation of Rs. 8 crores for Indira Mahila Yojna has not yet 
been approved. Therefore, the Committee recommends that until and unless spearate additional 
allocations are obtained for these additional components, ICDS should concentrate on strengthening 
and expansion of its own structure with whatever allocations it has. The proposal to entrust a 
percentage of !CDS schemes to NGOs should be properly assessed before it is implemented, because in 
the absence of community-based monitoring arrangements, it would be difficult to ensure accountability 
of these NGOs. 
30. With the usc of ICDS infrastructure, a special scheme for adolescent girls has been 
formulated, mainly for those who have been out of schools, to meet their nutritional, educational and 
recreational needs. 
31. Regarding education of adolescent girls, the Committee recommends that there should be a 
scheme to help meritorious girls enabling them to pursue their studies further. 
32. In order to meet the requirement of trained personnel for implementing the programmes for 
pre-school children, the Bal Scvika training programme was started in 1961-62. There are 25 Bal 
Scvika training Centres and each centre is provided with a sum of Rs. 1,74,750/- to train 50 Bal 
Sevikas each year. 
33. The Committee observes that out of the three components of ICDS, namely executive, workers 
and recipients, two do not appear to be happy with the service. Therefore, monitoring system should be 
strengthened to ensure proper functioning of the ICDS Scheme to the satisfaclion of all its components. 

of the population through ICDS, as well as nutritional education. In this context, the Committee 
recommends revival of the scheme of supply of milk to the under-nourished school Children. 
44. The Committee also feels that, year after year, the focus of attention of the Deptt. keeps on 
changing from one scheme to another and there seems to be no long-term perspective. Therefore, the 
Committee recommends that instead of framing new schemes every year and letting the earlier ones to 
just continue, the Department should concentrate on some major schemes and work to achieve the 
targets fixed through suitable action plans. The Department was set up in 1985 but its strerigth has 
remained the same although many new schemes have been introduced during this period. The 
Committee feels that strengthening of Departmental infrastructure is necessary inorder to ensure the 
effectiveness of the schemes.

AN OVERVIEW 
There are two main components of the Department i.e. Cult:ur~ and Arts. A . separate 
department, called the Department of Arts, was constitu ted in August, 1985 with the aim .,of setting 
up the Indira Gandhi National Centre for Arts (IGNCA)-a major centre for Arts, Humanities and 
Cultural heritage . The vast treasure of our culture is being preserved, promoted and propagated 
jointly by the Central and Srate Governments and Union Territory Administrations through out the 
country . The Archaeological survey of India is the largest and most important part of the Department 
of Culture engaged in conservation and excavation of old historical sites and about 25 per cent of the 
total budget provisions of the Department of Culture goes to this institution. Awareness generation 
and dissemination of information about our glorious past is done through exhibition of antiquities and 
artefacts preserved in museums spread throughout the country. Different Academies, National School 
of Drama, Centre for Cultural Resources and Training, Zonal Cultura l Centres ,' Libraries, Memorials 
like Gandhi Smriti and Darshan Samiti, Kalaksherra, Madras etc., functioning under the Department 
of Culture, cater to the artistic and literary needs of the people . The Anthmpological Survey of India, 
a subordinate office of the Department, has been carrying out researches on cultural aspects of Indian 
population. · 
2. The total outlay on culture during the Eighth Five Year Plan (as initially approved for the 
Department of Culture) amounts to Rs. 727 crores (including both Centra l as well as State sectors) . 
The Central sector share is Rs. 385.00 crores, supplemented by an additional allocation of Rs. 75.00 
crores, making it a total of Rs. 460.00 crores.

The Committee takes strong exception to the failure of the Department and recommends that 
henceforth budget allocations given to the Department should be fully utillsed and appropriated. The 
Committee also notes that the distribution of available funds is also not need-based. While on the one 
hand, funds are being blocked by allocaling them to such scheme where appropriation is less and are 
being surrendered on the other, some schemes where appropriation is cent percent and more grant is 
required, suffer from Jack of resources. Therefore, the Committee recommends that instead of 
surrendering the untilised funds the Deptt. should reallocate them for the needy schemes in time. 
7. The Secretary, Deptt. of Culture, during the course of his oral cvidehce tendered bef6re the 
Committee stated that this year the major thrust of the Deptt. are on the Scheme of setting up of 
rural libraries assistance to private museums, documentation and promotion of folk and tribal arts, 
attracting private sector in the field of arts and culture by according them tax exemptions etc., 
encouraging people's initiative and participation in the process of cultural development and organising 
festivals of India abroad. 
8. In order to give fillip to the culture and to restore and refurbish its dying facets, Govt. has 
drafted an Approach Paper on National Policy on Culture. Views/comments received from Members 
of Parliament, eminent person in the field of literature, arts and culture, critics and administrators, 
etc. on the Policy Paper have been discussed in the meetings of the Consultative Committee of the 
Department. Presently, by the Draft Approach Paper on National Policy on Culture is under 
consideration of this Standing Committee and it proposes to submit its report to the Parliament soon. 
REPORT 
9. The Committee, taking note of the revolutionary changes taking place in communications and 
mass media and threat to the Indian culture from outside, emphasises that culture should be seen in 
right perspective and stresses the need of countering cultural invasion from outside. The Secretary, 
during the course of his oral evidence before the Committee, while taking note of the concern of the 
Committee stated that efforts are being made to have parleys with the Secretaries of Ministry of 
Information and Broadcasting and Department of Tourism in order to ensure better coordination 
between them in this regard. The Commmittee urges upon the Government to make all-out efforts to 
contain cultural invasion and to restore our cullural ethos, ideals and values. 
10. The Committee expresses its concern over the neglect of the rural areas due to the· 
centralisation of programmes in the urban areas by the Department of Culture. More and more 
programmes of the department are concentrated in the major cities and the rural areas are being 
neglected in the process. It was admitted by the department that in our cultural programmes priority 
is being given to the urban areas due to reason that major cultural institutions are located in the cities 
and there are better transport and other facilities available in cities for the foreign delegates and 
dignatrics visiting these centres. The situation can improve only when more and more such facilities 
are provided in the rural areas to facilitate the establishment of cultural centre s in villages or semi­
urban areas. 
The Comm ittee was also informed that there is a provision with the Department to extend 
building grant of Rs. 10 lakhs to any organisation for setting up of auditorium at any place including 
the rural areas. if it has a piece of land and is ready to spend matching amount. During the year 1993-
94, fifty nine such institutions/organisations were given building grants to the tunc of Rs. 1.38 crores. 
But the logic of the Department does not appear to be sound enough in the sense that if the semi­
urban , under-developed and rural areas are neglected and rejected on this pretext, how the cultural 
needs of the vast majority of people living in these areas would be met. Therefore, the Committee 
recommends that the programmes and resources of the Department be considerably decentralised and 

taken to the backward, rural and und erdeveloped urban areas where ancient cultural heritage still 
holds· appeal and r equire s to be galvanised by the centre. 
Archaeological Surve y of India (ASI) 
11. Archaeological Survey of India, set up way back in 1861, is engaged in several activities, 
prominent among which are conservation and preservation of ancient monum ents, exploration and 
excavation of ancient sites, study of inscriptions, research and training in different areas of 
archaeology, etc. Povisions made for this head during the last two years are given in the table.
